periods.note: After the rising of 1857 the Crown ruled India directly. Gandhi's campaigns of non-violent resistance led the way to independence.

periods.name: Dominion and Islamic Republic of Pakistan
periods.note: Founded by Muhammad Ali Jinnah for the Muslims of British India; it lost its eastern half, Bangladesh, in 1971, and has swung between elected governments and army rule.

periods.name: First farmers
periods.note: At Mehrgarh, below the Bolan Pass, people farmed wheat and barley and herded cattle from about 7000 BC, the oldest farming in South Asia.

periods.name: Indus Valley Civilization
periods.note: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro: planned brick cities with drains and granaries, a script no one has read, and trade by sea with Mesopotamia.

periods.name: Vedic period
periods.note: Indo-Aryan herders composed the Vedas, India's oldest scriptures, and moved east into the Ganges plain, where kingdoms and the caste order took shape.

periods.name: Sixteen Great Kingdoms
periods.note: The mahajanapadas, kingdoms and republics of the Ganges plain, among which Magadha rose to lead. The Buddha and Mahavira taught here.

periods.name: Maurya Empire
periods.note: Chandragupta Maurya united most of India. His grandson Ashoka turned to Buddhism after the bloody conquest of Kalinga and carved his edicts on rocks and pillars.

periods.name: Middle kingdoms
periods.note: Shungas, Indo-Greeks, Sakas and Kushans in the north, the Satavahanas in the Deccan and the Tamil kingdoms in the south, trading with Rome.

periods.name: Gupta Empire
periods.note: The classical age: Kalidasa's plays, Aryabhata's astronomy, the decimal numbers with zero and the paintings of the Ajanta caves.

periods.name: Age of regional kingdoms
periods.note: Harsha of Kannauj, then the Palas of Bengal, the Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas fought over the Ganges plain, while the Pallavas built the shore temples of the south.

periods.name: Cholas and Rajputs
periods.note: The Chola navy reached Sumatra and the temple of Thanjavur rose, while Rajput kings built Khajuraho and Mahmud of Ghazni raided from the northwest.

periods.name: Delhi Sultanate
periods.note: Turkic and Afghan sultans ruled from Delhi and held off the Mongols; Timur sacked the city in 1398. In the south Vijayanagara grew rich.

periods.name: Mughal Empire
periods.note: Babur's heirs Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, who built the Taj Mahal, and Aurangzeb ruled one of the richest empires on earth.

periods.name: Marathas and the East India Company
periods.note: As the Mughals weakened, the Marathas, the Sikhs, Mysore and Hyderabad rose, and the British East India Company won Bengal at Plassey (1757) and most of India by 1818.

periods.name: British Raj
periods.note: After the rising of 1857 the Crown ruled India directly. Gandhi's campaigns of non-violent resistance led the way to independence.

periods.name: East Pakistan
periods.note: Bengal's Muslim east became the eastern wing of Pakistan, a thousand miles from the capital; the language movement of 1952 defended Bengali.

periods.name: Bangladesh
periods.note: Independent after the war of 1971 under Sheikh Mujibur Rahman; one of the world's most crowded countries, a leader in garment making.

periods.name: Coming of the Sinhalese
periods.note: The chronicles tell of Prince Vijaya, who came from north India in 543 BC with seven hundred followers; Indo-Aryan settlers founded villages along the rivers.

periods.name: Anuradhapura Kingdom
periods.note: Kings at Anuradhapura took up Buddhism from Ashoka's son Mahinda, built great dagobas and reservoirs, and kept the Buddha's tooth.

periods.name: Chola rule
periods.note: The Chola emperor Rajendra I carried off the last king of Anuradhapura in 1017, and for half a century the Cholas ruled the island from Polonnaruwa.

periods.name: Polonnaruwa Kingdom
periods.note: After Chola rule, Vijayabahu and then Parakramabahu the Great ruled from Polonnaruwa, building the Sea of Parakrama.

periods.name: Kingdoms of the southwest
periods.note: The capital moved southwest, to Dambadeniya, Gampola and Kotte, while a Tamil kingdom ruled Jaffna in the north.

periods.name: Kandy and the European coasts
periods.note: The kings of Kandy held the hills while the Portuguese, then the Dutch, took the cinnamon coasts.

periods.name: British Ceylon
periods.note: Britain took Kandy in 1815 and planted coffee, then tea, with Tamil workers brought from India.

periods.name: Sri Lanka
periods.note: Independent in 1948, renamed Sri Lanka in 1972; a civil war with the Tamil Tigers lasted from 1983 to 2009.

periods.name: Licchavi kings
periods.note: Kings of the Licchavi dynasty ruled the Kathmandu valley, where Buddhism and Hinduism grew up side by side.

periods.name: Thakuri and Malla kings
periods.note: The Malla kings filled Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur with temples and palace squares.

periods.name: Kingdom of Nepal
periods.note: Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha conquered the valley in 1768; the Rana prime ministers ruled in the kings' name from 1846 to 1951.

periods.name: Federal republic
periods.note: After a ten-year Maoist insurgency, the monarchy was abolished in 2008.

periods.name: Oxus civilization
periods.note: Walled towns of the Bronze Age along the Amu Darya (Oxus), trading lapis lazuli from Badakhshan as far as Egypt.

periods.name: Bactria and the Persian satrapies
periods.note: Iranian peoples settled Bactria and Arachosia, which became satrapies of the Persian Empire; Zoroaster may have preached here.

periods.name: Greco-Bactrian kingdom
periods.note: Alexander conquered Bactria; the Greek kings who followed ruled cities like Ai-Khanoum, with a theatre and a gymnasium on the Oxus.

periods.name: Kushan Empire
periods.note: The Yuezhi from the borders of China founded the Kushan Empire; under Kanishka Buddhism and Gandharan art spread toward China.

periods.name: Hephthalites and Shahis
periods.note: Kidarites and Hephthalite Huns, then the Turk and Hindu Shahis of Kabul and the Zunbils of the south; the Buddhas of Bamiyan were carved. Arab armies took Balkh and Herat.

periods.name: Ghaznavids and Ghurids
periods.note: Mahmud of Ghazni raided India and made his capital a centre of Persian poetry; the Ghurids of the mountains followed and conquered Delhi.

periods.name: Mongols and Timurids
periods.note: Genghis Khan destroyed Herat and Balkh. Timur's heirs later made Herat a capital of painting and poetry.

periods.name: Mughal and Safavid rule
periods.note: Babur ruled from Kabul before conquering India; the Mughals held Kabul and the Safavids Herat, and Kandahar changed hands.

periods.name: Durrani Empire
periods.note: Ahmad Shah Durrani, the founder of modern Afghanistan, built an empire from Khorasan to Kashmir and Delhi.

periods.name: Emirate of Afghanistan
periods.note: Caught between Britain and Russia in the Great Game; Britain lost the first Anglo-Afghan war in 1842 and took over its foreign policy in 1879.

periods.name: Kingdom of Afghanistan
periods.note: Amanullah Khan, who won full independence in 1919, made himself king; Zahir Shah reigned for forty years in peace.

periods.name: Republic, Soviet war and civil war
periods.note: A coup, a communist revolution, the Soviet invasion of 1979, civil war among the mujahideen, and from 1996 the Taliban.

periods.name: Islamic Republic and the Taliban
periods.note: After 9/11 an American-led war overthrew the Taliban; they returned to power when the last foreign troops left in 2021.

periods.name: Early Bhutan
periods.note: Local chiefs ruled the valleys under the sway of Tibet. Tradition says a Tibetan king built the first temples in the 600s and Guru Rinpoche flew to the cliff of the Tiger's Nest in the 700s; from the 1200s lamas of the Drukpa school founded monasteries here.

periods.name: Zhabdrung and the Drukpa state
periods.note: Ngawang Namgyal, the Zhabdrung, fled Tibet in 1616, beat back Tibetan invasions and united the land, building great fortress-monasteries (dzongs) and a double government of monks and lay rulers. Civil wars followed his death, and Bhutan lost its southern plains to Britain in the Duar War of 1864–65.

periods.name: Wangchuck kings
periods.note: Ugyen Wangchuck was chosen as the first king in 1907; Britain and then India guided Bhutan's foreign affairs. The fourth king made "Gross National Happiness" the country's goal; in the early 1990s about 100,000 Nepali-speaking Lhotshampa were forced out.

periods.name: Constitutional monarchy
periods.note: Led by its own kings, Bhutan adopted a constitution and elected its first parliament in 2008. Television and the internet had arrived only in 1999.

periods.name: Elam and the first Iranians
periods.note: Susa, one of the oldest cities, was the capital of Elam, which fought Sumer, Babylon and Assyria for three thousand years. Iranian peoples settled the plateau from about 1000 BC.

periods.name: Median Kingdom
periods.note: The Medes united the Iranian tribes, ruled from Ecbatana and helped destroy Assyria in 612 BC.

periods.name: Achaemenid Empire
periods.note: Cyrus the Great, Darius and Xerxes ruled the largest empire yet, from Egypt to the Indus, with royal roads, satraps and the palaces of Persepolis.

periods.name: Alexander and the Seleucids
periods.note: Alexander burned Persepolis; his general Seleucus inherited Iran, where Greek cities were planted along the old roads.

periods.name: Parthian Empire
periods.note: Horse archers of the Arsacid dynasty took Iran and Mesopotamia from the Seleucids and held off Rome for three centuries.

periods.name: Sasanian Empire
periods.note: Ardashir founded a Persian dynasty that made Zoroastrianism the state faith and fought Rome and Byzantium until both were worn out.

periods.name: Arab caliphates
periods.note: The Arab conquest brought Islam; Persian scribes and ideas shaped the Abbasid court in Baghdad.

periods.name: Iranian dynasties
periods.note: Tahirids, Saffarids, Samanids and Buyids ruled in the caliph's name; Ferdowsi wrote the Shahnameh and Persian became a literary language again.

periods.name: Seljuk Empire
periods.note: Turkish Seljuks ruled from Isfahan with Persian viziers such as Nizam al-Mulk; Omar Khayyam reformed the calendar.

periods.name: Ilkhanate
periods.note: The Mongols destroyed the cities of the east; Hulagu's heirs, the Ilkhans, became Muslims and patrons of Persian painting and history.

periods.name: Timurids and Turkmen
periods.note: Timur conquered Iran; his heirs at Herat and the Turkmen Black and White Sheep confederations at Tabriz divided it.
states: Emirate of the White Sheep Turks

periods.name: Safavid Empire
periods.note: Shah Ismail made Shi'a Islam the faith of Iran; Shah Abbas the Great built the squares and mosques of Isfahan.

periods.name: Afsharids and Zands
periods.note: Nader Shah sacked Delhi and carried off the Peacock Throne; Karim Khan Zand then ruled more gently from Shiraz.

periods.name: Qajar dynasty
periods.note: Qajar shahs ruled from Tehran, lost the Caucasus to Russia and granted a constitution after the revolution of 1906.

periods.name: Pahlavi dynasty
periods.note: Reza Shah and his son Mohammad Reza modernised Iran by force; oil wealth grew and so did opposition.

periods.name: Islamic Republic
periods.note: The revolution of 1979 brought Ayatollah Khomeini to power; eight years of war with Iraq followed.

periods.name: Sumer
periods.note: The first cities, Uruk, Ur and Lagash, between the Tigris and Euphrates: writing on clay, the wheel, ziggurats and the epic of Gilgamesh.

periods.name: Akkad and Ur
periods.note: Sargon of Akkad made the first empire; then the kings of Ur's third dynasty wrote the oldest surviving law code.

periods.name: Old Babylonian period
periods.note: Amorite kings ruled from Babylon; Hammurabi conquered Mesopotamia and set his laws in stone.

periods.name: Kassites and Middle Assyria
periods.note: Kassite kings ruled Babylon for four centuries while Assyria rose in the north around Ashur.

periods.name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
periods.note: From Nineveh the Assyrian kings, Tiglath-Pileser, Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal with his library, ruled from Egypt to Iran by terror.

periods.name: Neo-Babylonian Empire
periods.note: Nebuchadnezzar rebuilt Babylon with the Ishtar Gate, destroyed Jerusalem and carried the Judeans into exile.

periods.name: Persians, Greeks and Parthians
periods.note: Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC; Alexander died there in 323 BC; the Parthians ruled from Ctesiphon on the Tigris.

periods.name: Sasanian Mesopotamia
periods.note: Ctesiphon was the Sasanian capital, its great arch still standing; the Jewish academies wrote the Babylonian Talmud.

periods.name: Arab conquest and the Umayyads
periods.note: Arab armies won at Qadisiyya and founded Basra and Kufa; Karbala in 680 split Sunni and Shi'a.

periods.name: Abbasid Caliphate
periods.note: The Abbasids built Baghdad, the largest city of its age, with its House of Wisdom; later Buyid and Seljuk sultans ruled in the caliphs' name.

periods.name: Mongols and Turkmen
periods.note: Hulagu sacked Baghdad in 1258 and killed the last caliph there; Timur sacked it again in 1401.

periods.name: Ottoman Iraq
periods.note: Ottomans and Safavids fought over Baghdad; the Ottomans ruled it as three provinces: Mosul, Baghdad and Basra.

periods.name: British Mandate
periods.note: Britain took Mesopotamia in the First World War and made Faisal, a Hashemite prince, its king.

periods.name: Kingdom of Iraq
periods.note: Independent under the Hashemite kings, with oil flowing from Kirkuk, until the revolution of 1958.

periods.name: Republic of Iraq
periods.note: Coups led to Saddam Hussein, war with Iran and the invasion of Kuwait; the American invasion of 2003 brought him down.

periods.name: Early city-states
periods.note: Ebla, with its archive of clay tablets, and Mari on the Euphrates; Amorite kings later ruled from Aleppo.

periods.name: Arameans and empires
periods.note: Egypt, Mitanni and the Hittites fought over Syria; Aramean kingdoms such as Damascus followed, until Assyria took them. Aramaic became the common tongue of the Near East.

periods.name: Persian rule
periods.note: Syria was a Persian satrapy until Alexander took it in 333 BC.

periods.name: Seleucid Empire
periods.note: Seleucus, one of Alexander's generals, founded Antioch, the capital of a Greek kingdom reaching to India.

periods.name: Roman Syria
periods.note: Pompey made Syria a Roman province; caravan cities like Palmyra grew rich, and Queen Zenobia briefly defied Rome.

periods.name: Byzantine Syria
periods.note: A Christian land of monasteries and of Simeon on his pillar, fought over by Byzantium and Persia.

periods.name: Umayyad Caliphate
periods.note: Arab armies took Syria in 636; from 661 the Umayyad caliphs ruled from Damascus an empire from Spain to India, and built its Great Mosque.

periods.name: Abbasids, Fatimids and Seljuks
periods.note: The capital moved to Baghdad; Syria was fought over by Fatimids, Byzantines and finally the Seljuk Turks.

periods.name: Crusaders and Ayyubids
periods.note: Crusaders took Antioch and the coast; Nur ad-Din and then Saladin united Syria and Egypt against them.

periods.name: Mamluk Syria
periods.note: The Mamluks of Egypt stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut and drove out the last crusaders; Timur sacked Damascus in 1400.

periods.name: Ottoman Syria
periods.note: Four centuries as Ottoman provinces ruled from Damascus and Aleppo.

periods.name: French Mandate
periods.note: France ruled Syria under a League of Nations mandate and split off Lebanon.

periods.name: Syrian Republic
periods.note: Coups led to the Ba'ath party and the Assads, who ruled from 1970 through a civil war that began in 2011 until December 2024.

periods.name: Canaan
periods.note: Canaanite city-states such as Hazor, Megiddo and Jericho, long under Egyptian rule; the first alphabet grew up among them.

periods.name: United Monarchy
periods.note: The Bible tells of Saul, David, who made Jerusalem his capital, and Solomon, who built the First Temple.

periods.name: Kingdoms of Israel and Judah
periods.note: Two kingdoms: Israel in the north, taken by Assyria in 722 BC, and Judah, until Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple in 586 BC.

periods.name: Babylonian and Persian rule
periods.note: The exiles returned under Cyrus and built the Second Temple.

periods.name: Hellenistic rule and the Hasmoneans
periods.note: Ptolemies and Seleucids ruled until the Maccabees rose in 167 BC and founded a Jewish kingdom.

periods.name: Roman Judea
periods.note: Herod rebuilt the Temple; Jesus was crucified in Jerusalem; Rome destroyed the Temple in AD 70 and crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt.

periods.name: Byzantine Palestine
periods.note: A Christian Holy Land of pilgrims and churches.

periods.name: Caliphates
periods.note: The Arabs took Jerusalem in 638; the Dome of the Rock was built over the Temple Mount.

periods.name: Crusaders and Ayyubids
periods.note: The crusaders' Kingdom of Jerusalem, until Saladin retook the city in 1187.

periods.name: Mamluk rule
periods.note: The Mamluks took Acre, the last crusader city, in 1291.

periods.name: Ottoman rule
periods.note: Suleiman the Magnificent built Jerusalem's walls. Zionist settlers began arriving in the 1880s.

periods.name: British Mandate
periods.note: Britain promised a Jewish national home in the Balfour Declaration and ruled Palestine amid rising Arab and Jewish conflict.

periods.name: State of Israel
periods.note: Israel declared independence in 1948 and hundreds of thousands of Palestinians fled or were driven out; wars followed in 1967 and 1973, and occupation of the West Bank and Gaza.

periods.name: Ammon, Moab and Edom
periods.note: Small kingdoms east of the Jordan, named in the Bible and on the Mesha Stele.

periods.name: Nabataean Kingdom
periods.note: Arab traders who grew rich on incense caravans and carved their capital, Petra, from rose-red rock.

periods.name: Roman and Byzantine Arabia
periods.note: Trajan made Nabataea the province of Arabia; Jerash flourished as a Roman city.

periods.name: Caliphates and sultanates
periods.note: The Umayyads built desert palaces; crusader castles like Kerak guarded the road to Mecca.

periods.name: Ottoman rule
periods.note: A poor province crossed by the pilgrim road and, from 1908, the Hejaz railway.

periods.name: Emirate of Transjordan
periods.note: After the Arab Revolt, Britain made the Hashemite prince Abdullah emir of Transjordan.

periods.name: Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan
periods.note: Independent under Abdullah, then Hussein for nearly fifty years; it took in waves of Palestinian refugees.

periods.name: Predynastic Egypt
periods.note: Farming villages along the Nile grew into the kingdoms of Upper and Lower Egypt.

periods.name: Early Dynastic Period
periods.note: Narmer united Upper and Lower Egypt; hieroglyphs and the pharaohs' capital at Memphis followed.

periods.name: Old Kingdom
periods.note: The age of the pyramids: Djoser's step pyramid, then the Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza.

periods.name: First Intermediate Period
periods.note: Royal power broke down and local rulers fought for Egypt.

periods.name: Middle Kingdom
periods.note: Theban kings reunited Egypt; a classical age of literature and of forts in Nubia.

periods.name: Second Intermediate Period
periods.note: The Hyksos from Canaan ruled the north, bringing the horse and chariot.

periods.name: New Kingdom
periods.note: Egypt's empire: Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II, with tombs in the Valley of the Kings.

periods.name: Third Intermediate Period
periods.note: Priests, Libyan chiefs and the Nubian kings of Kush took turns as pharaohs.

periods.name: Late Period
periods.note: The last native dynasties, with two spells of Persian rule.

periods.name: Ptolemaic Kingdom
periods.note: Alexander founded Alexandria; the Greek Ptolemies ruled from it, with its Library and Lighthouse, until Cleopatra.

periods.name: Roman and Byzantine Egypt
periods.note: Rome's granary; Egypt became Christian, and its desert monks founded monasticism.

periods.name: Arab caliphates
periods.note: Amr ibn al-As conquered Egypt and founded Fustat; Arabic and Islam slowly spread.

periods.name: Fatimid Caliphate
periods.note: Shi'a caliphs founded Cairo and al-Azhar and ruled from Tunisia to Syria.

periods.name: Ayyubid Sultanate
periods.note: Saladin ended the Fatimids, built the Citadel of Cairo and retook Jerusalem from the crusaders.

periods.name: Mamluk Sultanate
periods.note: Slave soldiers who became sultans; they beat the Mongols and made Cairo the greatest city of Islam.

periods.name: Ottoman Egypt
periods.note: An Ottoman province where Mamluk beys kept real power; Napoleon invaded in 1798.

periods.name: Muhammad Ali's dynasty
periods.note: Muhammad Ali modernised Egypt's army and farming; the Suez Canal opened in 1869.

periods.name: British rule and the Kingdom
periods.note: Britain occupied Egypt in 1882; it became a kingdom in 1922 but British troops stayed by the canal.

periods.name: Republic
periods.note: The Free Officers' revolution: Nasser took the Suez Canal, Sadat made peace with Israel, Mubarak fell in 2011.

periods.name: Hattians and Assyrian traders
periods.note: Assyrian merchants traded tin and cloth at Kanesh, where the first Hittite words were written.

periods.name: Hittite Empire
periods.note: From Hattusa the Hittites ruled Anatolia, sacked Babylon and fought Egypt at Kadesh, then fell in the Bronze Age collapse.

periods.name: Phrygia, Lydia and Ionia
periods.note: King Midas of Phrygia; Lydia, where Croesus struck the first coins; and the Greek cities of Ionia, home of Homer and the first philosophers.

periods.name: Persian Anatolia
periods.note: Cyrus defeated Croesus; Anatolia became Persian satrapies.

periods.name: Hellenistic kingdoms
periods.note: Alexander's successors and local kingdoms, Pergamon with its great altar, Pontus, Bithynia and Cappadocia.

periods.name: Roman Anatolia
periods.note: Rich Roman provinces where Paul founded the first churches; Constantine made Byzantium his capital in 330.

periods.name: Byzantine Anatolia
periods.note: The heartland of the Byzantine Empire, ruled from Constantinople, where Hagia Sophia was built in 537.

periods.name: Seljuks of Rum
periods.note: After Manzikert the Seljuk Turks ruled from Konya, where Rumi wrote his poems; the Mongols humbled them in 1243.

periods.name: Rise of the Ottomans
periods.note: Osman's small beylik grew into a power that crossed into Europe; Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453.

periods.name: Ottoman Empire
periods.note: Suleiman the Magnificent ruled from Budapest to Baghdad; after 1683 the empire shrank, and it ended in the First World War.

periods.name: Republic of Turkey
periods.note: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk won the war of independence and built a secular republic with Ankara as its capital.

periods.name: Ancient Arabia
periods.note: Herders and oasis towns; Dilmun traded with Sumer, and caravans carried incense north past Dedan and Hegra.

periods.name: Muhammad and the first caliphs
periods.note: Muhammad was born in Mecca about 570; from Medina he united Arabia under Islam, and his successors carried it to Persia and Egypt.

periods.name: Arabia under the caliphs and sultans
periods.note: The capitals moved to Damascus, Baghdad and Cairo; Mecca and Medina, ruled by their sharifs, drew pilgrims from the whole Islamic world.

periods.name: Ottoman Hejaz
periods.note: The Ottoman sultans became guardians of the holy cities, while the tribes of the interior stayed free.

periods.name: First and Second Saudi States
periods.note: Muhammad ibn Saud allied with the preacher Ibn Abd al-Wahhab in 1744; their state took Mecca and was crushed by Egypt in 1818, then rose again.

periods.name: Rashidis and the rise of Ibn Saud
periods.note: The Rashidis of Hail ruled central Arabia until Ibn Saud retook Riyadh in 1902; he conquered the Hejaz in 1925.

periods.name: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
periods.note: Ibn Saud founded the kingdom in 1932; oil, found in 1938, made it one of the richest states in the world.

periods.name: Saba and the incense kingdoms
periods.note: Saba (Sheba), Qataban, Ma'in and Hadramaut grew rich on frankincense and myrrh; the great dam of Marib watered Saba.

periods.name: Himyarite Kingdom
periods.note: Himyar united Yemen; its last kings converted to Judaism, until Aksum invaded in 525.

periods.name: Aksumite and Persian rule
periods.note: Ethiopians and then Persians ruled Yemen until it accepted Islam.

periods.name: Islamic Yemen
periods.note: Zaydi imams in the highlands from 897, and the Rasulid sultans of Taiz, whose port of Aden traded with India.

periods.name: Ottomans and imams
periods.note: Ottomans and Zaydi imams fought over the highlands; Yemeni coffee from Mocha conquered the world; Britain took Aden in 1839.

periods.name: Kingdom of Yemen and Aden
periods.note: The imams ruled the north as a kingdom; Britain held Aden and the protectorates of the south.

periods.name: North and South Yemen
periods.note: A republican revolution in the north, and a Marxist state in the south after Britain left Aden in 1967.

periods.name: Republic of Yemen
periods.note: North and south united in 1990; a civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis took Sanaa.

periods.name: Magan and the frankincense coast
periods.note: Copper from Magan reached Sumer; frankincense from Dhofar was carried north by caravan.

periods.name: Ibadi imams and Muscat
periods.note: Oman took up Ibadi Islam under elected imams; its sailors traded from Sohar to China.

periods.name: Portuguese Muscat
periods.note: The Portuguese seized Muscat and the coast to control the Gulf.

periods.name: Omani Empire
periods.note: The Ya'ruba imams drove out the Portuguese; the Al Said ruled an empire reaching to Zanzibar on the East African coast.

periods.name: Muscat and Oman
periods.note: Zanzibar went its own way; the sultans of Muscat lived under British protection.

periods.name: Sultanate of Oman
periods.note: Sultan Qaboos overthrew his father in 1970 and built roads, schools and hospitals with oil money.

periods.name: Trucial States
periods.note: Britain signed truces with the sheikhs of the pirate coast; pearling was the living until oil was found in 1958.

periods.name: United Arab Emirates
periods.note: Seven emirates united in 1971; Abu Dhabi's oil and Dubai's trade built glass cities in the desert.

periods.name: Hayasa and Urartu
periods.note: The kingdom of Urartu around Lake Van built fortresses and canals and rivalled Assyria.

periods.name: Orontid Armenia
periods.note: Armenians ruled by the Orontid dynasty, first as a Persian satrapy.

periods.name: Artaxiad Kingdom
periods.note: Tigranes the Great briefly made Armenia an empire from the Caspian to the Mediterranean.

periods.name: Arsacid Armenia
periods.note: Armenia became the first Christian state in 301, and Mesrop Mashtots invented its alphabet.

periods.name: Persian, Byzantine and Arab rule
periods.note: Divided between Byzantium and Persia; Vartan Mamikonian died defending the faith at Avarayr in 451.

periods.name: Bagratid Armenia
periods.note: The Bagratid kings ruled from Ani, the city of a thousand and one churches.

periods.name: Cilicia and foreign rule
periods.note: Armenians founded a kingdom in Cilicia by the Mediterranean (1198 to 1375); the homeland was ruled by Turks, Persians and Russians. In 1915 the Ottoman genocide killed over a million.

periods.name: First Republic and Soviet Armenia
periods.note: A brief republic, then seventy years as a Soviet republic.

periods.name: Republic of Armenia
periods.note: Independent since 1991, after a war with Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh.

periods.name: Colchis and Iberia
periods.note: Colchis on the Black Sea, the land of the Golden Fleece, and the kingdom of Iberia inland.

periods.name: Christian Iberia
periods.note: Saint Nino converted King Mirian; Georgia was fought over by Persia, Byzantium and the Arabs.

periods.name: Kingdom of Georgia
periods.note: A golden age under David the Builder and Queen Tamar, when Rustaveli wrote The Knight in the Panther's Skin; Mongols and Timur ended it.

periods.name: Divided kingdoms
periods.note: Kartli, Kakheti and Imereti, squeezed between Ottomans and Persians.

periods.name: Russian rule
periods.note: Russia annexed the Georgian kingdoms one by one.

periods.name: Democratic Republic and Soviet Georgia
periods.note: Independent from 1918 to 1921, then a Soviet republic; Stalin was born in Gori.

periods.name: Georgia
periods.note: Independent since 1991; the Rose Revolution of 2003 and a war with Russia in 2008.

periods.name: Caucasian Albania
periods.note: A kingdom of the eastern Caucasus that took up Christianity in the 300s, under Persian overlords.

periods.name: Caliphs, Shirvanshahs and Persian rule
periods.note: Islam and Turkic speech came with Arabs and Seljuks; the Shirvanshahs ruled from Shamakhi and Baku under Persian empires.

periods.name: Russian rule
periods.note: Russia took the khanates north of the Aras; Baku's oil boom made it one of the world's oil capitals.

periods.name: Democratic Republic and Soviet Azerbaijan
periods.note: The first parliamentary republic of the Muslim world (1918 to 1920), then a Soviet republic.

periods.name: Republic of Azerbaijan
periods.note: Independent since 1991, rich in oil and gas; it took back Nagorno-Karabakh in 2020 and 2023.

periods.name: Canaanites and Phoenicians
periods.note: Byblos, Sidon and Tyre grew rich selling cedar wood to Egypt. From about 1200 BC their Phoenician sailors founded colonies across the Mediterranean, Carthage among them, and spread the alphabet that Greek and Latin letters come from.

periods.name: Persians, Greeks and Seleucids
periods.note: Phoenician fleets sailed for the Persian kings. Alexander took Tyre in 332 BC after a seven-month siege, building a causeway out to the island city; Ptolemies and Seleucids then fought over the coast.

periods.name: Roman and Byzantine rule
periods.note: Pompey made the coast part of Roman Syria. Berytus (Beirut) had a famous school of Roman law and Baalbek some of the largest temples the Romans built, until an earthquake and sea wave wrecked Beirut in 551.

periods.name: Caliphs and crusaders
periods.note: Arab armies took the coast in the 630s, while Maronite Christians held out in the mountains, where the Druze faith also took root in the 1000s. Crusaders held Tripoli and Beirut from 1109–10 until the Mamluks drove them out in 1289–91.

periods.name: Mamluk rule
periods.note: The Mamluk sultans of Cairo ruled the coast from Tripoli and Damascus. Venetian merchants came to Beirut for spices and silk, while the mountain clans kept their own lords.

periods.name: Ottoman Mount Lebanon
periods.note: The Druze emir Fakhr al-Din II, and after him the Shihab emirs, ruled the mountain almost on their own. After the massacres of 1860, Europe made the Ottomans give Mount Lebanon its own Christian governor; a famine in the First World War killed perhaps a third of its people.

periods.name: French Mandate
periods.note: France made Greater Lebanon in 1920, adding Beirut, Tripoli, the south and the Bekaa valley to the old province of Mount Lebanon, and gave it a constitution that shared power among its religious communities.

periods.name: Lebanese Republic
periods.note: An unwritten pact gave the presidency to a Maronite, the premiership to a Sunni and the speaker's chair to a Shia. Beirut was a banking and holiday capital until the civil war of 1975–90, which drew in Syrian and Israeli armies; wars with Israel, a financial collapse and the 2020 port explosion came after.

periods.name: Dilmun and Ikaros
periods.note: Ubaid potsherds at Bahra show seafarers here 7,000 years ago. Failaka island was a Dilmun trading post around 2000 BC, and later Ikaros, a Greek fort and temple of the Seleucid kings.

periods.name: Caliphs, Persians and Ottomans
periods.note: The Battle of Chains, fought near Kazma in 633, opened Iraq to the Muslim armies. For a thousand years the coast was ruled from Basra, Baghdad or Persia, and from the 1500s by the Ottomans and the Banu Khalid of al-Hasa.

periods.name: Sheikhdom of Kuwait
periods.note: Families of the Bani Utub settled here in the early 1700s and in the 1750s chose Sabah I as their sheikh; the Al Sabah still rule. Kuwait lived on pearling, boat-building and the desert caravans, under loose Ottoman overlordship.

periods.name: British protectorate
periods.note: Fearing the Ottomans, Sheikh Mubarak the Great signed a treaty with Britain in 1899. Oil was found at Burgan in 1938, and its exports from 1946 made Kuwait rich.

periods.name: State of Kuwait
periods.note: Kuwait became independent in 1961 and elected a parliament in 1963. Saddam Hussein's Iraq invaded and annexed it in August 1990, until a US-led coalition drove them out in February 1991; the retreating Iraqis set hundreds of oil wells on fire.

periods.name: Ancient Qatar
periods.note: Ubaid pottery from Mesopotamia shows people fishing and trading here 7,000 years ago. Ptolemy's map called the peninsula Catara; under Persian rule it was part of Beth Qatraye, a Christian land of monks and scholars.

periods.name: Islamic Qatar
periods.note: Qatar took up Islam in the 620s and was ruled from afar by caliphs and Gulf dynasties, among them the Qarmatians of al-Hasa and the kings of Hormuz. Its people lived from pearling, fishing and herding.

periods.name: Al Khalifa, Al Thani and the Ottomans
periods.note: The Al Khalifa founded Zubarah in 1766 and ruled Qatar from Bahrain after 1783. Britain recognised Mohammed bin Thani as its leader in 1868; his son Jassim, the founder of modern Qatar, accepted Ottoman rule but beat an Ottoman army at al-Wajbah in 1893.

periods.name: British protectorate
periods.note: When the Ottomans left, Qatar signed a protection treaty with Britain in 1916. The collapse of the pearl trade brought years of hunger, until oil was found at Dukhan in 1939.

periods.name: State of Qatar
periods.note: Independent since 1971, Qatar grew rich on its share of the world's largest gas field. It founded Al Jazeera in 1996, outlasted a blockade by its neighbours from 2017 to 2021 and hosted the 2022 World Cup.

periods.name: Prehistoric Italy
periods.note: Farmers had settled Italy by 6000 BC; Ötzi the Iceman died in the Alps around 3300 BC, and Bronze Age villages of the terramare lined the Po.

periods.name: Etruscans and Greek colonies
periods.note: Etruscan cities ruled central Italy, Greeks founded Naples, Syracuse and Taranto in the south, and Rome, by legend founded in 753 BC, was ruled by kings.

periods.name: Roman Republic
periods.note: Rome expelled its last king in 509 BC, conquered Italy, beat Carthage in three Punic Wars and took the Mediterranean, then tore itself apart in civil wars until Augustus.

periods.name: Roman Empire
periods.note: Augustus made himself the first emperor in 27 BC and two centuries of Pax Romana followed; then crisis, Diocletian's rule of four emperors, and Constantine's Christian empire with its new capital at Constantinople.

periods.name: Western Roman Empire
periods.note: After Theodosius the empire was split for good. The West, ruled from Milan and Ravenna, lost its provinces to Goths, Vandals and Franks; Rome was sacked in 410 and 455, and the last western emperor was deposed in 476.

periods.name: Ostrogothic Italy
periods.note: Odoacer deposed the last emperor; Theodoric the Ostrogoth ruled Italy from Ravenna until Justinian's generals destroyed the Gothic kingdom in a twenty-year war.

periods.name: Byzantines and Lombards
periods.note: The Lombards took most of Italy from 568, while Byzantium kept Ravenna, Rome, Naples and the south, and the popes grew into the rulers of Rome.

periods.name: Franks, popes and emirs
periods.note: Charlemagne conquered the Lombards in 774 and was crowned emperor in Rome in 800. The Papal States took shape around Rome, Arab emirs ruled Sicily from 831, and Venice grew rich in Byzantium's shadow.

periods.name: Emperors, Normans and communes
periods.note: German kings crowned in Rome ruled the north as emperors; Normans took the south and Sicily, a kingdom from 1130; Venice, Genoa, Pisa and Milan grew rich and free, and fought Frederick Barbarossa.

periods.name: City-states and the Renaissance
periods.note: Florence, Venice, Milan, the papacy and Naples balanced each other while Dante, Giotto, Brunelleschi and Botticelli made the Renaissance.

periods.name: Italian Wars and Spanish rule
periods.note: France and Spain fought over Italy from 1494. Spain won Milan, Naples and Sicily, and Rome was sacked in 1527; Leonardo, Michelangelo and Galileo worked through the wars and the Counter-Reformation.

periods.name: Austrian and Bourbon Italy
periods.note: After the War of the Spanish Succession Austria held Milan, Bourbon kings ruled Naples and Sicily, and the House of Savoy became kings of Sardinia.

periods.name: Napoleonic Italy
periods.note: Napoleon conquered Italy, ended the thousand-year Republic of Venice in 1797 and made a Kingdom of Italy in the north.

periods.name: Risorgimento
periods.note: Mazzini's conspiracies, Garibaldi's Thousand and Cavour's diplomacy united Italy under the King of Sardinia; Venice followed in 1866 and Rome in 1870.

periods.name: Kingdom of Italy
periods.note: A new kingdom with Rome as its capital from 1871. Millions emigrated to the Americas, colonies were taken in Africa, and 600,000 Italians died in the First World War.

periods.name: Fascist Italy
periods.note: Mussolini's Fascists ruled from 1922, conquered Ethiopia and joined Hitler's war; the Allies invaded in 1943, and partisans shot Mussolini in 1945.

periods.name: Italian Republic
periods.note: Italians voted out the monarchy in 1946; the economic miracle of the 1950s and 60s made Italy a founder of the European Union and one of the largest economies.

periods.name: Megalith builders
periods.note: Farmers raised the standing stones of Carnac; Bronze Age and then Celtic Hallstatt chiefs traded tin, salt and amber across the land.

periods.name: Celtic Gaul
periods.note: Greeks founded Massalia (Marseille) around 600 BC. Celtic Gauls of the La Tène culture lived in tribes with hill-forts, druids and coins, until Julius Caesar conquered them in 58–51 BC and beat Vercingetorix at Alesia.

periods.name: Roman Gaul
periods.note: Gaul became Roman, with Lyon as its capital and Latin as its tongue. From 406 Franks, Visigoths and Burgundians crossed the Rhine and carved it up.

periods.name: Merovingian Franks
periods.note: Clovis united the Franks, took Gaul and was baptised a Catholic; his Merovingian heirs divided the kingdom among sons, and Charles Martel stopped an Arab army near Poitiers in 732.

periods.name: Carolingian Empire
periods.note: Pepin the Short took the crown in 751; his son Charlemagne ruled most of western Europe and was crowned emperor in 800. His grandsons split the empire at Verdun in 843, and Vikings rowed up the Seine.

periods.name: Capetian France
periods.note: Hugh Capet's heirs grew from a small domain around Paris into the strongest kingdom in Europe: Philip Augustus took Normandy from the English and the Albigensian Crusade won the south. Gothic cathedrals rose at Saint-Denis, Chartres and Notre-Dame.

periods.name: Hundred Years' War
periods.note: English kings claimed the French crown; the Black Death and a century of war followed, until Joan of Arc relieved Orléans in 1429 and the English were driven out.

periods.name: Renaissance and Wars of Religion
periods.note: Valois kings fought the Habsburgs in Italy and brought the Renaissance home to the châteaux of the Loire; at home Catholics fought Protestant Huguenots, and thousands were killed on Saint Bartholomew's Day in 1572.

periods.name: Bourbon monarchy
periods.note: Henry IV ended the wars of religion; Louis XIV, the Sun King, built Versailles and fought the rest of Europe; Louis XV lost Canada and India to Britain.

periods.name: Revolution and Napoleon
periods.note: The Revolution of 1789 abolished the monarchy and executed the king; Napoleon crowned himself emperor in 1804 and conquered most of Europe before his defeat at Waterloo.

periods.name: Restoration and Second Empire
periods.note: Bourbon kings returned, then the July Monarchy of Louis-Philippe; after the revolution of 1848, Napoleon's nephew made himself Emperor Napoleon III, until Prussia beat him at Sedan.

periods.name: Third Republic
periods.note: The republic survived the Paris Commune, built an empire in Africa and Indochina, and won the First World War at the cost of 1.4 million dead.

periods.name: Occupation and Vichy
periods.note: Germany conquered France in six weeks. Pétain's Vichy regime collaborated, while de Gaulle led the Free French from London and the Resistance fought at home.

periods.name: Fourth and Fifth Republics
periods.note: After the liberation France lost its empire in Indochina and Algeria; de Gaulle's Fifth Republic of 1958 made a strong presidency, and France and Germany built the European Union together.

periods.name: Prehistoric Iberia
periods.note: Copper Age towns such as Los Millares; the Bell Beaker culture spread from Iberia across western Europe, and El Argar ruled the south-east in the Bronze Age.

periods.name: Iberians, Celts and Phoenicians
periods.note: Phoenicians founded Gadir (Cádiz) around 1100 BC; Iberians lived in the east and south, Celts in the centre and west. Carthage conquered the south, from where Hannibal set out for Italy.

periods.name: Roman Hispania
periods.note: Rome took Iberia from Carthage in 218–206 BC and needed two centuries to conquer it all. Hispania gave Rome the emperors Trajan and Hadrian and the writers Seneca and Martial.

periods.name: Visigothic kingdom
periods.note: Vandals, Suebi and Alans crossed the Pyrenees in 409; the Visigoths ruled from Toledo, became Catholic in 589, and Isidore of Seville wrote his encyclopedia.

periods.name: Al-Andalus
periods.note: Arab and Berber armies took Iberia in 711. An Umayyad prince who escaped the Abbasids founded the Emirate of Córdoba in 756; under Abd al-Rahman III it became a caliphate and Córdoba the largest city in Europe, while Christian Asturias held out in the north.

periods.name: Taifas and the Reconquista
periods.note: The caliphate broke into taifa kingdoms. Castile took Toledo in 1085, while Almoravid and then Almohad Berbers came from Morocco to defend al-Andalus; after Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, Christians took Córdoba, Seville and Valencia.

periods.name: Castile, Aragon and Granada
periods.note: Granada, the last Muslim kingdom, built the Alhambra; Aragon took Sicily, Sardinia and Naples by sea, and Castile grew rich on wool.

periods.name: Catholic Monarchs
periods.note: Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon took Granada in January 1492, expelled the Jews, and sent Columbus west the same year.

periods.name: Habsburg Spain
periods.note: Charles V and Philip II ruled an empire on which the sun never set, from Mexico and Peru to the Netherlands, Naples and the Philippines. Silver from Potosí paid for their wars, and Cervantes and Velázquez made a Golden Age.

periods.name: Bourbon Spain
periods.note: The War of the Spanish Succession brought a French Bourbon king, Philip V, who centralised the state; Charles III reformed it in the spirit of the Enlightenment.

periods.name: Napoleon and the loss of the empire
periods.note: Napoleon put his brother on the throne in 1808 and Spain rose against him. The American colonies won their independence, and civil wars between liberals and Carlists followed.

periods.name: Restoration
periods.note: The Bourbons returned under a constitution; Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines to the United States in 1898.

periods.name: Republic and Civil War
periods.note: The Second Republic of 1931 split Spain between left and right; General Franco's rising in 1936 began a civil war that killed half a million people.

periods.name: Franco dictatorship
periods.note: Franco ruled as Caudillo and kept Spain out of the Second World War; from the 1960s tourism and industry brought growth.

periods.name: Democratic Spain
periods.note: On Franco's death King Juan Carlos led the change to democracy, with a constitution in 1978; Spain joined the European Community in 1986.

periods.name: Megaliths and Lusitanians
periods.note: Megalith builders raised the Almendres stone circle near Évora; later the Lusitanians and other Celtic peoples held the west of the peninsula and traded with Phoenicians at Lisbon.

periods.name: Roman Lusitania
periods.note: The Lusitanian chief Viriathus fought Rome until his murder in 139 BC; Augustus made Lusitania a province, with Mérida as its capital and Olisipo (Lisbon) as its port.

periods.name: Suebi and Visigoths
periods.note: The Germanic Suebi made a kingdom in the north-west with Braga as its capital, until the Visigoths absorbed it in 585.

periods.name: Gharb al-Andalus
periods.note: Lisbon, Santarém and the Algarve (al-Gharb, "the west") were Muslim for four centuries, while the County of Portugal around Porto grew up under the kings of León.

periods.name: Kingdom of Portugal
periods.note: Afonso Henriques made himself king in 1139 and took Lisbon with crusaders' help in 1147; the conquest of the Algarve in 1249 fixed borders that have barely changed since, and victory at Aljubarrota in 1385 kept Portugal free of Castile.

periods.name: Age of Discovery
periods.note: From the capture of Ceuta in 1415 Prince Henry's ships worked down Africa; Dias rounded the Cape in 1488, Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498 and Cabral Brazil in 1500. Lisbon became the spice market of Europe.

periods.name: Iberian Union
periods.note: When King Sebastian died in Morocco without an heir, Philip II of Spain took the crown, and Portugal lost much of its eastern trade to the Dutch.

periods.name: Braganza monarchy
periods.note: The revolt of 1640 brought the Braganza kings. Brazilian gold paid for the Baroque, the earthquake of 1755 destroyed Lisbon, the court fled to Brazil from Napoleon in 1807, and Brazil became independent in 1822.

periods.name: First Republic
periods.note: A revolution ended the monarchy in 1910; the republic had forty-five governments in sixteen years.

periods.name: Estado Novo
periods.note: Salazar's dictatorship ruled for four decades and fought long colonial wars in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea.

periods.name: Democratic Portugal
periods.note: The Carnation Revolution of 1974 brought democracy at home and freedom to the colonies; Portugal joined the European Community in 1986.

periods.name: Stone and Bronze Age Britain
periods.note: Farmers crossed from the continent around 4000 BC and raised Stonehenge and Avebury; Beaker people brought metalworking around 2400 BC.

periods.name: Celtic Britain
periods.note: Iron Age Britons lived in tribes with hill-forts such as Maiden Castle; Julius Caesar landed twice, in 55 and 54 BC.

periods.name: Roman Britain
periods.note: Claudius invaded in AD 43; Boudica's revolt burned London; Hadrian built his wall in 122, and Constantine was proclaimed emperor at York in 306. The legions left around 410.

periods.name: Anglo-Saxon kingdoms
periods.note: Angles, Saxons and Jutes settled the east and south, and kingdoms such as Kent, Mercia, Northumbria and Wessex fought for overlordship. Augustine converted Kent in 597; Bede wrote his history at Jarrow.

periods.name: Vikings and the Kingdom of England
periods.note: The Great Heathen Army of Danes conquered most of England from 865; Alfred the Great of Wessex held out, and his grandson Athelstan united England in 927. Cnut the Dane ruled it from 1016.

periods.name: Normans and Angevins
periods.note: William the Conqueror won at Hastings in 1066 and surveyed his kingdom in the Domesday Book; Henry II ruled from the Scottish border to the Pyrenees; King John lost Normandy and sealed Magna Carta in 1215.

periods.name: Plantagenet England
periods.note: Parliament took shape and Edward I conquered Wales; the Hundred Years' War with France, the Black Death and the Peasants' Revolt followed, then the Wars of the Roses between York and Lancaster.

periods.name: Tudor England
periods.note: Henry VII ended the Wars of the Roses; Henry VIII broke with Rome to end his marriage; under Elizabeth I the Armada was beaten and Shakespeare wrote.

periods.name: Stuarts and the Civil War
periods.note: James VI of Scotland became James I of England; civil war ended with Charles I beheaded in 1649 and Cromwell's republic, and the Glorious Revolution of 1688 put Parliament above the crown.

periods.name: Great Britain
periods.note: The Act of Union joined England and Scotland in 1707. Britain won Canada and India, lost its American colonies, beat Napoleon, and became the first industrial nation; Ireland was joined in 1801.
states: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

periods.name: Victorian Britain
periods.note: Under Queen Victoria the British Empire grew to cover a quarter of the world; railways, factories and cities spread, and reforms slowly widened the vote.
states: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

periods.name: World wars
periods.note: Britain fought both world wars and lost most of Ireland in 1922; under Churchill it stood alone against Hitler in 1940.
states: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

periods.name: Post-war Britain
periods.note: The welfare state and the National Health Service; the empire became the Commonwealth. Britain joined the European Community in 1973 and voted to leave the European Union in 2016.

periods.name: Prehistoric Scotland
periods.note: Neolithic farmers built the stone village of Skara Brae and the great tomb of Maeshowe on Orkney.

periods.name: Caledonians and Romans
periods.note: Iron Age Scots built brochs and crannogs. Rome beat the Caledonians at Mons Graupius in AD 83 but never held the north, building Hadrian's and the Antonine walls instead.

periods.name: Picts and Gaels
periods.note: Picts held the north and east; Gaels from Ireland founded Dál Riata in the west, and Columba founded Iona in 563; Britons ruled Strathclyde and Angles took Lothian. Kenneth MacAlpin, king of the Picts from about 843, began the line of Scottish kings.

periods.name: Kingdom of Alba
periods.note: From around 900 the Gaelic kingdom of Alba took shape and added Lothian and Strathclyde. Macbeth ruled from 1040 to 1057; David I brought in Norman knights, abbeys and burghs.

periods.name: Wars of Independence
periods.note: When Alexander III died, Edward I of England tried to rule Scotland; William Wallace and Robert the Bruce fought him, Bruce winning at Bannockburn in 1314, and the Declaration of Arbroath asserted Scottish freedom in 1320.

periods.name: Stewart Scotland
periods.note: The Stewart kings ruled a turbulent kingdom; James IV died at Flodden in 1513, John Knox led the Reformation in 1560, and Mary, Queen of Scots, was deposed and later executed in England.

periods.name: Union of the Crowns
periods.note: James VI became king of England too in 1603; Scotland kept its own parliament and church through the Covenanter wars and the Darien disaster.

periods.name: Scotland in Great Britain
periods.note: The Treaty of Union of 1707 merged the parliaments. The Jacobite risings ended at Culloden in 1746; the Enlightenment of Hume and Adam Smith and the shipyards of Glasgow followed.
states: ~United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

periods.name: Devolved Scotland
periods.note: A Scottish Parliament opened in Edinburgh in 1999; Scots voted against independence in 2014.

periods.name: Prehistoric Ireland
periods.note: Farmers built the passage tomb of Newgrange around 3200 BC, older than the pyramids; Bronze Age smiths made gold collars and lunulae.

periods.name: Celtic Ireland
periods.note: Gaelic-speaking tribes and petty kings ruled from royal sites such as Tara; Rome traded with Ireland but never invaded.

periods.name: Early Christian Ireland
periods.note: Patrick and other missionaries converted Ireland in the 5th century; its monasteries kept Latin learning alive and made the Book of Kells, and Irish monks such as Columba and Columbanus carried it to Scotland and Europe.

periods.name: Viking age
periods.note: Viking raids began in 795 and the Norse founded Dublin, Waterford and Limerick. Brian Boru became high king and broke Norse power at Clontarf in 1014.

periods.name: Gaelic kingdoms
periods.note: The provincial kings of Munster, Leinster, Connacht and Ulster fought to be high king of Ireland.

periods.name: Anglo-Norman lordship
periods.note: Norman knights invaded in 1169 and Henry II claimed the lordship of Ireland; the English Pale around Dublin then shrank as Gaelic lords won back most of the island.

periods.name: Kingdom of Ireland
periods.note: Henry VIII made himself King of Ireland in 1541. Tudor conquest, the Plantation of Ulster, Cromwell's massacres and the Williamite war put land and power in Protestant hands.

periods.name: Union with Britain
periods.note: The Act of Union of 1801 joined Ireland to Britain. The Great Famine of 1845–1852 killed a million people and drove a million more abroad; the Easter Rising of 1916 led to a war of independence.
states: ~United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

periods.name: Irish Free State
periods.note: The treaty of 1921 created the Irish Free State without six counties of Ulster, and a civil war followed; the constitution of 1937 named the state Éire.
states: ~United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

periods.name: Republic of Ireland
periods.note: Ireland left the Commonwealth as a republic in 1949, joined the European Community in 1973 and grew rich as the "Celtic Tiger"; the Good Friday Agreement of 1998 brought peace to Northern Ireland.

periods.name: Prehistoric Low Countries
periods.note: Farmers of the Funnelbeaker culture built the hunebedden, megalithic tombs of Drenthe; later Celtic and Germanic tribes, the Belgae and the Frisians, lived along the deltas.

periods.name: Roman frontier
periods.note: Caesar conquered the Belgae and the Rhine became the frontier of the empire, with forts at Nijmegen and Utrecht, while the Frisians lived free to the north.

periods.name: Frisians and Franks
periods.note: Frisians traded along the coast from Dorestad; the Franks conquered them in the 8th century, and Charlemagne ruled from Aachen nearby.

periods.name: Counties of the Empire
periods.note: After the Carolingian split the Low Countries fell to the Empire, apart from Flanders. Counts of Holland, dukes of Brabant and bishops of Utrecht ruled, while Bruges, Ghent and Dordrecht grew on trade and cloth.

periods.name: Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands
periods.note: The dukes of Burgundy gathered the provinces in the 15th century; by marriage they passed to the Habsburgs, and Charles V, born in Ghent, ruled them as the Seventeen Provinces. Philip II's taxes and persecution of Protestants drove them to revolt in 1568.

periods.name: Dutch Republic
periods.note: Seven northern provinces declared independence from Spain in 1581. In the Golden Age the Dutch East India Company traded from Japan to Brazil, Amsterdam was the market of the world, and Rembrandt and Vermeer painted.

periods.name: Batavian Republic and French rule
periods.note: French revolutionaries made the Batavian Republic in 1795; Napoleon made his brother Louis King of Holland and then annexed the country to France.

periods.name: Kingdom of the Netherlands
periods.note: The Congress of Vienna made a kingdom under the House of Orange, with Belgium until it broke away in 1830; the Netherlands stayed neutral in the First World War.

periods.name: German occupation
periods.note: Germany invaded in May 1940 and bombed Rotterdam; three quarters of Dutch Jews, Anne Frank among them, were murdered, and the Hunger Winter of 1944–45 killed 20,000.

periods.name: Modern Netherlands
periods.note: Indonesia became independent in 1949; the Delta Works were built after the flood of 1953, and the Netherlands helped found NATO and the European Union.

periods.name: Spanish Netherlands
periods.note: The southern provinces stayed Spanish and Catholic after the Dutch revolt; Antwerp's trade moved to Amsterdam, and the land became the battlefield of Europe.

periods.name: Austrian Netherlands
periods.note: The peace treaties of 1713–14 passed the southern Netherlands to Austria.

periods.name: French rule
periods.note: Revolutionary France annexed the country; Napoleon was beaten at Waterloo, south of Brussels, in 1815.

periods.name: United Kingdom of the Netherlands
periods.note: The Congress of Vienna joined the south to the Dutch kingdom, whose rule Catholics and liberals resented.

periods.name: Kingdom of Belgium
periods.note: The revolution of 1830 made Belgium independent under King Leopold I. It was among the first industrial countries, and Leopold II ruled the Congo as his private colony, where millions died.

periods.name: World wars
periods.note: Germany invaded neutral Belgium in 1914 and again in 1940; the trenches of Ypres and the Battle of the Bulge were fought on its soil.

periods.name: Modern Belgium
periods.note: Brussels became the seat of the European Union and NATO; the Congo became independent in 1960, and Belgium became a federal state of Flemings and Walloons in 1993.

periods.name: Roman and Frankish
periods.note: The land of the Treveri was ruled from Trier in Roman times, then by the Frankish kings.

periods.name: County of Luxembourg
periods.note: Count Siegfried built a castle on the Bock rock in 963; his heirs became Holy Roman Emperors, and Henry VII, Charles IV and Sigismund all came from the House of Luxembourg.

periods.name: Burgundian and Spanish rule
periods.note: Philip the Good of Burgundy took the duchy in 1443; it passed with the Netherlands to the Habsburgs and Spain, and France besieged its fortress again and again.

periods.name: Austrian rule
periods.note: Austria held the duchy and its fortress, among the strongest in Europe.

periods.name: French rule
periods.note: Revolutionary France annexed Luxembourg as the department of the Forests.

periods.name: Grand Duchy
periods.note: The Congress of Vienna made a grand duchy under the Dutch king. It lost its western half to Belgium in 1839, became neutral in 1867, and has had its own dynasty since 1890.

periods.name: German occupation
periods.note: Germany invaded in 1940 and annexed the country; a general strike in 1942 was crushed.

periods.name: Modern Luxembourg
periods.note: A founder of the European Communities and home to their court and bank, Luxembourg became one of the richest countries in the world per person.

periods.name: Lake dwellers and Helvetii
periods.note: Neolithic villages on stilts lined the lakes; the site of La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel gave its name to Celtic art, and the Celtic Helvetii gave the country its Latin name.

periods.name: Roman Helvetia
periods.note: Caesar turned back the migrating Helvetii in 58 BC; Roman towns such as Aventicum (Avenches) and Augusta Raurica grew along the roads over the Alps.

periods.name: Alemanni and Burgundians
periods.note: When Rome withdrew, Alemanni settled the north and east, bringing German speech, and Burgundians the west, who kept Latin: a language border that still runs through the country. The Franks ruled both.

periods.name: Burgundy and the Empire
periods.note: The land passed to the Kingdom of Burgundy and in 1033 to the Holy Roman Empire, ruled by lords such as the Zähringer, who founded Bern and Fribourg, and the Habsburgs, whose castle stood in Aargau.

periods.name: Old Swiss Confederacy
periods.note: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden swore an alliance in 1291. The confederates beat the Habsburgs at Morgarten and Sempach and Charles the Bold of Burgundy at Grandson and Morat, and Zwingli and Calvin led the Reformation from Zurich and Geneva.

periods.name: Helvetic Republic
periods.note: France invaded in 1798 and made a centralised Helvetic Republic; Napoleon's Act of Mediation of 1803 gave the cantons back much of their power.

periods.name: Restoration
periods.note: The Congress of Vienna guaranteed Swiss neutrality; Catholic and Protestant cantons fought a short civil war in 1847.

periods.name: Federal Switzerland
periods.note: The constitution of 1848 made a federal state with direct democracy. Switzerland stayed out of both world wars; the Red Cross and the United Nations work from Geneva.

periods.name: Prehistoric Germany
periods.note: Farmers of the Linear Pottery culture; the Únětice culture of the Bronze Age made the Nebra sky disc, the oldest known picture of the sky, around 1600 BC.

periods.name: Germanic tribes and Rome
periods.note: Celts lived in the south and Germanic tribes in the north. Rome held the Rhine and the Danube and lost three legions in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9; in the 5th century Franks, Alemanni, Saxons and Thuringians took the west.

periods.name: Franks and Saxons
periods.note: The Frankish kings conquered the Alemanni, Thuringians and Bavarians, and Boniface converted the Germans; Charlemagne crushed the Saxons in thirty years of war and ruled his empire from Aachen.

periods.name: East Francia
periods.note: The Treaty of Verdun gave Louis the German the lands east of the Rhine. When his line died out the dukes elected Conrad and then Henry the Fowler of Saxony, whose son Otto beat the Magyars at the Lechfeld in 955.

periods.name: Holy Roman Empire
periods.note: Otto the Great was crowned emperor in Rome in 962. Salian and Hohenstaufen emperors fought the popes over bishops and Italy; Frederick Barbarossa drowned on crusade in 1190.

periods.name: Princes and cities
periods.note: After the Hohenstaufen fell, princes, bishops and free cities ruled. The Golden Bull of 1356 named seven electors to choose the emperor; the Hanseatic League ruled Baltic trade, and Gutenberg printed his Bible in Mainz around 1455.

periods.name: Reformation and Thirty Years' War
periods.note: Luther's 95 theses of 1517 split Germany between Catholic and Protestant princes; the Thirty Years' War of 1618–1648 killed perhaps a third of its people.

periods.name: Rise of Prussia
periods.note: Brandenburg-Prussia, ruled from Berlin by the Hohenzollerns, became a kingdom in 1701, and Frederick the Great took Silesia from Austria. Bach, Kant and Goethe; Napoleon dissolved the Empire in 1806.

periods.name: German Confederation
periods.note: Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine was followed after 1815 by a German Confederation of 39 states. The revolution of 1848 failed, and Bismarck united Germany through wars against Denmark, Austria and France.

periods.name: German Empire
periods.note: Wilhelm I of Prussia was proclaimed emperor at Versailles in 1871. Germany became an industrial giant, took colonies in Africa and the Pacific, and lost the First World War.

periods.name: Weimar Republic
periods.note: A democratic republic lived through the Versailles treaty, the hyperinflation of 1923 and mass unemployment after 1929.

periods.name: Nazi Germany
periods.note: Hitler's dictatorship rearmed Germany, annexed Austria and Czechoslovakia, started the Second World War and murdered six million Jews in the Holocaust.

periods.name: Divided Germany
periods.note: The Allies divided Germany into four zones; in 1949 they became the Federal Republic in the west and the communist German Democratic Republic in the east, split by the Berlin Wall from 1961.

periods.name: Reunified Germany
periods.note: The Wall fell in November 1989, and Germany was reunited on 3 October 1990 with Berlin as its capital.

periods.name: Hallstatt and Noricum
periods.note: The salt mines of Hallstatt gave their name to the early Iron Age of Europe; later the Celtic kingdom of Noricum traded its iron with Rome.

periods.name: Roman Noricum and Pannonia
periods.note: Rome took the Alpine lands in 15 BC; Vindobona (Vienna) and Carnuntum guarded the Danube, and Marcus Aurelius died on campaign there in 180.

periods.name: Migrations
periods.note: Rome evacuated Noricum in 488; Lombards, Avars, the Slavs of Carantania and the Bavarians took the land.

periods.name: Frankish march
periods.note: Charlemagne destroyed the Avars and set up an eastern march, which the Magyars overran until their defeat in 955.

periods.name: Babenberg Austria
periods.note: The Babenbergs ruled Ostarrichi, first named in 996, as margraves and from 1156 as dukes; Richard the Lionheart was held for ransom at Dürnstein.

periods.name: Habsburg Austria
periods.note: Rudolf of Habsburg took Austria in 1278; his heirs were emperors from 1438, and Maximilian's marriages won Burgundy, Spain and Hungary for the family.

periods.name: Habsburg Monarchy
periods.note: Ferdinand I added Bohemia and Hungary in 1526; Vienna held out against Ottoman sieges in 1529 and 1683. Maria Theresa reformed the state, and Haydn and Mozart worked in Vienna.

periods.name: Austrian Empire
periods.note: Francis I took the title Emperor of Austria in 1804; Metternich hosted the Congress of Vienna and held nationalism down until the revolutions of 1848.

periods.name: Austria-Hungary
periods.note: After defeat by Prussia, the Compromise of 1867 made a dual monarchy with Hungary: the Vienna of Freud, Klimt and Mahler. The heir Franz Ferdinand's murder at Sarajevo in 1914 began the First World War, which destroyed the empire.

periods.name: First Republic
periods.note: A small German-speaking republic was left; civil strife ended in Dollfuss' dictatorship in 1934.

periods.name: Annexed to Germany
periods.note: Hitler, born in Austria, annexed it in the Anschluss of March 1938.

periods.name: Allied occupation
periods.note: Four powers occupied Austria and Vienna until the State Treaty of 1955 made it free and neutral.

periods.name: Second Republic
periods.note: Neutral Austria grew prosperous and joined the European Union in 1995.

periods.name: Temple builders
periods.note: Farmers from Sicily reached the islands about 5900 BC. Between about 3600 and 2500 BC their descendants raised great stone temples such as Ġgantija, older than the pyramids of Egypt, and carved the underground Hypogeum; Bronze Age newcomers followed.

periods.name: Phoenicians and Carthage
periods.note: Phoenician traders settled the islands around 700 BC and worshipped Astarte at the old temple site of Tas-Silġ; from the 500s BC Malta was ruled by Carthage.

periods.name: Roman Malta
periods.note: Rome took Malta from Carthage in 218 BC. Tradition says the apostle Paul was shipwrecked here around AD 60 and converted the islanders; the catacombs of Rabat date from the late empire, before Vandals and Goths took the islands.

periods.name: Byzantine Malta
periods.note: Belisarius won Malta for the Byzantine Empire in 535, and for three centuries it was a naval outpost and a place of exile.

periods.name: Arab Malta
periods.note: The Aghlabids of Tunisia took Malta in 870 and left it almost empty, until Muslims from Sicily resettled it about 1048. They brought new crops and irrigation, and their Arabic grew into the Maltese language.

periods.name: Normans and the Kingdom of Sicily
periods.note: Count Roger the Norman landed in 1091, and in 1127 his son made Malta part of Sicily. It passed with Sicily to the Swabians, the Angevins and the kings of Aragon, while the local nobles ruled from Mdina.

periods.name: Knights of St John
periods.note: Charles V gave Malta to the Knights Hospitaller in 1530. They beat off the Ottoman Great Siege of 1565, then built Valletta and the Co-Cathedral of St John, and ruled as crusading monks until Napoleon took the island in 1798.

periods.name: British Malta
periods.note: The Maltese rose against the French, and Britain, called in to help, kept the islands as the base of its Mediterranean fleet. Malta held out through two years of bombing and siege in the Second World War, and the whole island was awarded the George Cross in 1942.

periods.name: Independent Malta
periods.note: Malta became independent in 1964 and a republic in 1974; the last British forces left in 1979. It joined the European Union in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2008.

periods.name: Stone and Bronze Age Denmark
periods.note: Farmers built dolmens and passage graves; Bronze Age chiefs were buried in oak coffins, and the Trundholm sun chariot was made around 1400 BC.

periods.name: Iron Age Danes
periods.note: Bog bodies such as Tollund Man and the silver Gundestrup cauldron; Angles and Jutes left for Britain, and by the 6th century the Danes ruled from Lejre.

periods.name: Viking age
periods.note: Danish Vikings raided and settled England and Normandy. Harald Bluetooth united Denmark and made it Christian around 965, and Cnut the Great ruled Denmark, England and Norway.

periods.name: Medieval Denmark
periods.note: Valdemar the Great and his sons made Denmark a Baltic power and conquered Estonia in 1219, where by legend the Dannebrog flag fell from the sky.

periods.name: Kalmar Union
periods.note: Queen Margaret united Denmark, Norway and Sweden under one crown at Kalmar in 1397; Sweden broke away for good under Gustav Vasa in 1523.

periods.name: Denmark-Norway
periods.note: Lutheran from 1536, the twin kingdom fought Sweden for the Baltic and lost Skåne in 1658; Christian IV built Copenhagen's towers, and Danish trading posts reached the Caribbean, India and Greenland.

periods.name: Kingdom of Denmark
periods.note: Denmark lost Norway to Sweden in 1814 and Schleswig-Holstein to Prussia and Austria in 1864, and became a constitutional monarchy in 1849. Hans Christian Andersen and Kierkegaard wrote in Copenhagen.

periods.name: German occupation
periods.note: Germany occupied Denmark in 1940; in 1943 Danes ferried almost all of the country's Jews to safety in Sweden.

periods.name: Modern Denmark
periods.note: A founder of NATO, Denmark joined the European Community in 1973 and built one of the world's most generous welfare states.

periods.name: Stone and Bronze Age Norway
periods.note: Hunters carved thousands of pictures of reindeer, boats and people into the rocks at Alta; farming reached the south around 4000 BC.

periods.name: Iron Age Norway
periods.note: Chieftains ruled from farms along the fjords and were buried in ships, as at Oseberg in 834.

periods.name: Viking age
periods.note: Norwegian Vikings raided Britain and Ireland and settled Iceland; Harald Fairhair united Norway around 872, and Olaf Haraldsson, later Saint Olaf, made it Christian.

periods.name: Kingdom of Norway
periods.note: After civil wars, the reign of Haakon IV brought a golden age; Norway ruled Iceland, Greenland, Orkney and Shetland. The Black Death of 1349 killed half its people.

periods.name: Union with Denmark
periods.note: Norway was ruled from Copenhagen for four centuries, first in the Kalmar Union and from 1536 as a part of Denmark.

periods.name: Union with Sweden
periods.note: Norway wrote its own constitution at Eidsvoll on 17 May 1814 but had to take the Swedish king; Ibsen, Grieg and Munch made its culture known.

periods.name: Independent Norway
periods.note: Norway ended the union peacefully in 1905 and chose a Danish prince as King Haakon VII; Amundsen reached the South Pole in 1911.

periods.name: German occupation
periods.note: Germany invaded in April 1940; the king led resistance from London while Quisling governed for the Nazis.

periods.name: Modern Norway
periods.note: North Sea oil, found in 1969, made Norway one of the richest countries; it twice voted not to join the European Union.

periods.name: Stone and Bronze Age Sweden
periods.note: Rock carvings at Tanum show the ships, chariots and ploughs of the Bronze Age.

periods.name: Iron Age Sweden
periods.note: The Svear around Uppsala and the Geats to the south, whose king Hygelac appears in Beowulf; rich boat graves at Vendel and Valsgärde.

periods.name: Viking age
periods.note: Swedish Vikings, the Varangians, sailed the rivers of Russia to Constantinople and Baghdad; Sweden became Christian slowly, and Uppsala's pagan temple lasted into the 1080s.

periods.name: Medieval Sweden
periods.note: Sweden conquered Finland in crusades; Birger Jarl founded Stockholm around 1252, and Saint Birgitta founded her order.

periods.name: Kalmar Union
periods.note: Sweden joined Denmark and Norway at Kalmar in 1397 but often fought the union kings; the Stockholm Bloodbath of 1520 led to revolt.

periods.name: Vasa Sweden
periods.note: Gustav Vasa was elected king in 1523, broke with Rome and built a Lutheran state.

periods.name: Swedish Empire
periods.note: Gustavus Adolphus made Sweden a great power in the Thirty Years' War. It ruled Finland, Estonia, Livonia and northern Germany until Charles XII's defeat by Peter the Great at Poltava in 1709.

periods.name: Age of Liberty and the Gustavians
periods.note: Parliament ruled in the Age of Liberty; Linnaeus named the plants and Celsius made his thermometer. Gustav III took power back for the crown and was shot at a masked ball.

periods.name: Sweden–Norway
periods.note: Sweden lost Finland to Russia in 1809 and won Norway in 1814; Napoleon's marshal Bernadotte founded the present royal house. A million Swedes emigrated to America.

periods.name: Modern Sweden
periods.note: Neutral in both world wars, Sweden built the "people's home" welfare state under the Social Democrats, joined the European Union in 1995 and NATO in 2024.

periods.name: Finnic peoples
periods.note: Hunters and fishers of the Comb Ceramic culture; later Finnic tribes, the Finns proper, Tavastians and Karelians, farmed, hunted and traded furs.

periods.name: Swedish Finland
periods.note: Swedish crusades from about 1150 brought Finland under Sweden for six centuries; Turku was its capital, and Mikael Agricola wrote the first book in Finnish in 1543.

periods.name: Grand Duchy of Finland
periods.note: Russia took Finland in 1809 as a grand duchy with its own laws; Helsinki became the capital, Lönnrot gathered the Kalevala, and Sibelius wrote Finlandia.

periods.name: Independent Finland
periods.note: Finland declared independence in December 1917, fought a bitter civil war, and twice fought the Soviet Union, in the Winter War of 1939–40 and the Continuation War, losing Karelia but keeping its freedom.

periods.name: Modern Finland
periods.note: Neutral between East and West, Finland built a welfare state and joined the European Union in 1995 and NATO in 2023.

periods.name: Settlement
periods.note: Norse settlers, many from Norway, and their Irish slaves settled Iceland from 874, as the Book of Settlements records.

periods.name: Icelandic Commonwealth
periods.note: Iceland governed itself without a king through the Althing, founded in 930, one of the oldest parliaments; Leif Erikson sailed from here to North America around 1000, and the sagas were written down.

periods.name: Norwegian and Danish rule
periods.note: Iceland accepted the Norwegian king in 1262 and passed with Norway to Denmark; volcanoes, famine and a Danish trade monopoly kept it poor.

periods.name: Kingdom of Iceland
periods.note: Iceland became a sovereign kingdom in union with Denmark in 1918.

periods.name: Republic of Iceland
periods.note: Iceland declared a republic in 1944 while Denmark was occupied, and won the "Cod Wars" with Britain over its fishing waters.

periods.name: Paleo-Inuit
periods.note: Arctic hunters of the Saqqaq and Dorset cultures lived on the coasts for three thousand years.

periods.name: Norse Greenland
periods.note: Erik the Red founded Norse farms in the south-west in 985; perhaps 2,000 people lived there at the height, but the settlements had died out by about 1450, as the Inuit of the Thule culture spread along the coasts.

periods.name: Inuit Greenland
periods.note: The Inuit, ancestors of today's Greenlanders, had the island to themselves, apart from European whalers.

periods.name: Danish colony
periods.note: The missionary Hans Egede founded Godthåb (Nuuk) in 1721; Greenland was a Danish trade monopoly, and the United States built bases there in the Second World War.

periods.name: Home rule
periods.note: Greenland became a county of Denmark in 1953, won home rule in 1979 and self-government in 2009, and left the European Community in 1985.

periods.name: Hunters of the north
periods.note: Hunters and fishers of the far north carved rock art at Alta over thousands of years.

periods.name: Early Sámi
periods.note: Sámi speech and ways of life took shape across the north; Tacitus wrote of the "Fenni" around AD 98, and later writers of skiing "Skridfinns".

periods.name: Sámi and the Norse
periods.note: Sámi hunted wild reindeer and traded furs with Norse chieftains such as Ottar, who described them to King Alfred around 890, and paid tribute to Norwegian, Swedish, Karelian and Russian collectors alike.

periods.name: Divided Sápmi
periods.note: From the 16th century the states taxed, converted and settled the Sámi lands, and reindeer herding grew; the border treaty of 1751 guaranteed herders' crossings. Sámi parliaments have sat in Finland, Norway and Sweden since 1973–1993.

periods.name: Finnic Estonia
periods.note: Finnic farmers lived in counties with hill-forts, such as Saaremaa and Ugandi, and raided Scandinavia as the Vikings raided them.

periods.name: Danish and Teutonic rule
periods.note: German crusaders and Danes conquered Estonia between 1208 and 1227; Tallinn became a Hanseatic town, and German barons ruled Estonian peasants for seven centuries.

periods.name: Swedish Estonia
periods.note: Sweden took Tallinn in 1561 and, after Poland-Lithuania gave up the south in 1629, founded the university of Tartu in 1632.

periods.name: Russian Estonia
periods.note: Peter the Great took Estonia in 1710; serfdom ended in 1816, and a national awakening followed, with song festivals from 1869.

periods.name: Independent Estonia
periods.note: Estonia declared independence on 24 February 1918 and won it in a war against Soviet Russia and German forces.

periods.name: Soviet Estonia
periods.note: Occupied by the Soviet Union in 1940, by Germany in 1941 and by the Soviets again in 1944; tens of thousands were deported to Siberia.

periods.name: Restored Estonia
periods.note: The Singing Revolution restored independence in 1991; Estonia joined NATO and the European Union in 2004 and led the world in digital government.

periods.name: Baltic and Finnic tribes
periods.note: Baltic tribes, the Curonians, Semigallians, Selonians and Latgalians, with Finnic Livs on the coast, traded amber and fought the Vikings.

periods.name: Livonia
periods.note: Bishop Albert founded Riga in 1201, and the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, later a branch of the Teutonic Order, conquered the land; German merchants and barons ruled it.

periods.name: Polish and Swedish rule
periods.note: When the Livonian Order fell, Poland-Lithuania and Sweden divided the land; Riga was Sweden's largest city, and the Duchy of Courland even had colonies in Tobago and Gambia.

periods.name: Russian Latvia
periods.note: Russia took Riga in 1710 and Courland, still a Polish fief, in 1795; Riga grew into a great industrial port.

periods.name: Independent Latvia
periods.note: Latvia declared independence on 18 November 1918 and won it in a war of independence by 1920.

periods.name: Soviet Latvia
periods.note: Soviet occupation in 1940, German occupation and the Holocaust from 1941, and Soviet rule again from 1944, with mass deportations.

periods.name: Restored Latvia
periods.note: Latvia regained its independence in 1991 and joined NATO and the European Union in 2004.

periods.name: Baltic tribes
