periods.note: Baltic tribes lived in the forests, the last pagans of Europe; Lithuania is first named in a chronicle of 1009.

periods.name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania
periods.note: Mindaugas united the tribes and was crowned king in 1253; Gediminas founded Vilnius, and his heirs, still pagan, conquered Belarus and Ukraine.

periods.name: Union with Poland
periods.note: Grand Duke Jogaila married Queen Jadwiga of Poland in 1386 and was baptised; Vytautas and the Poles beat the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410, and Lithuania stretched to the Black Sea.

periods.name: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
periods.note: The Union of Lublin made one Commonwealth with an elected king; its neighbours partitioned it out of existence between 1772 and 1795.

periods.name: Russian Lithuania
periods.note: Russia crushed risings in 1831 and 1863 and banned books in Lithuanian in Latin letters from 1864 to 1904, so book smugglers carried them in from Prussia.

periods.name: Independent Lithuania
periods.note: Lithuania declared independence on 16 February 1918, but Poland seized Vilnius, so Kaunas served as the capital.

periods.name: Soviet Lithuania
periods.note: Soviet occupation, then the Nazis, who with local collaborators murdered almost all of Lithuania's 200,000 Jews; Soviet rule again from 1944.

periods.name: Restored Lithuania
periods.note: Lithuania was the first Soviet republic to declare independence, on 11 March 1990; it joined NATO and the European Union in 2004.

periods.name: Early peoples
periods.note: Farmers, then the Lusatian culture of the Bronze Age, which built the wooden fortified town of Biskupin around 740 BC; later Celts, Goths and Vandals passed through.

periods.name: Slavic tribes
periods.note: Slavic tribes settled the land from the 6th century: the Polans around Gniezno, the Vistulans around Kraków and others.

periods.name: Piast Poland
periods.note: Mieszko I of the Polans was baptised in 966, the founding date of Poland, and Bolesław the Brave was crowned king in 1025. Split among dukes from 1138 and ravaged by the Mongols in 1241, it was reunited by Casimir the Great, who founded the university of Kraków.

periods.name: Jagiellonian Poland
periods.note: Queen Jadwiga married Jogaila of Lithuania in 1386, and together they beat the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410. Copernicus studied in Kraków and published his sun-centred universe in 1543.

periods.name: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
periods.note: A republic of nobles with an elected king and wide religious tolerance; John Sobieski saved Vienna from the Turks in 1683. The constitution of 3 May 1791 came too late: Russia, Prussia and Austria partitioned Poland out of existence by 1795.

periods.name: Partitions
periods.note: Napoleon's Duchy of Warsaw raised hopes; risings against Russia in 1830 and 1863 failed. Chopin and Marie Curie left for Paris.

periods.name: Second Republic
periods.note: Poland was reborn on 11 November 1918 and beat the Red Army at Warsaw in 1920.

periods.name: Occupation
periods.note: Germany and the Soviet Union invaded in September 1939. The Nazis murdered three million Polish Jews in camps such as Auschwitz and Treblinka, and Warsaw rose in 1944 and was razed.

periods.name: Communist Poland
periods.note: Moved west by the Allies, Poland became a Soviet satellite; the Solidarity union, born in the Gdańsk shipyard in 1980, forced free elections in 1989.

periods.name: Third Republic
periods.note: A democracy and market economy, Poland joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004.

periods.name: Celts and Marcomanni
periods.note: The Celtic Boii gave Bohemia its name; then the Germanic Marcomanni under King Maroboduus made a kingdom here that fought Rome.

periods.name: Slavs and Samo
periods.note: Slavs settled after 568; the Frankish merchant Samo led them against the Avars in the 7th century.

periods.name: Great Moravia
periods.note: Great Moravia united the western Slavs; the Byzantine missionaries Cyril and Methodius came in 863 and made the first Slavic alphabet.

periods.name: Přemyslid Bohemia
periods.note: The Přemyslid dukes, Saint Wenceslas among them, ruled from Prague; Bohemia became a kingdom of the Holy Roman Empire, and Ottokar II stretched it to the Adriatic.

periods.name: Luxembourg Bohemia and the Hussites
periods.note: Charles IV made Prague an imperial capital with its university and bridge; Jan Hus was burned for heresy in 1415, and his followers beat five crusades.

periods.name: Habsburg Bohemia
periods.note: The Habsburgs inherited Bohemia in 1526. The Defenestration of Prague began the Thirty Years' War, and defeat at the White Mountain in 1620 ended Czech independence for three centuries.

periods.name: Czechoslovakia
periods.note: Tomáš Masaryk founded a democratic Czechoslovakia in 1918; at Munich in 1938 Britain and France let Hitler take the Sudetenland.

periods.name: German occupation
periods.note: Hitler occupied Prague in March 1939 and ruled the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia.

periods.name: Communist Czechoslovakia
periods.note: Communists seized power in 1948; the Prague Spring of 1968 was crushed by Soviet tanks.

periods.name: Czech Republic
periods.note: The Velvet Revolution of 1989 made Václav Havel president; Czechs and Slovaks parted peacefully on 1 January 1993.

periods.name: Celts and Quadi
periods.note: Celtic hill-towns, then the Germanic Quadi on Rome's Danube frontier; Marcus Aurelius wrote part of his Meditations on campaign among them.

periods.name: Slavs and Great Moravia
periods.note: Slavs settled in the 6th century; the Principality of Nitra joined Great Moravia, where Cyril and Methodius taught.

periods.name: Kingdom of Hungary
periods.note: For a thousand years Slovakia was Upper Hungary. When the Turks took Buda, Pressburg (Bratislava) became Hungary's capital, where its kings were crowned from 1563 to 1830.

periods.name: Czechoslovakia
periods.note: Slovaks joined the Czechs in the new state of 1918.

periods.name: Slovak State
periods.note: A Slovak state under Jozef Tiso was Hitler's ally; the Slovak National Uprising of 1944 was crushed.

periods.name: Communist Czechoslovakia
periods.note: Slovakia was industrialised under communism; Alexander Dubček, a Slovak, led the Prague Spring of 1968.

periods.name: Slovak Republic
periods.note: Independent from 1 January 1993, Slovakia joined NATO and the European Union in 2004 and took the euro in 2009.

periods.name: Early Pannonia
periods.note: Farmers built tell villages on the Great Plain; later Celts and Illyrian Pannonians lived here.

periods.name: Roman Pannonia
periods.note: Pannonia was a frontier province on the Danube, with Aquincum (Budapest) as a legionary fortress.

periods.name: Huns and Avars
periods.note: Attila ruled the Huns from the Hungarian plain until 453; then came Gepids and Lombards, and the Avars ruled a khaganate here from 568 until Charlemagne destroyed it in 796.

periods.name: Magyar conquest
periods.note: Seven Magyar tribes under Árpád crossed the Carpathians around 895 and raided as far as Spain until their defeat at the Lechfeld in 955.

periods.name: Kingdom of Hungary
periods.note: Stephen I was crowned with a crown from the pope on Christmas Day 1000. The Mongols devastated Hungary in 1241; under Matthias Corvinus it was a Renaissance power, until the Ottomans killed King Louis II at Mohács in 1526.

periods.name: Ottoman and Habsburg Hungary
periods.note: Hungary was split three ways: the Ottomans held Buda and the centre, the Habsburgs a strip of Royal Hungary in the west and north, and Transylvania was a principality under the Sultan.

periods.name: Habsburg Hungary
periods.note: Once the Ottomans were driven out the Habsburgs ruled all of Hungary; Rákóczi's war of independence failed in 1711, and Kossuth's revolution of 1848 was crushed with Russian help.

periods.name: Austria-Hungary
periods.note: The Compromise of 1867 made Hungary an equal partner in a dual monarchy; Budapest was united in 1873 and boomed.

periods.name: Kingdom without a king
periods.note: Defeat in 1918, a short Soviet republic, then Admiral Horthy's regency; the Treaty of Trianon took two thirds of Hungary's land. Allied with Hitler, Hungary was occupied in 1944 and 430,000 Jews were sent to Auschwitz.

periods.name: Communist Hungary
periods.note: A Soviet-backed state; the revolution of 1956 was crushed by Soviet tanks, then Kádár's "goulash communism" eased life.

periods.name: Republic of Hungary
periods.note: Hungary opened its border with Austria in 1989, helping to bring down the Iron Curtain; it joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004.

periods.name: Steppe and forest peoples
periods.note: Finno-Ugric hunters lived in the forests, while on the steppe Cimmerians, Scythians, Sarmatians, Huns and Turkic khaganates followed each other. From the 7th century the Khazars ruled the lower Volga, and Slavs moved into the forests.

periods.name: Kyivan Rus'
periods.note: Varangians led by Rurik took Novgorod around 862 and Oleg moved to Kyiv; Vladimir the Great was baptised in 988. Kyivan Rus' broke into rival principalities, and Vladimir-Suzdal and Novgorod rose in the north.

periods.name: Mongol rule
periods.note: Batu's Mongols burned the Rus' cities in 1237–1240, and the princes paid tribute to the Golden Horde at Sarai. Moscow rose as the khans' tax collector, and Dmitry Donskoy beat the Tatars at Kulikovo in 1380.

periods.name: Grand Duchy of Moscow
periods.note: Ivan III took Novgorod in 1478 and stopped paying the Horde after the stand on the Ugra in 1480; he married a Byzantine princess, and Moscow was called the "third Rome".

periods.name: Tsardom of Russia
periods.note: Ivan the Terrible was crowned tsar in 1547, took Kazan and Astrakhan and began the conquest of Siberia; after the Time of Troubles the Romanovs were chosen in 1613, and Russians reached the Pacific by 1639.

periods.name: Russian Empire
periods.note: Peter the Great built St Petersburg and took the title emperor in 1721; Catherine the Great took Crimea and much of Poland, and Napoleon burned Moscow in 1812. Alexander II freed the serfs in 1861; defeat in the First World War ended the monarchy.

periods.name: Soviet Union
periods.note: Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in 1917 and won a civil war; Stalin's forced industrialisation, famines and purges killed millions. The Soviet Union lost 27 million people beating Nazi Germany, then faced America in the Cold War and put the first man in space in 1961.

periods.name: Russian Federation
periods.note: The Soviet Union broke up in December 1991; Yeltsin's chaotic 1990s gave way to Vladimir Putin, whose Russia seized Crimea in 2014 and invaded Ukraine in 2022.

periods.name: Trypillia and the steppe
periods.note: Farmers of the Trypillia culture built some of the largest settlements in the world around 4000 BC; horse-riding herders of the Yamnaya culture spread Indo-European languages, and the Cimmerians followed.

periods.name: Scythians and Greek colonies
periods.note: Scythian horsemen buried their kings with gold in great mounds; Greeks founded Olbia, Chersonesus and the Bosporan Kingdom on the Black Sea coast and shipped grain to Athens. Sarmatians followed the Scythians.

periods.name: Goths, Huns and Khazars
periods.note: Goths settled the steppe in the 3rd century until the Huns arrived around 370; Bulgars, Avars and Khazars followed, and East Slavic tribes, the Polianians around Kyiv among them, settled the forest-steppe.

periods.name: Kyivan Rus'
periods.note: Oleg made Kyiv the capital of the Rus' in 882; Volodymyr the Great was baptised in 988, and Yaroslav the Wise built Saint Sophia. Kyiv was the greatest city of eastern Europe until the Mongols sacked it in 1240.

periods.name: Galicia-Volhynia and the Horde
periods.note: Danylo of Galicia was crowned king in 1253 and held the west, while the steppe paid tribute to the Golden Horde.

periods.name: Lithuanian and Polish rule
periods.note: Lithuania took Kyiv after beating the Tatars at Blue Waters in 1362; after 1569 Ukraine passed to Poland, whose nobles made its peasants serfs. Free Cossacks gathered beyond the Dnieper rapids at the Zaporozhian Sich, and the Crimean Khanate raided for slaves.

periods.name: Cossack Hetmanate
periods.note: Bohdan Khmelnytsky's Cossack uprising of 1648 made a Cossack state, which took the tsar's protection at Pereiaslav in 1654; Hetman Mazepa sided with Sweden and lost at Poltava in 1709.

periods.name: Russian and Austrian rule
periods.note: Catherine the Great abolished the Hetmanate, destroyed the Sich and annexed Crimea in 1783, while Galicia in the west went to Austria. Taras Shevchenko's poems woke a national feeling that the tsars tried to ban.

periods.name: Revolution and Soviet Ukraine
periods.note: The Ukrainian People's Republic declared independence in 1918 but lost to the Bolsheviks; Stalin's famine, the Holodomor, killed millions in 1932–33, and the Second World War killed millions more. Chernobyl exploded in 1986.

periods.name: Independent Ukraine
periods.note: Ukraine voted for independence in December 1991; the Orange Revolution of 2004 and the Maidan of 2014 turned it to the West. Russia seized Crimea in 2014 and launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.

periods.name: Baltic and Slavic tribes
periods.note: Baltic tribes, then East Slavs, the Krivichs, Dregovichs and Radimichs, settled the forests and marshes.

periods.name: Principality of Polotsk
periods.note: Polotsk was a principality of the Rus', often at war with Kyiv; Euphrosyne of Polotsk founded convents and schools in the 12th century.

periods.name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania
periods.note: From the 13th century the Grand Duchy of Lithuania took in the Belarusian lands; Old Belarusian was its language of government, and Francysk Skaryna printed the Bible in it in 1517.

periods.name: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
periods.note: Belarus was part of the Commonwealth and was fought over by Russia and Sweden.

periods.name: Russian rule
periods.note: The partitions of Poland gave Belarus to Russia; Napoleon's army was destroyed crossing the Berezina in 1812.

periods.name: Soviet Belarus
periods.note: A Belarusian People's Republic was declared in 1918, but the Bolsheviks made a Soviet Belarus; the Second World War killed a quarter of its people.

periods.name: Republic of Belarus
periods.note: Independent from 1991; Alexander Lukashenko has ruled since 1994.

periods.name: Cucuteni and Hamangia
periods.note: Farmers of the Cucuteni culture made painted pottery and huge villages; the Hamangia culture made the clay figure known as the Thinker around 5000 BC.

periods.name: Dacians
periods.note: The Getae and Dacians, Thracian peoples, built mountain fortresses; King Burebista united them around 60 BC, and Decebalus fought Rome.

periods.name: Roman Dacia
periods.note: Trajan conquered Dacia in 106, as his column in Rome shows. Rome withdrew in 271, leaving behind the Latin speech that became Romanian.

periods.name: Migrations
periods.note: Goths, Huns, Gepids, Avars, Slavs, Bulgars, Pechenegs and Cumans crossed the land; Transylvania became part of Hungary from the 11th century.

periods.name: Wallachia and Moldavia
periods.note: Basarab founded Wallachia around 1310 and Bogdan Moldavia in 1359. Vlad the Impaler and Stephen the Great fought the Turks, but both principalities became Ottoman vassals, ruled in the 18th century by Greek Phanariot princes.

periods.name: Bessarabia under Russia
periods.note: Russia took the eastern half of Moldavia, Bessarabia, from the Ottomans in 1812.

periods.name: Greater Romania
periods.note: Bessarabia joined Romania in 1918.

periods.name: Moldavian SSR
periods.note: The Soviet Union took Bessarabia in 1940 and made it the Moldavian Soviet republic, writing its Romanian language in Cyrillic letters.

periods.name: Republic of Moldova
periods.note: Moldova became independent in 1991; Transnistria broke away in a short war in 1992.

periods.name: Cycladic and Minoan
periods.note: Islanders of the Cyclades carved marble figures; on Crete the Minoans built the palace of Knossos, wrote Linear A and traded across the Aegean.

periods.name: Mycenaean Greece
periods.note: Warrior kings ruled from Mycenae, Pylos and Thebes, wrote Greek in Linear B and, by tradition, sacked Troy.

periods.name: Dark Age and Archaic Greece
periods.note: After the palaces fell, Greeks rebuilt in city-states. Homer's epics were written down, the first Olympic Games were held in 776 BC, colonies were founded from Spain to the Black Sea, and Athens became a democracy in 508 BC.

periods.name: Classical Greece
periods.note: Athens and Sparta beat the Persians at Marathon, Salamis and Plataea. Athens built the Parthenon, and Socrates, Plato, Sophocles and Thucydides lived there, until the Peloponnesian War ruined it.

periods.name: Macedonian Greece
periods.note: Philip II of Macedon beat Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BC; his son Alexander conquered Persia, Egypt and the Indus. His generals divided the empire, and Macedon ruled Greece until Rome came.

periods.name: Roman Greece
periods.note: Rome sacked Corinth in 146 BC; Greek became the culture of the Roman elite, and Paul preached in Athens and Corinth.

periods.name: Byzantine Empire
periods.note: Constantine founded Constantinople in 330. The eastern Roman empire spoke Greek, built Hagia Sophia and outlived the West by a thousand years.

periods.name: Crusaders and the last Byzantines
periods.note: The Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204, and Franks and Venetians divided Greece; a shrunken Byzantium fell to the Ottomans on 29 May 1453.

periods.name: Ottoman Greece
periods.note: Greece was Ottoman for nearly four centuries; Venice held Crete until 1669 and the Ionian Islands until 1797, and the Orthodox Church kept Greek identity alive.

periods.name: Independence and the kingdom
periods.note: The revolution of 1821, helped by Britain, France and Russia at Navarino, won independence in 1830. The kingdom grew by stages to take Thessaly, Crete, Macedonia and Epirus, but defeat in Anatolia in 1922 ended in an exchange of peoples with Turkey.

periods.name: Republic, dictatorship and war
periods.note: Republic and monarchy took turns; then the Metaxas dictatorship, German occupation from 1941, a civil war won by the right in 1949, and the colonels' junta of 1967–74.

periods.name: Third Hellenic Republic
periods.note: Democracy returned in 1974 and the monarchy was abolished; Greece joined the European Community in 1981 and the euro in 2001, and lived through a deep debt crisis after 2009.

periods.name: Varna and the first gold
periods.note: The Varna necropolis, from around 4500 BC, holds the oldest worked gold in the world.

periods.name: Thracians
periods.note: Thracian tribes, whom Herodotus called the most numerous people after the Indians, buried their kings with gold; the Odrysian kingdom was the strongest of them. Spartacus was a Thracian.

periods.name: Roman and Byzantine Thrace
periods.note: Rome made Thrace and Moesia provinces; Serdica (Sofia) was a favourite city of Constantine. Slavs settled from the 6th century.

periods.name: First Bulgarian Empire
periods.note: Khan Asparukh's Bulgars crossed the Danube and won recognition from Byzantium in 681. Boris I became Christian in 864, the Cyrillic alphabet was made at Preslav and Ohrid, and Tsar Simeon nearly took Constantinople; Basil II, the "Bulgar-slayer", conquered the empire in 1018.

periods.name: Byzantine rule
periods.note: Bulgaria was a Byzantine province for 170 years.

periods.name: Second Bulgarian Empire
periods.note: The brothers Asen and Peter rebelled in 1185 and ruled from Tarnovo; Ivan Asen II made Bulgaria the strongest Balkan power again, until the Ottomans took Tarnovo in 1393.

periods.name: Ottoman Bulgaria
periods.note: Five centuries of Ottoman rule; the April Uprising of 1876 and its bloody repression led to the Russo-Turkish War.

periods.name: Principality and Tsardom
periods.note: Russia's victory in 1878 made an autonomous principality, independent as a tsardom in 1908; Bulgaria then lost the Second Balkan War and both world wars.

periods.name: People's Republic
periods.note: Todor Zhivkov ruled the most loyal of the Soviet satellites for 35 years.

periods.name: Republic of Bulgaria
periods.note: Multi-party democracy from 1990; Bulgaria joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007.

periods.name: Cucuteni and Hamangia
periods.note: Farmers of the Cucuteni culture made painted pottery and huge villages; the Hamangia culture made the clay figure known as the Thinker around 5000 BC.

periods.name: Dacians
periods.note: The Getae and Dacians, Thracian peoples, built mountain fortresses; King Burebista united them around 60 BC, and Decebalus fought Rome.

periods.name: Roman Dacia
periods.note: Trajan conquered Dacia in 106, as his column in Rome shows. Rome withdrew in 271, leaving behind the Latin speech that became Romanian.

periods.name: Migrations
periods.note: Goths, Huns, Gepids, Avars, Slavs, Bulgars, Pechenegs and Cumans crossed the land; Transylvania became part of Hungary from the 11th century.

periods.name: Wallachia and Moldavia
periods.note: Basarab founded Wallachia around 1310 and Bogdan Moldavia in 1359. Vlad the Impaler and Stephen the Great fought the Turks, but both principalities became Ottoman vassals, ruled in the 18th century by Greek Phanariot princes.

periods.name: United Principalities and Kingdom
periods.note: Alexandru Ioan Cuza was elected prince of both principalities in 1859; independence came in 1878 and a king in 1881. After the First World War Transylvania and Bessarabia joined to make Greater Romania.

periods.name: Communist Romania
periods.note: The king was forced out in 1947; Nicolae Ceaușescu ruled from 1965, starving the people to pay off foreign debts.

periods.name: Democratic Romania
periods.note: A revolution in December 1989 overthrew and executed Ceaușescu; Romania joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007.

periods.name: Vinča and the Danube
periods.note: Lepenski Vir on the Danube was a fishing village with carved stone heads by 7000 BC; the Vinča culture, around 5500–4500 BC, smelted copper and made clay figures.

periods.name: Illyrians, Thracians and Celts
periods.note: Illyrian, Thracian and Dacian tribes lived here; the Celtic Scordisci founded Singidunum, today Belgrade, in the 3rd century BC.

periods.name: Roman Moesia
periods.note: Rome conquered the land by 29 BC; Sirmium was an imperial capital, and seventeen emperors, Constantine the Great among them, were born in what is now Serbia.

periods.name: Slavs and Byzantium
periods.note: Slavs settled the Balkans in the 6th and 7th centuries. Serbian princes such as Vlastimir ruled Raška and Duklja between Byzantium and Bulgaria and became Christian in the 9th century.

periods.name: Nemanjić Serbia
periods.note: Stefan Nemanja founded a dynasty in 1166, and his son Sava made the Serbian church independent; Stefan Dušan was crowned emperor of the Serbs and Greeks in 1346 and wrote a law code.

periods.name: Kosovo and the Despotate
periods.note: Prince Lazar died fighting the Ottomans at Kosovo Polje in 1389, a battle at the heart of Serbian memory; the despots held out at Smederevo until 1459.

periods.name: Ottoman Serbia
periods.note: Ottoman rule lasted three and a half centuries. Belgrade changed hands between Turks and Austrians, and in 1690 thousands of Serbs fled north to Habsburg lands.

periods.name: Principality and Kingdom of Serbia
periods.note: Karađorđe's rising of 1804 and Miloš Obrenović's of 1815 won self-rule, and independence came in 1878. Serbia won the Balkan Wars, and a Bosnian Serb's shots at Sarajevo in 1914 led Austria-Hungary to attack it.

periods.name: Yugoslavia
periods.note: The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes of 1918 became Yugoslavia. After German occupation and civil war, Tito's partisans made a communist federation that stayed out of the Soviet bloc.

periods.name: Republic of Serbia
periods.note: Under Slobodan Milošević Serbia fought wars as Yugoslavia broke apart, and NATO bombed it in 1999 over Kosovo. Montenegro left in 2006, and Kosovo declared independence in 2008, which Serbia does not accept.

periods.name: Vučedol and the Illyrians
periods.note: The Vučedol culture made its famous dove vessel around 2800 BC; later Illyrian tribes held the coast, where Greeks founded colonies on Vis and Korčula.

periods.name: Roman Dalmatia and Pannonia
periods.note: Rome made Dalmatia and Pannonia provinces; Diocletian retired to the palace he built at Split, inside which the old town still lives.

periods.name: Avars, Slavs and Franks
periods.note: Croats arrived in the 7th century; their dukes ruled Dalmatia and Pannonia between the Franks and Byzantium.

periods.name: Kingdom of Croatia
periods.note: Tomislav was crowned the first king of Croatia around 925; the kingdom ruled the Adriatic coast and Slavonia.

periods.name: Union with Hungary
periods.note: In 1102 Croatia took the Hungarian king, keeping its own ban and diet; Venice took most of Dalmatia, and Dubrovnik (Ragusa) was a free merchant republic.

periods.name: Habsburg Croatia
periods.note: Croatian nobles elected the Habsburgs in 1527, and much of the land became a military frontier against the Ottomans.

periods.name: Yugoslavia
periods.note: Croatia joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. In the Second World War the fascist Ustaše ran a Nazi puppet state with death camps such as Jasenovac; Tito, himself half Croat, made Croatia a republic of communist Yugoslavia.

periods.name: Republic of Croatia
periods.note: Croatia declared independence in 1991 and won a war against Serb rebels and the Yugoslav army by 1995; it joined NATO in 2009 and the European Union in 2013.

periods.name: Pile-dwellers and Celts
periods.note: Pile-dwellers of the Ljubljana Marshes made the oldest known wooden wheel, about 5,150 years ago; later Celts of Noricum lived in the Alps.

periods.name: Roman Slovenia
periods.note: Emona (Ljubljana) and Celeia (Celje) were Roman towns on the road from Italy to the Danube.

periods.name: Carantania
periods.note: Alpine Slavs, ancestors of the Slovenes, founded Carantania in the 7th century, whose dukes were installed on the Prince's Stone; it accepted Bavarian and then Frankish rule.

periods.name: Empire and Habsburgs
periods.note: Carniola, Styria and Carinthia were lands of the Empire, under the Habsburgs from 1278 to 1918; Primož Trubar printed the first books in Slovene in the Reformation.

periods.name: Yugoslavia
periods.note: Slovenia joined Yugoslavia and was the richest of its republics.

periods.name: Republic of Slovenia
periods.note: Slovenia won its independence in a ten-day war in 1991 and joined the European Union and NATO in 2004.

periods.name: Butmir and the Illyrians
periods.note: Neolithic villages of the Butmir culture; later the Illyrian Daesitiates, who fought Rome in the great revolt of AD 6–9.

periods.name: Roman Dalmatia
periods.note: The province of Dalmatia had silver mines and spas such as Ilidža.

periods.name: Slavs, Byzantium and Hungary
periods.note: Slavs settled in the 7th century, and the land passed between Byzantium, Croatia, Serbia and Hungary.

periods.name: Banate and Kingdom of Bosnia
periods.note: Bans such as Kulin ruled Bosnia under Hungarian overlordship, with its own Bosnian Church; Tvrtko I was crowned king in 1377, and the carved stećak tombstones date from this age.

periods.name: Ottoman Bosnia
periods.note: The Ottomans took Bosnia in 1463 and Herzegovina in 1482. Many Bosnians became Muslim, and Sarajevo and Mostar, with its bridge of 1566, grew into Ottoman cities.

periods.name: Austro-Hungarian rule
periods.note: Austria-Hungary occupied Bosnia in 1878 and annexed it in 1908; Gavrilo Princip shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914.

periods.name: Yugoslavia
periods.note: Part of Yugoslavia; in the Second World War it was a battlefield of partisans, Chetniks and Ustaše, and Sarajevo hosted the Winter Olympics in 1984.

periods.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
periods.note: Independence in 1992 brought a war of Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats, with the siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica genocide of 1995; the Dayton Agreement ended it.

periods.name: Illyrians and Romans
periods.note: Illyrian kings, Queen Teuta among them, ruled the Bay of Kotor until Rome took it; Doclea was a Roman town.

periods.name: Duklja and Zeta
periods.note: Slavs settled. Duklja became a kingdom in 1077; as Zeta it was part of Nemanjić Serbia and later ruled by the Balšić and Crnojević families.

periods.name: Prince-bishops
periods.note: In the mountains around Cetinje the Montenegrins kept a free Orthodox state under prince-bishops of the Petrović-Njegoš family, among them the poet Njegoš.

periods.name: Principality and Kingdom
periods.note: Danilo made himself a secular prince in 1852; independence was recognised in 1878, and Nikola I became king in 1910.

periods.name: Yugoslavia
periods.note: Montenegro joined Serbia and then Yugoslavia in 1918, and stayed with Serbia when Yugoslavia broke up.

periods.name: Independent Montenegro
periods.note: Montenegrins voted for independence in 2006; the country joined NATO in 2017.

periods.name: Paeonians and Macedon
periods.note: Paeonian tribes lived along the Vardar and Dardanians to the north; Philip II of Macedon conquered them in the 4th century BC.

periods.name: Roman province
periods.note: Rome made Macedonia a province in 148 BC, and the Via Egnatia crossed it from the Adriatic to Thessaloniki; Justinian was born near Skopje.

periods.name: Slavs, Bulgaria and Byzantium
periods.note: Slavs settled in the 6th century. Clement and Naum taught at Ohrid in the 9th century, and Tsar Samuel ruled from Ohrid until Byzantium destroyed his state in 1018; Stefan Dušan was crowned in Skopje in 1346.

periods.name: Ottoman Macedonia
periods.note: Five centuries of Ottoman rule; the Ilinden Uprising of 1903 against the Turks failed.

periods.name: Serbia and Yugoslavia
periods.note: The Balkan Wars of 1912–13 divided Macedonia between Serbia, Greece and Bulgaria; in 1944 Tito made the Yugoslav part a republic with its own Macedonian language.

periods.name: Independent North Macedonia
periods.note: Independent from 1991; a dispute with Greece over its name ended in 2019 with "North Macedonia", and it joined NATO in 2020.

periods.name: Illyrians
periods.note: Illyrian tribes and kingdoms held the western Balkans, while Greeks founded Epidamnus (Durrës) and Apollonia on the coast; Queen Teuta's raiders provoked Rome in 229 BC.

periods.name: Roman and Byzantine Albania
periods.note: Rome took the last Illyrian king, Gentius, in 168 BC, and the Via Egnatia ran from Durrës to Constantinople. Byzantium held the land through Slav and Bulgar invasions.

periods.name: Medieval principalities
periods.note: The Principality of Arbanon of 1190 was the first Albanian state; then came Angevins, Serbs and Venetians. Skanderbeg held off the Ottomans from Krujë for 25 years until his death in 1468.

periods.name: Ottoman Albania
periods.note: Most Albanians became Muslim under the Ottomans, and many rose high in their service; Ali Pasha of Tepelena ruled almost on his own around 1800.

periods.name: Independent Albania
periods.note: Albania declared independence at Vlorë in 1912; Ahmet Zogu made himself King Zog in 1928, and Italy invaded in 1939.

periods.name: Communist Albania
periods.note: Enver Hoxha's dictatorship broke with Yugoslavia, the Soviet Union and China in turn, banned religion and built 170,000 bunkers.

periods.name: Republic of Albania
periods.note: Communism fell in 1991, and Albania joined NATO in 2009.

periods.name: Ancient Cyprus
periods.note: Copper, which may take its name from the island, made Cyprus rich from the Bronze Age; Phoenician and Greek city-kingdoms followed, under Assyria, Egypt and Persia, then Ptolemy's Egypt.

periods.name: Roman and Byzantine Cyprus
periods.note: Rome annexed Cyprus in 58 BC, and Paul and Barnabas preached there; Arabs and Byzantines shared the island's taxes for three centuries after 688.

periods.name: Lusignan Kingdom
periods.note: Richard the Lionheart took Cyprus on the Third Crusade in 1191 and sold it; French Lusignan kings ruled it for three centuries.

periods.name: Venetian Cyprus
periods.note: Venice took the island in 1489 and fortified Nicosia and Famagusta, which fell to the Ottomans in 1571 after a long siege.

periods.name: Ottoman Cyprus
periods.note: Turkish settlers joined the Greek population under Ottoman rule.

periods.name: British Cyprus
periods.note: Britain took over the island in 1878 and made it a colony in 1925; Greek Cypriots fought for union with Greece in the 1950s.
states: ~United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

periods.name: Republic of Cyprus
periods.note: Independent in 1960; after fighting between Greek and Turkish Cypriots and a Greek-backed coup, Turkey invaded in 1974, and the island has been divided ever since. Cyprus joined the European Union in 2004.

periods.name: Ancient Berbers
periods.note: Berber (Amazigh) farmers and herders lived here long before written history; Phoenicians, then Carthage, kept trading posts on the coast at Lixus and Mogador.

periods.name: Kingdom of Mauretania
periods.note: Moorish kings ruled from Volubilis and Tingis (Tangier). Bocchus handed Jugurtha over to Rome, and Juba II and his wife Cleopatra Selene, daughter of Cleopatra and Mark Antony, ruled as Rome's clients until Caligula had their son killed in AD 40.

periods.name: Roman Mauretania
periods.note: Rome made the province of Mauretania Tingitana, rich in olive oil, around the city of Volubilis; in the 280s it pulled back to the north around Tangier.

periods.name: Berber kingdoms
periods.note: After Rome, Berber princes ruled the land and the Byzantines held only Ceuta; Uqba ibn Nafi's Arab raiders reached the Atlantic in 681.

periods.name: Arab conquest and the Berber revolt
periods.note: Musa ibn Nusayr conquered Morocco around 705, and his Berber general Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed to Spain in 711. The Berbers rose against the caliphs in 740, and the Barghawata founded a kingdom of their own on the Atlantic plains.

periods.name: Idrisid dynasty
periods.note: Idris I, a descendant of the Prophet fleeing the Abbasids, was made imam by Berbers at Volubilis in 788; his son founded Fez, where Fatima al-Fihri founded the mosque-university of al-Qarawiyyin in 859.

periods.name: Córdoba, the Fatimids and the Zenata
periods.note: The caliphs of Córdoba and the Fatimids fought over Morocco through Zenata Berber chiefs, who ruled Fez and the caravan town of Sijilmasa.

periods.name: Almoravid dynasty
periods.note: Veiled Sanhaja Berbers from the Sahara, led by Yusuf ibn Tashfin, founded Marrakesh around 1070, crossed to Spain to beat Castile at Sagrajas in 1086 and ruled from the Senegal river to the Ebro.

periods.name: Almohad Caliphate
periods.note: Followers of the reformer Ibn Tumart took Marrakesh in 1147 and ruled from the Atlantic to Tripoli and in al-Andalus; they built the Koutoubia, and Averroes was their judge and doctor. Defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 began their fall.

periods.name: Marinid dynasty
periods.note: Zenata Berbers took Marrakesh in 1269 and ruled from Fez, which they filled with madrasas; Ibn Battuta set out from Tangier in 1325, and Portugal took Ceuta in 1415.

periods.name: Wattasid dynasty
periods.note: The Wattasids, viziers of the Marinids, ruled a shrunken kingdom from Fez while Portugal seized Asilah, Safi and Agadir on the coast.

periods.name: Saadi dynasty
periods.note: Sharifs from the Draa valley took Fez in 1554, crushed Portugal at the Battle of the Three Kings in 1578 and, under Ahmad al-Mansur, conquered Songhai across the Sahara in 1591.

periods.name: Alaouite sultanate
periods.note: The Alaouites, who still reign, took Fez in 1666; Moulay Ismail built Meknes and an army of slave soldiers, and in 1777 Morocco was the first state to recognise the United States. France beat it at Isly in 1844 and Spain in 1860.

periods.name: French and Spanish protectorates
periods.note: The Treaty of Fez made Morocco a French protectorate in 1912, with a Spanish zone in the north, where Abd el-Krim's Rif Republic routed Spain at Annual in 1921 before France and Spain crushed it in 1926.

periods.name: Kingdom of Morocco
periods.note: Mohammed V won independence in 1956. Hassan II ruled through the "years of lead" and sent the Green March into Western Sahara in 1975; Mohammed VI has reigned since 1999.

periods.name: Ancient Berbers
periods.note: Herders painted the rocks of Tassili n'Ajjer when the Sahara was green; Berber farmers lived in the north, and Carthage kept ports on the coast.

periods.name: Numidia
periods.note: Two Berber kingdoms, of Syphax in the west and Gala in the east, sided with Carthage and Rome in turn. Gala's son Masinissa, Rome's ally at Zama, united them and ruled from Cirta (Constantine); his grandson Jugurtha fought Rome, and Caesar annexed Numidia in 46 BC.

periods.name: Roman Africa
periods.note: Roman towns such as Timgad, Djemila and Tipasa covered the north; Augustine was bishop of Hippo (Annaba) and died there in 430 while the Vandals besieged it.

periods.name: Vandals, Byzantines and Berber kingdoms
periods.note: The Vandals took the coast, the Byzantines won part of it back in 534, and Berber kingdoms ruled the Aurès mountains and the interior.

periods.name: Arab conquest
periods.note: Arab armies met fierce resistance from Kusaila and then from Dihya, the "Kahina", queen of the Aurès, who fell around 701; the Berbers became Muslims but rose against the caliphs in 740.

periods.name: Rustamids and Aghlabids
periods.note: The Ibadi imams of the Rustamid dynasty ruled the west from Tahert, and the Aghlabids of Kairouan the east.

periods.name: Fatimids, Zirids and Hammadids
periods.note: Kutama Berbers of Kabylia carried the Fatimids to power in 909. Their Zirid governors founded Algiers, and the Hammadids ruled from the Qal'a of Beni Hammad and Béjaïa, while the Almoravids took the west.

periods.name: Almohads
periods.note: The Almohads took Béjaïa in 1152 and ruled the whole Maghreb; Ibadi Muslims kept their towns in the desert valley of the Mzab.

periods.name: Kingdom of Tlemcen
periods.note: The Zayyanid (Abd al-Wadid) dynasty ruled the west from Tlemcen and fought off the Marinids of Fez, while the Hafsids of Tunis held the east.

periods.name: Regency of Algiers
periods.note: The corsair brothers Oruç and Hayreddin Barbarossa took Algiers and put it under the Ottoman sultan. For three centuries its corsairs raided Mediterranean ships and coasts, under deys chosen by the janissaries.

periods.name: French Algeria
periods.note: France took Algiers in 1830 and needed decades to conquer the country against Emir Abdelkader; Algeria was made part of France and settled by Europeans. The war of independence from 1954 cost hundreds of thousands of lives.

periods.name: People's Democratic Republic
periods.note: Independent from 5 July 1962, Algeria was ruled by the FLN and the army. A civil war with Islamist rebels in the 1990s killed some 150,000, and the Hirak protests of 2019 ended Bouteflika's twenty years in power.

periods.name: Berbers and Phoenician traders
periods.note: Capsian hunters, then Berber farmers; Phoenicians from Tyre founded Utica around 1100 BC.

periods.name: Carthage
periods.note: Founded by Tyre, by legend under Queen Dido, Carthage grew into a sea empire from Libya to Spain. It lost three Punic Wars to Rome, despite Hannibal's march over the Alps in 218 BC, and was razed in 146 BC.

periods.name: Roman Africa
periods.note: Rebuilt by Augustus, Carthage became the greatest city of the Latin West after Rome; the amphitheatre of El Djem dates from this time, and Tertullian and Cyprian wrote here.

periods.name: Vandal kingdom
periods.note: Gaiseric's Vandals took Carthage in 439 and sailed from it to sack Rome in 455.

periods.name: Byzantine Africa
periods.note: Belisarius won Africa back for Justinian in 534; Carthage fell to the Arabs in 698.

periods.name: Umayyads and Aghlabids
periods.note: Uqba ibn Nafi had founded Kairouan in 670. From 800 the Aghlabid emirs ruled Ifriqiya from it, built its Great Mosque and conquered Sicily.

periods.name: Fatimids and Zirids
periods.note: The Fatimid caliphate was proclaimed here in 909 and built Mahdia before moving to Cairo in 973; its Zirid governors broke away and were ruined by the Banu Hilal nomads after 1050.

periods.name: Almohads and Hafsids
periods.note: The Almohads took Tunis in 1159, and their Hafsid governors made it the capital of a caliphate of their own from 1249. Louis IX of France died besieging Tunis in 1270, and Ibn Khaldun was born there in 1332.

periods.name: Ottoman Tunis
periods.note: The Ottomans took Tunis from Spain in 1574. The Husainid beys ruled almost on their own from 1705, abolished slavery in 1846 and gave the Arab world its first constitution in 1861.

periods.name: French protectorate
periods.note: France imposed a protectorate by the Treaty of Bardo in 1881; Habib Bourguiba's Neo-Destour party led the fight for independence.

periods.name: Republic of Tunisia
periods.note: Bourguiba ruled until 1987 and Ben Ali until the revolution of 2010–11, which began the Arab Spring.

periods.name: Libyans and Garamantes
periods.note: Libyan tribes fought and served the pharaohs, and Libyan chiefs ruled Egypt as its 22nd dynasty; in the Fezzan the Garamantes later built a desert kingdom watered by underground channels.

periods.name: Greeks, Phoenicians and Carthage
periods.note: Greeks from Thera founded Cyrene in 631 BC. In the west the Phoenician towns of Oea (Tripoli), Leptis and Sabratha came under Carthage; Cyrenaica passed to the Ptolemies and in 96 BC to Rome.

periods.name: Roman Libya
periods.note: Leptis Magna grew rich on olive oil and was rebuilt in marble by its own son, the emperor Septimius Severus.

periods.name: Vandals and Byzantines
periods.note: The Vandals took Tripolitania; Justinian won it back in 533.

periods.name: Caliphs and Berber dynasties
periods.note: Amr ibn al-As took Tripoli in 643. It was ruled from Kairouan, Cairo and Tunis in turn, and Spain and the Knights of St John held it from 1510 to 1551.

periods.name: Ottoman Tripoli
periods.note: The corsair Turgut Reis took Tripoli for the Ottomans in 1551. The Karamanli pashas ruled on their own from 1711 to 1835 and fought the United States in the First Barbary War, and the Senussi order spread through Cyrenaica.

periods.name: Italian Libya
periods.note: Italy invaded in 1911. Omar Mukhtar led the resistance in Cyrenaica until he was hanged in 1931, and the desert war of 1940–43 was fought across the coast.

periods.name: Kingdom of Libya
periods.note: Britain and France ran the country after the war; it became independent in 1951 under King Idris, and oil was found in 1959.

periods.name: Gaddafi and after
periods.note: Muammar Gaddafi seized power in 1969 and ruled for 42 years; the uprising of 2011 ended in his death, and rival governments have fought over the country since.

periods.name: Saharan nomads
periods.note: Sanhaja Berber and later Arab, Hassaniya-speaking nomads herded camels here; the Almoravid movement began among them in the 11th century.

periods.name: Spanish Sahara
periods.note: Spain claimed the coast in 1884 and ruled Río de Oro and Saguia el-Hamra as a colony; phosphate was found at Bou Craa in 1947.

periods.name: Disputed territory
periods.note: When Spain left in 1975, Morocco sent 350,000 marchers in the Green March and took over. The Polisario Front fought for independence until a ceasefire in 1991, and the territory's status is still unsettled.

periods.name: Nubian cultures and Kerma
periods.note: Kerma, by the Nile's third cataract, was the capital of the first kingdom of Kush, rival of Middle Kingdom Egypt; its kings were buried under great mounds with hundreds of servants.

periods.name: Egyptian Nubia
periods.note: New Kingdom pharaohs conquered Kush as far as the fourth cataract and ruled it through a viceroy, the "King's Son of Kush".

periods.name: Kingdom of Kush
periods.note: The kings of Napata, by the holy mountain of Jebel Barkal, conquered Egypt and ruled it as its 25th dynasty, from about 744 to 656 BC, until the Assyrians drove them out.

periods.name: Meroë
periods.note: The capital moved south to Meroë, a centre of iron-working with its own script and more pyramids than Egypt; Rome raided it but never conquered it, and it fell around 350.

periods.name: Christian Nubia
periods.note: Aksum's armies reached Meroë around 350. Three kingdoms, Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia, became Christian in the 6th century. Makuria held off the Arabs and signed the baqt treaty with them in 652, and Christian Nubia lasted into the 15th century.

periods.name: Funj Sultanate
periods.note: The Funj founded a sultanate at Sennar in 1504 and became Muslim, while the Ottomans held the Red Sea port of Suakin and Lower Nubia; to the west the Fur sultans ruled Darfur from the Jebel Marra.

periods.name: Turkiyya
periods.note: Muhammad Ali's Egypt conquered Sudan in 1820–21 and founded Khartoum; slave raiding grew, and Egypt took Darfur in 1874.

periods.name: Mahdist state
periods.note: Muhammad Ahmad, the Mahdi, rose against Egyptian rule and took Khartoum in January 1885, killing General Gordon; his successor the Khalifa ruled from Omdurman until Kitchener crushed his army there in 1898.

periods.name: Anglo-Egyptian Sudan
periods.note: Britain and Egypt ruled Sudan jointly from 1899, in practice as a British colony that governed the Arab north and the African south apart.

periods.name: Republic of the Sudan
periods.note: Independent in 1956, Sudan fought two long civil wars with the south, which broke away as South Sudan in 2011. Omar al-Bashir ruled from 1989 to 2019, and war between the army and the RSF broke out in 2023.

periods.name: Highland farmers
periods.note: Farmers of the highlands domesticated teff and finger millet and herded cattle. Much earlier the Afar had been home to some of the oldest human ancestors, among them "Lucy", 3.2 million years old.

periods.name: Dʿmt
periods.note: The kingdom of Dʿmt, with its temple at Yeha, wrote in a South Arabian script and traded across the Red Sea.

periods.name: Kingdom of Aksum
periods.note: Aksum traded ivory and gold through the port of Adulis, minted its own coins and raised giant stone stelae. King Ezana became Christian around 340, and Aksum sheltered early followers of Muhammad.

periods.name: Zagwe dynasty
periods.note: From the 10th century power moved south from Aksum. The Agaw Zagwe kings ruled from Roha, renamed Lalibela after the king who had eleven churches carved down into its rock around 1200.

periods.name: Solomonic Ethiopia
periods.note: Yekuno Amlak claimed descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba and founded a dynasty that lasted until 1974. Amda Seyon beat the Muslim sultanates, but in 1529–43 Ahmad Gragn of Adal nearly conquered the empire, until Portuguese musketeers helped save it; Oromo peoples then moved into the south and centre.

periods.name: Gondar
periods.note: Fasilides expelled the Jesuits and built the castles of Gondar, the capital for over a century.

periods.name: Era of the Princes
periods.note: In the Zemene Mesafint the emperors were puppets of regional lords, many of them Oromo.

periods.name: Modern empire
periods.note: Tewodros II reunited the country. Menelik II conquered the south, founded Addis Ababa and beat Italy at Adwa in 1896, keeping Ethiopia independent; Haile Selassie was crowned in 1930.

periods.name: Italian occupation
periods.note: Mussolini's army conquered Ethiopia with poison gas in 1935–36; British and Ethiopian forces freed it in 1941.

periods.name: Haile Selassie
periods.note: The emperor came back, annexed Eritrea in 1962 and made Addis Ababa the seat of the Organisation of African Unity.

periods.name: Derg
periods.note: A Marxist junta under Mengistu Haile Mariam overthrew the emperor; the Red Terror and the famine of 1983–85 killed hundreds of thousands.

periods.name: Federal Republic
periods.note: Rebels took Addis Ababa in 1991 and Eritrea left in 1993. Ethiopia became a federation of ethnic regions, and the Tigray war of 2020–22 was one of the deadliest of the century.

periods.name: Highland farmers
periods.note: Farmers of the highlands domesticated teff and finger millet and herded cattle. Much earlier the Afar had been home to some of the oldest human ancestors, among them "Lucy", 3.2 million years old.

periods.name: Dʿmt
periods.note: The kingdom of Dʿmt, with its temple at Yeha, wrote in a South Arabian script and traded across the Red Sea.

periods.name: Kingdom of Aksum
periods.note: Aksum traded ivory and gold through the port of Adulis, minted its own coins and raised giant stone stelae. King Ezana became Christian around 340, and Aksum sheltered early followers of Muhammad.

periods.name: Zagwe dynasty
periods.note: From the 10th century power moved south from Aksum. The Agaw Zagwe kings ruled from Roha, renamed Lalibela after the king who had eleven churches carved down into its rock around 1200.

periods.name: Solomonic Ethiopia
periods.note: Yekuno Amlak claimed descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba and founded a dynasty that lasted until 1974. Amda Seyon beat the Muslim sultanates, but in 1529–43 Ahmad Gragn of Adal nearly conquered the empire, until Portuguese musketeers helped save it; Oromo peoples then moved into the south and centre.

periods.name: Medri Bahri and Ottoman Massawa
periods.note: The Ottomans took the port of Massawa in 1557, while the highlands, Medri Bahri, the "land of the sea", were ruled by their own lord, the bahri negash; Egypt held Massawa from 1865.

periods.name: Italian Eritrea
periods.note: Italy proclaimed the colony in 1890 and built Asmara, now a World Heritage city of modernist buildings.

periods.name: British rule and federation
periods.note: Britain ran Eritrea after 1941; in 1952 the UN federated it with Ethiopia, which annexed it in 1962.

periods.name: War of independence
periods.note: Eritrean fronts fought Ethiopia for thirty years, the longest war in Africa's modern history.

periods.name: State of Eritrea
periods.note: Independent after a referendum in 1993 and ruled since by Isaias Afwerki; a border war with Ethiopia in 1998–2000 killed tens of thousands.

periods.name: Punt and the incense coast
periods.note: Egyptians sailed to the "land of Punt", on this coast or across the sea from it, for incense and myrrh; Greek and Roman traders later called at its ports.

periods.name: Cushitic herders and early Islam
periods.note: Somali herders spread over the land, and Islam came early to the ports of Zeila, Berbera and Mogadishu.

periods.name: Ajuran and Adal
periods.note: Mogadishu, which Ibn Battuta visited in 1331, grew rich on trade; the Ajuran sultanate ruled the south, and Adal, ruled from Zeila and Harar, fought Ethiopia under Ahmad Gragn.

periods.name: Sultanates and clans
periods.note: Clan sultanates such as the Geledi, Majeerteen and Hobyo ruled the interior and coast, while the sultans of Zanzibar held Mogadishu and the southern ports; Egypt held the northern coast and Harar from 1875.

periods.name: British and Italian Somaliland
periods.note: Britain took the north in 1884 and Italy the south from 1889; the "Mad Mullah", Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, fought the British for twenty years until 1920.

periods.name: Somali Republic
periods.note: The two colonies united at independence in 1960; Siad Barre seized power in 1969 and lost the Ogaden War with Ethiopia in 1977–78.

periods.name: Civil war and rebuilding
periods.note: The state collapsed in 1991 and Somaliland declared itself independent; a federal government has fought al-Shabaab since the 2000s.

periods.name: Afar and Issa lands
periods.note: Afar and Somali Issa herders lived here; the sultanates of Adal, Tadjourah and Aussa traded across the Gulf of Aden.

periods.name: French Somaliland
periods.note: France bought Obock in 1862 and founded Djibouti in 1888; the railway to Addis Ababa, finished in 1917, made it Ethiopia's port.

periods.name: Republic of Djibouti
periods.note: Independent in 1977, it hosts French, American, Chinese and Japanese military bases.

periods.name: Herders and farmers
periods.note: The shores of Lake Turkana hold some of the oldest human fossils; Cushitic and Nilotic herders and Bantu farmers later settled the land.

periods.name: Swahili coast
periods.note: Swahili trading towns, Lamu, Malindi, Mombasa and Gedi, grew rich on the Indian Ocean trade; Zheng He's Chinese fleet called at Malindi in 1418.

periods.name: Portuguese and Omani coast
periods.note: Vasco da Gama found a pilot at Malindi in 1498. Portugal built Fort Jesus at Mombasa in 1593 and lost it to Oman in 1698, and the coast passed to the sultans of Zanzibar.

periods.name: British East Africa
periods.note: Britain built the Uganda Railway from Mombasa, founding Nairobi in 1899, and gave the highlands to white settlers; the Mau Mau uprising of 1952–60 was crushed with mass detentions.

periods.name: Republic of Kenya
periods.note: Jomo Kenyatta led Kenya to independence in 1963; Daniel arap Moi ruled from 1978 to 2002, and a disputed election in 2007 set off deadly violence.

periods.name: Early peoples
periods.note: Olduvai Gorge holds stone tools nearly two million years old; Bantu farmers who worked iron settled the land in the last millennium BC.

periods.name: Swahili city-states
periods.note: Kilwa Kisiwani grew into the richest of the Swahili towns by controlling the gold trade of Sofala; Ibn Battuta admired it in 1331.

periods.name: Portuguese and Omani coast
periods.note: Portugal sacked Kilwa in 1505; Omani Arabs drove the Portuguese out by 1698 and ruled the coast.

periods.name: Sultanate of Zanzibar
periods.note: Sultan Said moved his capital from Muscat to Zanzibar in 1840. Its clove plantations and caravans to the interior ran on slavery, while Mirambo built a kingdom in Unyamwezi and Ngoni invaders settled in the south.

periods.name: German East Africa
periods.note: Germany took the mainland and crushed the Abushiri revolt and the Maji Maji rising of 1905–07. Zanzibar became British in 1890 and lost the shortest war in history to Britain in 1896.

periods.name: British Tanganyika
periods.note: Tanganyika was a British mandate after the First World War.

periods.name: United Republic of Tanzania
periods.note: Julius Nyerere led Tanganyika to independence in 1961 and joined it with Zanzibar in 1964; his ujamaa socialism grouped farmers into villages.

periods.name: Farmers and herders
periods.note: Bantu farmers and Nilotic herders settled around Lake Victoria, growing bananas and working iron.

periods.name: Great Lakes kingdoms
periods.note: Legend tells of the Chwezi rulers of Kitara; from its heir Bunyoro, Buganda rose by the 1700s to be the strongest kingdom, ruled by its kabaka. Kabaka Mutesa I welcomed Stanley and the missionaries in the 1870s.

periods.name: Uganda Protectorate
periods.note: Britain made Buganda a protectorate in 1894 and ruled the rest of the country through it.

periods.name: Republic of Uganda
periods.note: Independent in 1962; Idi Amin's rule from 1971 to 1979 killed perhaps 300,000, and Yoweri Museveni has ruled since 1986.

periods.name: Early peoples
periods.note: Twa hunters of the forest were joined by Bantu farmers, and later by cattle herders.

periods.name: Kingdom of Rwanda
periods.note: The mwami ruled a kingdom of Hutu farmers and Tutsi cattle herders that grew through the 1700s and 1800s, strongest under Kigeli IV Rwabugiri.

periods.name: German and Belgian rule
periods.note: Germany, then from 1916 Belgium, ruled through the Tutsi monarchy, and Belgium issued identity cards by ethnic group in 1933; the Hutu revolution of 1959 drove many Tutsi into exile.

periods.name: Republic of Rwanda
periods.note: In 1994 Hutu extremists murdered some 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu in a hundred days, until the Tutsi-led RPF took the country; Paul Kagame has led it since.

periods.name: Early peoples
periods.note: Twa hunters, then Bantu farmers and cattle herders.

periods.name: Kingdom of Burundi
periods.note: The mwami Ntare I founded the kingdom in the late 1600s; princes of the royal family, the ganwa, ruled its provinces.

periods.name: German and Belgian rule
periods.note: Part of German East Africa, then from 1916 of Belgian Ruanda-Urundi.

periods.name: Republic of Burundi
periods.note: Independent as a kingdom in 1962 and a republic from 1966; massacres in 1972 and a civil war from 1993 to 2005 set Hutu and Tutsi against each other.

periods.name: First settlers
periods.note: Sailors from Borneo crossed the Indian Ocean in the first millennium AD and, joined by Bantu Africans, became the Malagasy; legend remembers the Vazimba as the island's first people.

periods.name: Malagasy kingdoms
periods.note: Arab and Swahili traders called at the northern ports; the Sakalava built kingdoms in the west, the Betsimisaraka on the east coast and the Merina in the central highlands.

periods.name: Merina kingdom
periods.note: Andrianampoinimerina united Imerina from Antananarivo; his son Radama I, allied with Britain, conquered most of the island, and Queen Ranavalona I persecuted the Christians.

periods.name: French Madagascar
periods.note: France conquered the island in 1895 and abolished the monarchy; the uprising of 1947 was put down at the cost of tens of thousands of lives.

periods.name: Republic of Madagascar
periods.note: Independent in 1960; Didier Ratsiraka's socialist revolution of 1975 was followed by coups and disputed elections.

periods.name: Saharan herders
periods.note: When the Sahara was greener, herders and farmers left rock art and the stone villages of Dhar Tichitt, from around 2000 BC.

periods.name: Ghana Empire
periods.note: The Soninke kings of Wagadu, the Ghana Empire, grew rich on the Saharan gold trade; their capital is thought to have been Koumbi Saleh, in the far southeast of today's Mauritania.

periods.name: Almoravids and the caravan towns
periods.note: The Almoravid movement began among the Sanhaja Berbers of the western Sahara around 1040 and is said to have taken the Ghana capital in 1076; Chinguetti and Ouadane became caravan towns of scholars, and Mali ruled the south, with the trading town of Walata.

periods.name: Emirates of the Moors
periods.note: After the Char Bouba war of 1644–74 Arab warrior tribes ruled over Berber scholars. The emirates of Trarza, Brakna, Adrar and Tagant sold gum arabic to the French at Saint-Louis.

periods.name: French Mauritania
periods.note: France made Mauritania a protectorate in 1903 and a colony of French West Africa in 1920, ruled from Saint-Louis in Senegal.

periods.name: Islamic Republic of Mauritania
periods.note: Independent in 1960 under Moktar Ould Daddah; it fought the Polisario over Western Sahara until 1979, and in 1981 it became the last country to abolish slavery.

periods.name: Early peoples
periods.note: Farmers domesticated African rice in the inner Niger delta, and Jenne-jeno, founded around 250 BC, became one of the first towns south of the Sahara.

periods.name: Ghana Empire
periods.note: The Soninke kingdom of Wagadu, which Arab writers called Ghana after its king's title, grew rich by taxing the trade of Saharan salt for West African gold.

periods.name: Mali Empire
periods.note: Sundiata Keita beat the Sosso king at Kirina around 1235 and founded the Mali Empire. Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, with so much gold that he lowered its price in Cairo, made Mali famous, and Timbuktu became a city of scholars.

periods.name: Songhai Empire
periods.note: Sunni Ali took Timbuktu in 1468, and Askia Muhammad built the largest empire in West Africa's history; a Moroccan army with guns crushed it at Tondibi in 1591.

periods.name: Pashalik and Bambara kingdoms
periods.note: Moroccan soldiers, the Arma, ruled Timbuktu as pashas; Bambara kings ruled Ségou from the 1710s and Kaarta to its west, while Mali shrank to its Manding heartland.

periods.name: Toucouleur Empire
periods.note: The jihad leader El Hadj Umar Tall took Ségou in 1861, and his son Ahmadu ruled his empire until the French took it.

periods.name: French Sudan
periods.note: France conquered the land and ruled it as French Sudan, a colony of French West Africa.

periods.name: Republic of Mali
periods.note: Independent in 1960 under Modibo Keïta; Moussa Traoré's dictatorship fell in 1991, and since 2012 Tuareg and jihadist rebellions and coups have shaken the country.

periods.name: Early peoples
periods.note: The stone circles of Senegambia, raised from around the 3rd century BC, mark the graves of chiefs.

periods.name: Takrur
periods.note: Takrur, on the Senegal river, was one of the first West African kingdoms to become Muslim, in the 11th century; in the 13th it fell under Mali.

periods.name: Jolof Empire
periods.note: The Wolof empire of Jolof ruled the land between the Senegal and Gambia rivers until its coastal kingdoms broke away after 1549.

periods.name: Wolof kingdoms and the slave trade
periods.note: Kajoor, Bawol, Waalo and Siin ruled on their own; the French at Saint-Louis and on the island of Gorée bought slaves and gum.

periods.name: French Senegal
periods.note: Governor Faidherbe conquered the interior from 1854. Dakar became the capital of French West Africa, and its four communes sent the first black African deputy, Blaise Diagne, to Paris in 1914.

periods.name: Republic of Senegal
periods.note: The poet Léopold Sédar Senghor led Senegal from independence in 1960 to 1980; it has never had a coup.

periods.name: River kingdoms
periods.note: Mandinka kingdoms along the river paid tribute to Mali; the Portuguese, then the English and the French, came up it to trade for slaves.

periods.name: British Gambia
periods.note: Britain founded Bathurst (Banjul) in 1816 to stop the slave trade, and later ruled a narrow strip along the river.

periods.name: Republic of the Gambia
periods.note: Independent in 1965; Yahya Jammeh ruled from a coup in 1994 until he lost an election in 2016.

periods.name: Kaabu
periods.note: The Mandinka kingdom of Kaabu, first a province of Mali, ruled the land from the 13th century until 1867.

periods.name: Portuguese Guinea
periods.note: Portugal founded Cacheu in 1588 as a slave port but conquered the interior only in the 1910s; Amílcar Cabral's PAIGC fought for independence from 1963.

periods.name: Republic of Guinea-Bissau
periods.note: Portugal recognised independence in 1974; coups and a civil war in 1998–99 have marked it since.

periods.name: Mali and its heirs
periods.note: The heartland of Mali, and by tradition its capital Niani, lay in what is now northeastern Guinea; as Mali declined, Fulani herders moved into the Fouta Djallon highlands, and Susu and Baga peoples lived on the coast.

periods.name: Fouta Djallon and Samori
periods.note: Fulani Muslims declared a holy war in 1725 and founded an imamate ruled from Timbo. In the 1870s Samori Touré built the Wassoulou empire in the east and fought the French for seventeen years, until they caught him in 1898.

periods.name: French Guinea
periods.note: France ruled Guinea as a colony of French West Africa.

periods.name: Republic of Guinea
periods.note: Guinea alone voted No to de Gaulle's French Community in 1958 and became independent at once. Ahmed Sékou Touré ruled until 1984, and the army has seized power several times since, most recently in 2021.

periods.name: Peoples of the coast
periods.note: The Portuguese sailor Pedro de Sintra named the "lion mountains" in 1462; Temne and Mende peoples traded with Europeans, and Bunce Island became a slave fort.

periods.name: Colony and protectorate
periods.note: British abolitionists founded Freetown in 1787 for freed slaves from London, Nova Scotia and Jamaica, and the Royal Navy landed there the Africans it freed from slave ships; the interior became a protectorate in 1896.

periods.name: Republic of Sierra Leone
periods.note: Independent in 1961; the civil war of 1991–2002, fought over diamonds, was one of the cruellest of its time.

periods.name: Peoples of the Pepper Coast
periods.note: Kru, Bassa, Vai and Gola peoples traded malagueta pepper, the "grains of paradise", with European ships.

periods.name: Americo-Liberian republic
periods.note: The American Colonization Society settled freed African Americans at Monrovia from 1822; they declared Africa's first republic in 1847 and ruled the native peoples for over a century.

periods.name: Coups, civil wars and peace
periods.note: Samuel Doe's coup of 1980 ended settler rule; Charles Taylor's wars followed from 1989 to 2003, and in 2006 Ellen Johnson Sirleaf became Africa's first elected woman president.

periods.name: Forest and savanna peoples
periods.note: Mande traders reached the northern savanna from Mali; Akan, Kru and Senufo peoples farmed the forest and the north.

periods.name: Kong and the Baoulé
periods.note: The Dyula traders of Kong built a Muslim kingdom in the north around 1710, and Akan people led by Queen Abla Pokou founded the Baoulé kingdom; the French traded on the coast from 1843.

periods.name: French Côte d'Ivoire
periods.note: France made it a colony in 1893, and Samori burned Kong in 1897; cocoa and coffee plantations grew on forced labour.

periods.name: Republic of Côte d'Ivoire
periods.note: Félix Houphouët-Boigny ruled from 1960 to 1993 over the "Ivorian miracle"; civil wars broke out in 2002 and after the election of 2010.

periods.name: Early peoples
periods.note: The farmers of the Kintampo culture, from around 2500 BC, were among the first in West Africa to keep cattle and live in villages.

periods.name: Akan forest states
periods.note: Akan peoples mined the gold that gave the coast its European name; Bono-Manso and Begho traded it north to Mali, and in 1482 Portugal built Elmina castle.

periods.name: Asante Empire
periods.note: Osei Tutu united the Asante at Kumasi around 1701 around the Golden Stool; Asante sold gold and slaves and fought the Fante and the British for the coast.

periods.name: Gold Coast colony
periods.note: Britain made the coast a colony in 1874, exiled the Asantehene in 1896 and annexed Asante after the War of the Golden Stool in 1900; cocoa made the Gold Coast rich.

periods.name: Republic of Ghana
periods.note: Kwame Nkrumah led the first colony south of the Sahara to independence in 1957 and named it after the old empire; after coups, Jerry Rawlings brought back democracy in 1992.

periods.name: Ewe and Kabye peoples
periods.note: Ewe people settled the south after leaving Notsé in the 1600s; the coast was a slave-trading shore between the Gold Coast and Dahomey.

periods.name: German Togoland
periods.note: Germany made Togoland a "model colony" of railways and cash crops.

periods.name: French Togo
periods.note: Britain and France split Togoland in 1914; the British west joined Ghana in 1957, and the French east became Togo.

periods.name: Togolese Republic
periods.note: Independent in 1960; its first president, Sylvanus Olympio, was murdered in 1963, and Gnassingbé Eyadéma and then his son Faure have ruled since 1967.

periods.name: Allada, Whydah and Oyo
periods.note: The Aja kingdoms of Allada and Whydah sold slaves to European ships, under the shadow of Oyo to the north.

periods.name: Kingdom of Dahomey
periods.note: From Abomey, Dahomey conquered Allada in 1724 and Whydah in 1727 and became a great slave-trading state, with women soldiers, the Agojie, in its army; it paid tribute to Oyo until 1823.

periods.name: French Dahomey
periods.note: France conquered Dahomey in 1892–94 and exiled King Béhanzin.

periods.name: Dahomey and Benin
periods.note: Independent as Dahomey in 1960; after coups, Mathieu Kérékou's Marxist regime renamed it Benin in 1975, and in 1990 it led Africa back to multi-party democracy.

periods.name: Nok culture
periods.note: The Nok people of the central plateau smelted iron and made terracotta heads from around 1000 BC or earlier.

periods.name: Igbo-Ukwu, Ife and Kanem
periods.note: The bronzes of Igbo-Ukwu date from the 9th century, and Ile-Ife, holy city of the Yoruba, cast lifelike brass heads in the 12th to 15th centuries; Kanem's kings ruled the northeast.

periods.name: Kingdoms of the forest and savanna
periods.note: Benin's obas ruled a walled city famed for its bronzes, Oyo's cavalry built a Yoruba empire, and the Hausa city-states of Kano, Katsina and Zaria traded across the Sahara; the coast became a centre of the Atlantic slave trade.

periods.name: Sokoto Caliphate
periods.note: Usman dan Fodio's jihad of 1804 overthrew the Hausa kings and founded the Sokoto Caliphate, the largest state in 19th-century West Africa. Oyo fell apart in the Yoruba wars, Britain annexed Lagos in 1861 and sacked Benin City in 1897, carrying off its bronzes.

periods.name: British Nigeria
periods.note: Britain conquered Sokoto in 1903 and joined north and south as Nigeria in 1914, ruling through emirs and chiefs.

periods.name: Federal Republic of Nigeria
periods.note: Independent in 1960; the Biafran war of 1967–70 killed perhaps a million people, and the army ruled for most of the years until 1999. Nigeria is Africa's most populous country.

periods.name: Mossi kingdoms
periods.note: Mossi horsemen founded kingdoms by the 1400s; the Mogho Naaba of Ouagadougou, whose court ceremonies still go on, raided Timbuktu and held off Mali and Songhai.

periods.name: French Upper Volta
periods.note: France took Ouagadougou in 1896. Upper Volta was made a colony in 1919, divided among its neighbours in 1932 and remade in 1947.

periods.name: Upper Volta and Burkina Faso
periods.note: Independent in 1960; Captain Thomas Sankara renamed it Burkina Faso, "land of upright people", in 1984 and was killed in 1987. Jihadist war and coups have followed since 2015.

periods.name: Saharan herders
periods.note: The Aïr and the Ténéré were once green enough for cattle herders, who carved the giraffes of Dabous into the rock.

periods.name: Mali, Songhai, Kanem and the Hausa
periods.note: The river valley was ruled by Mali in the 1300s and then by the Songhai kingdom of Gao, which grew into an empire under Sunni Ali and Askia Muhammad; the east came under Kanem-Bornu and the Hausa states.

periods.name: Dendi and the Sahel sultanates
periods.note: After Morocco crushed Songhai in 1591 its princes held out in Dendi, down the Niger; the Tuareg sultanate of Agadez ruled the Aïr, Damagaram rose at Zinder, and the south came under the Sokoto Caliphate after 1804.

periods.name: French Niger
periods.note: The French conquest began with the murderous Voulet–Chanoine mission of 1899; Niger became a colony of French West Africa in 1922.

periods.name: Republic of Niger
periods.note: Independent in 1960; uranium mines, droughts and several coups, the latest in 2023.

periods.name: Lake Chad and the Sahel
periods.note: "Toumaï", a skull some seven million years old found in the Djurab desert in 2001, is among the oldest human ancestors known; Lake Chad was far larger then.

periods.name: Kanem
periods.note: The Sayfawa kings of Kanem ruled from Njimi, became Muslim in the 11th century and held the trade route north to Libya.

periods.name: Bornu, Bagirmi and Wadai
periods.note: The Sayfawa moved west to Bornu; Bagirmi and Wadai rose as slave-raiding sultanates, and in the 1890s the warlord Rabih az-Zubayr conquered Bornu.

periods.name: French Chad
periods.note: France beat Rabih at Kousséri in 1900 and ruled Chad as part of French Equatorial Africa; in 1940 its governor Félix Éboué was the first to rally to Free France.

periods.name: Republic of Chad
periods.note: Independent in 1960; civil wars from 1965, Libya's occupation of the Aouzou strip, Hissène Habré's dictatorship and three decades of Idriss Déby followed.

periods.name: Early peoples
periods.note: The Bantu languages are thought to have spread from the grasslands here, from around 3000 BC, over most of Africa south of the equator.

periods.name: Kingdoms and the coast
periods.note: Portuguese sailors named the Wouri estuary Rio dos Camarões, "river of prawns"; the Bamum and Bamileke kingdoms ruled the grasslands, and the Fulani emirate of Adamawa the north.

periods.name: German Kamerun
periods.note: Germany made Kamerun a colony in 1884.

periods.name: French and British Cameroons
periods.note: After the First World War France ruled most of it and Britain two strips along Nigeria; the UPC's rising against French rule was crushed in the 1950s and 60s.

periods.name: Republic of Cameroon
periods.note: French Cameroun became independent in 1960 and joined the southern British strip in 1961; Paul Biya has ruled since 1982, and an anglophone rebellion began in 2017.

periods.name: Savanna and forest peoples
periods.note: The megaliths of Bouar date from before 500 BC; Ubangian-speaking farmers, among them the Zande and the Banda, settled the land.

periods.name: Slave raiders
periods.note: Raiders from Bagirmi, Wadai and Darfur, and later Rabih az-Zubayr, emptied much of the land of its people.

periods.name: Ubangi-Shari
periods.note: France founded Bangui in 1889; concession companies forced the people to gather rubber, and the Kongo-Wara rebellion of 1928–31 was crushed.

periods.name: Central African Republic
periods.note: Independent in 1960; Jean-Bédel Bokassa crowned himself emperor in 1977, and coups and civil wars have followed.

periods.name: Portuguese islands
periods.note: Fernão do Pó sighted Bioko in 1472; Portugal held the islands, home of the Bubi people, until it traded them to Spain in 1778.

periods.name: Spanish Guinea
periods.note: Spain ruled Fernando Po (Bioko), with its cocoa plantations, and the mainland Río Muni.

periods.name: Republic of Equatorial Guinea
periods.note: Independent in 1968; Francisco Macías Nguema's terror drove a third of the people abroad, and his nephew Teodoro Obiang, who overthrew him in 1979, has ruled on oil ever since.

periods.name: Forest peoples
periods.note: Pygmy hunter-gatherers were joined by Bantu farmers who worked iron.

periods.name: Coastal trade
periods.note: Portuguese sailors reached the estuary in 1472 and named it after a hooded cloak, gabão; the Mpongwe traded ivory and slaves.

periods.name: French Gabon
periods.note: France signed treaties from 1839 and founded Libreville in 1849 for freed slaves; the Fang moved in from the north, and Albert Schweitzer opened his hospital at Lambaréné in 1913.

periods.name: Gabonese Republic
periods.note: Omar Bongo ruled for 41 years on oil wealth and his son Ali for 14, until a coup in 2023.

periods.name: Forest peoples
periods.note: Hunter-gatherers of the rainforest were joined by Bantu farmers who worked iron.

periods.name: Loango, Kongo and Teke
periods.note: The Vili kingdom of Loango traded on the coast, through which the Atlantic slave trade passed, and the Teke kingdom ruled the plateaus north of the Pool.

periods.name: French Congo
periods.note: The Teke king Makoko signed a treaty with Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza in 1880. Brazzaville became the capital of French Equatorial Africa and, in 1940, of de Gaulle's Free France.

periods.name: Republic of the Congo
periods.note: Independent in 1960; a Marxist people's republic from 1969 to 1991 and civil wars in the 1990s, with Denis Sassou Nguesso in power for most of the years since 1979.

periods.name: Forest and savanna peoples
periods.note: Hunter-gatherers of the rainforest were joined by Bantu farmers, who spread iron-working and farming across the Congo basin from around 1000 BC.

periods.name: Kingdoms of the savanna
periods.note: The Kongo kingdom ruled the lower river and the Teke the Pool, where Kinshasa began as a Teke market town; inland lay the Luba and Lunda empires and the Kuba, famed for their raffia cloth and carvings, and in the 1800s the trader-kings Msiri and Tippu Tip carved out states in the east.

periods.name: Congo Free State
periods.note: King Leopold II of Belgium ruled the Congo as his own property; forced rubber collection, enforced with hostages and severed hands, killed millions until an international outcry.

periods.name: Belgian Congo
periods.note: Belgium took the colony over in 1908 and ran it with the Church and the mining companies; the copper of Katanga and the uranium of the first atomic bombs came from here.

periods.name: Independence and Mobutu's Zaire
periods.note: Independence in 1960 brought Katanga's secession and the murder of Patrice Lumumba; Mobutu Sese Seko seized power in 1965, renamed the country Zaire and plundered it for 32 years.

periods.name: Democratic Republic of the Congo
periods.note: Laurent Kabila overthrew Mobutu in 1997; the wars of 1996–2003 drew in nine African countries and killed millions, and fighting goes on in the east.

periods.name: Early peoples
periods.note: Khoisan hunters, then Bantu farmers, who came in the first millennium AD.

periods.name: Kongo and Ndongo
periods.note: The Kingdom of Kongo, ruled from Mbanza Kongo, met the Portuguese in 1483; its king Afonso I became Christian and wrote to Portugal's king against the slave trade. To the south lay Ndongo, whose king's title, ngola, gave Angola its name.

periods.name: Portuguese Angola and Queen Njinga
periods.note: Portugal founded Luanda in 1575 and made it the greatest slave port of Africa, shipping millions to Brazil; Queen Njinga of Ndongo and Matamba fought the Portuguese for forty years.

periods.name: Conquest of the interior
periods.note: After the Berlin Conference Portugal conquered the interior, crushing the Ovimbundu kingdom of Mbailundu in 1902 and ending the Kongo kingdom in 1914.

periods.name: Colonial Angola
periods.note: Under Salazar's Estado Novo, Portuguese settlers poured in and Africans were forced to grow cotton and coffee.

periods.name: War of independence
periods.note: Risings in 1961 began a guerrilla war by the MPLA, FNLA and UNITA that ended with Portugal's revolution of 1974.

periods.name: Civil war
periods.note: Independence in 1975 brought civil war between the MPLA, backed by Cuba and the Soviet Union, and UNITA, backed by South Africa and the United States, until Jonas Savimbi was killed in 2002.

periods.name: Peace and oil
periods.note: Oil made Luanda one of the most expensive cities in the world, under José Eduardo dos Santos until 2017.

periods.name: Early peoples
periods.note: The Kabwe skull, of an early human some 300,000 years old, was found here; Bantu farmers and iron-workers spread from the first millennium AD.

periods.name: Lozi, Kazembe and Bemba
periods.note: The Lozi ruled the Zambezi floodplain, the Kazembe kingdom, an offshoot of the Lunda, the Luapula valley, and the Bemba the northeast; David Livingstone reached the Victoria Falls in 1855.

periods.name: Northern Rhodesia
periods.note: Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company took the land by treaties from 1890, and Britain ruled it from 1924; its Copperbelt became one of the world's great copper fields.

periods.name: Republic of Zambia
periods.note: Kenneth Kaunda led Zambia from independence in 1964 until 1991, as a one-party state from 1972, when free elections returned.

periods.name: Maravi kingdoms
periods.note: The Maravi confederacy of the Chewa ruled around the lake from the 1400s. In the 1800s Ngoni invaders and Yao and Swahili slave traders raided it, and Livingstone reached the lake in 1859.

periods.name: Nyasaland
