periods.note: Britain made it a protectorate in 1891; John Chilembwe led a rising against it in 1915.

periods.name: Republic of Malawi
periods.note: Hastings Banda ruled from independence in 1964 until 1994, from 1971 as "president for life".

periods.name: Early peoples and Sofala
periods.note: Bantu farmers settled the land in the first millennium AD, and Swahili traders at Sofala shipped the gold of the Zimbabwe plateau.

periods.name: Portuguese forts and prazos
periods.note: Vasco da Gama landed in 1498. Portugal held the coast and the Zambezi valley, where its settlers ruled great estates called prazos, and only conquered the Gaza kingdom of the south in 1895.

periods.name: Portuguese colony
periods.note: Chartered companies ran much of the colony on forced labour, and many men went to work in South Africa's gold mines.

periods.name: War of independence
periods.note: Frelimo, led by Eduardo Mondlane and then Samora Machel, fought Portugal from 1964 until its revolution of 1974.

periods.name: People's Republic and peace
periods.note: Independent in 1975 under Samora Machel; a civil war against Renamo, backed by Rhodesia and South Africa, killed about a million people until peace in 1992.

periods.name: Early peoples
periods.note: San hunters painted the rocks of the Matobo hills; Bantu farmers arrived in the first millennium AD.

periods.name: Great Zimbabwe
periods.note: Shona kings built Great Zimbabwe, the largest stone ruins south of the Sahara, and traded gold to the Swahili coast.

periods.name: Mutapa and Rozvi
periods.note: The Mutapa kingdom ruled the north and traded with the Portuguese, who tried and failed to conquer it; the Rozvi Changamire dynasty drove them from the plateau in the 1690s.

periods.name: Ndebele kingdom
periods.note: Mzilikazi's Ndebele, fleeing the Zulu, settled in the southwest and ruled from Bulawayo; his son Lobengula signed away mineral rights to Cecil Rhodes in 1888.

periods.name: Rhodesia
periods.note: Rhodes's company occupied Mashonaland in 1890 and crushed the Ndebele and Shona risings. White settlers ran the colony, declared independence from Britain in 1965 and fought a bush war against African guerrillas.

periods.name: Republic of Zimbabwe
periods.note: Independent in 1980 under Robert Mugabe, who ruled until 2017; massacres in Matabeleland, land seizures and hyperinflation marked his rule.

periods.name: San and Tswana
periods.note: San hunters have lived in the Kalahari for tens of thousands of years; Tswana chiefdoms, among them the Bangwato, settled the east from the 1700s.

periods.name: Bechuanaland Protectorate
periods.note: Three Tswana chiefs, Khama III among them, went to London in 1895 to keep their land out of Cecil Rhodes's hands, and Britain kept it as a protectorate.

periods.name: Republic of Botswana
periods.note: Seretse Khama led it to independence in 1966; diamonds found in 1967 made one of the world's poorest countries one of Africa's richest, and it has held free elections ever since.

periods.name: San, Nama and Herero
periods.note: San hunters painted the rocks of the Brandberg; Nama and Herero herders and Ovambo farmers later shared the land.

periods.name: German South West Africa
periods.note: Germany took the land in 1884; its war against the Herero and Nama in 1904–08, with the order to exterminate the Herero, is called the first genocide of the 20th century.

periods.name: South African rule
periods.note: South Africa conquered it in 1915 and ruled it under a League of Nations mandate, imposing apartheid; SWAPO fought for independence from 1966.

periods.name: Republic of Namibia
periods.note: Independent in 1990 under Sam Nujoma; Walvis Bay joined it in 1994.

periods.name: San and Khoikhoi
periods.note: Caves on the Cape coast hold some of the oldest signs of modern human thought, such as the engraved ochre of Blombos, 75,000 years old; San hunters and later Khoikhoi herders lived here.

periods.name: Bantu farmers and Mapungubwe
periods.note: Bantu-speaking farmers settled the east from about AD 300; the kingdom of Mapungubwe on the Limpopo, around 1075–1220, traded gold and ivory to the Indian Ocean.

periods.name: Dutch Cape Colony
periods.note: Jan van Riebeeck founded Cape Town for the Dutch East India Company in 1652. Settlers and slaves from Asia and Africa followed, and the frontier pushed into Khoikhoi and Xhosa lands.

periods.name: British Cape and the Great Trek
periods.note: Britain took the Cape in 1806. Shaka built the Zulu kingdom in the 1810s and 1820s, and from 1835 Boer trekkers left the Cape to found Natal, the Orange Free State and the Transvaal.

periods.name: Diamonds, gold and war
periods.note: Diamonds at Kimberley and gold on the Witwatersrand drew Britain in: it broke the Zulu kingdom in 1879 and conquered the Boer republics in the war of 1899–1902, in which some 26,000 Boer women and children died in British camps.

periods.name: Union of South Africa
periods.note: The four colonies united as a British dominion in 1910; the ANC was founded in 1912, and the Natives Land Act of 1913 kept most of the land for whites.

periods.name: Apartheid
periods.note: The National Party made racial segregation law. Police killed 69 protesters at Sharpeville in 1960, Nelson Mandela was jailed for 27 years, and the Soweto uprising of 1976 began the final struggle.

periods.name: Democratic South Africa
periods.note: The first free elections, in 1994, made Mandela president, and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission heard the crimes of apartheid.

periods.name: Kingdom of Moshoeshoe
periods.note: Moshoeshoe I gathered refugees of the wars of the 1820s on the mountain fortress of Thaba Bosiu and founded the Basotho nation.

periods.name: Basutoland
periods.note: Moshoeshoe asked Britain for protection from the Boers in 1868; Basutoland stayed a British protectorate, kept out of the Union of South Africa.

periods.name: Kingdom of Lesotho
periods.note: Independent in 1966, a mountain kingdom wholly surrounded by South Africa.

periods.name: Swazi kingdom
periods.note: Ngwane III led the Dlamini clan here around 1745; Sobhuza I and Mswati II built the Swazi kingdom, and Mswati gave it his name.

periods.name: British protectorate
periods.note: Britain ruled it after the Anglo-Boer War, keeping the king on his throne.

periods.name: Kingdom of Eswatini
periods.note: Independent in 1968 under Sobhuza II, who reigned for 82 years; his son Mswati III, an absolute monarch, renamed it Eswatini in 2018.

periods.name: Archaic peoples
periods.note: People had come from Asia across the Bering land bridge in the last Ice Age, and Clovis hunters chased mammoths around 11,000 BC. Archaic peoples raised the mounds of Watson Brake around 3500 BC and the great earthworks of Poverty Point around 1600 BC.

periods.name: Woodland cultures
periods.note: The Adena and then the Hopewell peoples of the Ohio valley built burial mounds and great earthworks, and traded copper from Lake Superior, obsidian from the Rockies and shells from the Gulf of Mexico.

periods.name: Ancestral Puebloans and Mississippians
periods.note: In the Southwest the Ancestral Puebloans built the great houses of Chaco Canyon and the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde. In the Mississippi valley maize farmers built Cahokia, a town of perhaps 15,000 people around its great mound, around 1050–1200.

periods.name: Native nations and Spanish explorers
periods.note: Hundreds of Native nations lived here, from the Haudenosaunee confederacy to the Pueblos. Spaniards explored from Florida to Kansas and founded St Augustine in 1565, and European diseases killed most of the people.

periods.name: Colonial America
periods.note: England founded Jamestown in 1607 and the Pilgrims Plymouth in 1620; the Dutch held New Amsterdam until 1664. By 1732 there were thirteen British colonies along the coast, while France claimed the Mississippi and Spain Florida and the Southwest.

periods.name: Independence and the early republic
periods.note: The colonies declared independence on 4 July 1776 and won it at Yorktown in 1781. The republic bought Louisiana from France in 1803 and took the Southwest from Mexico in 1848, while the Native nations were driven west on the Trail of Tears.

periods.name: Civil War and Reconstruction
periods.note: Eleven slave states seceded as the Confederacy; the Union's victory in 1865, at the cost of some 620,000 lives, ended slavery, and Reconstruction briefly gave the freed people the vote.

periods.name: Industrial and world power
periods.note: Railways, steel and immigrants made the United States the largest economy by 1900. It took Hawaii and the Philippines in 1898, joined the First World War in 1917, lived through the Depression and the New Deal, and fought the Second World War from 1941.

periods.name: Cold War superpower
periods.note: The United States led the West against the Soviet Union, from the Marshall Plan to Korea and Vietnam; the civil rights movement ended legal segregation in the 1960s, and Apollo 11 landed on the Moon in 1969.

periods.name: Since the Cold War
periods.note: The only superpower after 1991; the attacks of 11 September 2001 led to wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, and Barack Obama became the first black president in 2009.

periods.name: First peoples
periods.note: People came from Asia during the last Ice Age; as the ice melted, hunters and fishers spread over the land, and the first Arctic peoples arrived around 2500 BC.

periods.name: Paleo-Inuit and Woodland peoples
periods.note: The Dorset people hunted seals across the Arctic; in the south, Woodland peoples made pottery, built burial mounds and fished the Great Lakes.

periods.name: Thule and the Norse
periods.note: Around 1000 Norse Greenlanders led by Leif Erikson landed at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland. The Thule people, ancestors of the Inuit, spread east from Alaska and replaced the Dorset, Iroquoian farmers grew maize by the St Lawrence, and John Cabot reached Newfoundland in 1497.

periods.name: New France
periods.note: Jacques Cartier claimed the St Lawrence for France in 1534, and Champlain founded Quebec in 1608; French fur traders and missionaries allied with the Wendat and Algonquin. Britain chartered the Hudson's Bay Company in 1670 and took Acadia in 1713.

periods.name: British North America
periods.note: Britain took New France in 1763. Loyalists fleeing the American Revolution settled Ontario and the Maritimes, Canadians beat off American invasions in 1812–14, and the rebellions of 1837–38 led to self-government.

periods.name: Dominion of Canada
periods.note: Confederation in 1867 made Canada a self-governing dominion. It bought Rupert's Land, hanged the Métis leader Louis Riel in 1885, built the railway to the Pacific, and lost 60,000 men in the First World War, winning fame at Vimy Ridge.

periods.name: Modern Canada
periods.note: The Statute of Westminster made Canada fully independent in 1931; Newfoundland joined in 1949, the Charter of Rights came with the Constitution of 1982, and Quebec voted narrowly to stay in 1995.

periods.name: Archaic farmers
periods.note: Maize had been bred from wild teosinte by about 7000 BC; farmers in the valleys of Oaxaca and Tehuacán grew it with beans and squash.

periods.name: Olmec
periods.note: The Olmecs of the Gulf coast, Mesoamerica's first civilisation, carved colossal stone heads at San Lorenzo and La Venta.

periods.name: Classic Mesoamerica
periods.note: Teotihuacan, with its Pyramids of the Sun and Moon, was one of the largest cities in the world around AD 500; the Zapotecs ruled Oaxaca from Monte Albán, and the Maya built city-states in the south and east.

periods.name: Toltecs and city-states
periods.note: After Teotihuacan fell, Tula became the capital of the Toltecs, remembered by the Aztecs as masters of every art; El Tajín flourished on the Gulf, Mixtec lords ruled Oaxaca, and Mogollon villagers farmed the north.

periods.name: Aztec Empire
periods.note: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco in 1325 and, through the Triple Alliance of 1428, built an empire that taxed most of central Mexico; the Purépecha of Michoacán held them off.

periods.name: New Spain
periods.note: Hernán Cortés and his Tlaxcalan allies took Tenochtitlan in 1521, and Mexico City was built on its ruins as the capital of New Spain. Epidemics killed most of the native people, and silver from Zacatecas and Guanajuato flowed to Spain and China.

periods.name: Independence and the Reform
periods.note: Miguel Hidalgo's revolt of 1810 led to independence in 1821. Mexico lost Texas in 1836 and half its land to the United States in 1848, and Benito Juárez's liberals beat the French-backed emperor Maximilian in 1867.

periods.name: Porfiriato and Revolution
periods.note: Porfirio Díaz ruled for 35 years; the Revolution of 1910–20, the war of Madero, Zapata, Villa and Carranza, killed perhaps a million people.

periods.name: Rule of the PRI
periods.note: The party later called the PRI ruled for 71 years; Lázaro Cárdenas nationalised oil in 1938, and NAFTA came in 1994.

periods.name: Democratic Mexico
periods.note: Vicente Fox's election in 2000 ended one-party rule; the drug war since 2006 has cost hundreds of thousands of lives.

periods.name: Early Maya
periods.note: Maya farmers settled the lowlands and highlands, and by 600 BC they were building cities such as Nakbe.

periods.name: Preclassic Maya
periods.note: El Mirador, in the Petén forest, raised some of the largest pyramids ever built, and the Maya developed their script and calendar.

periods.name: Classic Maya
periods.note: Tikal, Calakmul and dozens of rival city-states, ruled by holy kings, raised temples and dated their monuments in the Long Count calendar; most were abandoned in the 9th century.

periods.name: Postclassic Maya
periods.note: Chichén Itzá and then Mayapán led the north, in Yucatán; in the highlands the Kʼicheʼ and Kaqchikel kingdoms fought for power, and the Kʼicheʼ book of creation, the Popol Vuh, was written down after the conquest.

periods.name: Spanish Guatemala
periods.note: Pedro de Alvarado conquered the highlands in 1524, and the Captaincy General of Guatemala ruled Central America from Antigua; the last independent Maya city, Nojpetén of the Itza, fell in 1697.

periods.name: Independence and the liberal republic
periods.note: Independent in 1821 and part of the Central American Federation until 1839, Guatemala was ruled by strongmen such as Rafael Carrera and Jorge Ubico, while the United Fruit Company grew powerful.

periods.name: Revolution, coup and civil war
periods.note: The democratic revolution of 1944 ended in a coup backed by the CIA in 1954; the civil war of 1960–96 killed some 200,000 people, most of them Maya.

periods.name: Peace
periods.note: Peace accords ended the war in 1996.

periods.name: Maya cities
periods.note: Caracol, Lamanai, Altun Ha and Xunantunich were Maya cities; Caracol beat Tikal in war in 562.

periods.name: Spanish claims
periods.note: Spain claimed the land from the 1540s and sent friars, but the Maya of Tipu drove them out in 1638.

periods.name: Baymen and British Honduras
periods.note: British log-cutters, the Baymen, settled the coast in the 1600s and beat off a Spanish attack at St George's Caye in 1798; it became the colony of British Honduras in 1862.

periods.name: Belize
periods.note: Independent in 1981; Guatemala's claim to the country is before the International Court of Justice.

periods.name: Copán and the chiefdoms
periods.note: Copán, in the west, was one of the great Classic Maya cities, famed for its hieroglyphic stairway; Lenca and other peoples lived in the rest of the land.

periods.name: Spanish Honduras
periods.note: Spaniards conquered the land against the Lenca chief Lempira, who died in 1537; the British and the Miskito held the Caribbean coast.

periods.name: Republic of Honduras
periods.note: Independent in 1821 and from the Central American Federation in 1838; American banana companies made it the first "banana republic".

periods.name: Democratic Honduras
periods.note: Civilian rule returned in 1982; a coup ousted President Zelaya in 2009.

periods.name: Maya and Pipil
periods.note: Maya villages such as Joya de Cerén, buried by a volcano around 600, and later the Nahua-speaking Pipil kingdom of Cuzcatlan.

periods.name: Spanish rule
periods.note: Pedro de Alvarado's men conquered Cuzcatlan from 1524; indigo plantations made the colony's wealth.

periods.name: Republic of El Salvador
periods.note: Coffee planters ruled the republic; in 1932 the army killed thousands of peasants in La Matanza.

periods.name: Civil war and peace
periods.note: Archbishop Óscar Romero was murdered in 1980, and a civil war killed some 75,000 people until peace in 1992.

periods.name: Chiefdoms
periods.note: Nicarao and Chorotega chiefdoms lived by the great lakes, and the Miskito and Mayangna on the Caribbean coast.

periods.name: Spanish Nicaragua
periods.note: Francisco Hernández de Córdoba founded Granada and León in 1524; Britain kept a protectorate over the Miskito on the Mosquito Coast.

periods.name: Republic and American intervention
periods.note: The American adventurer William Walker made himself president in 1856; US Marines occupied the country from 1912 to 1933, fought by Augusto Sandino.

periods.name: Somoza dynasty
periods.note: The Somoza family ruled for 43 years, until the Sandinista revolution of 1979.

periods.name: Sandinistas and after
periods.note: The Sandinistas fought the American-backed Contras in the 1980s; Daniel Ortega returned to power in 2007.

periods.name: Chiefdoms
periods.note: The Diquís culture of the south carved the famous stone spheres; Huetar and other chiefdoms lived on the central plateau.

periods.name: Spanish Costa Rica
periods.note: Columbus landed in 1502; it was a poor, remote province of farmers, settled from Cartago in 1563.

periods.name: Republic of Costa Rica
periods.note: Coffee and then bananas brought wealth after independence.

periods.name: Second Republic
periods.note: José Figueres abolished the army after the civil war of 1948; Costa Rica has been a stable democracy since, and Óscar Arias won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1987.

periods.name: Chiefdoms
periods.note: Cueva and Guna chiefdoms lived on the isthmus, and the Coclé culture made fine gold work.

periods.name: Spanish Panama
periods.note: Balboa crossed the isthmus and saw the Pacific in 1513. Panama City, founded in 1519, shipped Peru's silver to Spain, and the buccaneer Henry Morgan sacked it in 1671.

periods.name: Part of Colombia
periods.note: Panama joined Gran Colombia in 1821; the Panama Railroad of 1855 carried gold-rush travellers, and a French canal company failed in the 1880s.

periods.name: Republic and the canal
periods.note: The United States backed Panama's break from Colombia in 1903 and built the canal, opened in 1914, keeping the Canal Zone; it invaded in 1989 to depose Manuel Noriega.

periods.name: Panama
periods.note: Panama took over the canal on 31 December 1999.

periods.name: Taíno and Guanahatabey
periods.note: Taíno farmers lived on most of the island, and the Guanahatabey in the far west.

periods.name: Spanish Cuba
periods.note: Diego Velázquez conquered Cuba in 1511, and the cacique Hatuey was burned alive. Havana guarded the treasure fleets, slaves grew sugar from the 1790s, and wars of independence began in 1868 and 1895.

periods.name: American occupation and the republic
periods.note: The United States intervened in 1898 and ruled until 1902; the Platt Amendment, the Guantánamo base and dictators such as Gerardo Machado and Fulgencio Batista followed.

periods.name: Revolutionary Cuba
periods.note: Fidel Castro's revolution won in 1959. Cuba allied with the Soviet Union, survived the Bay of Pigs invasion and the missile crisis of 1962, and is still ruled by the Communist Party.

periods.name: Taíno Hispaniola
periods.note: Taíno chiefdoms ruled the island, which they called Ayiti, "land of mountains".

periods.name: Spanish Hispaniola
periods.note: Columbus built La Navidad on this coast in 1492; within decades the Taíno were nearly wiped out.

periods.name: Saint-Domingue
periods.note: Spain ceded the west to France in 1697. Saint-Domingue, with half a million slaves, became the richest colony in the world, until the slave revolt of 1791 led by Toussaint Louverture.

periods.name: Independent Haiti
periods.note: Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared the first black republic in 1804, after the only successful slave revolution in history; France forced Haiti to pay it a huge indemnity in 1825.

periods.name: American occupation and the Duvaliers
periods.note: US Marines occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934; François "Papa Doc" Duvalier and his son ruled by terror from 1957 to 1986.

periods.name: Since the Duvaliers
periods.note: Coups, Jean-Bertrand Aristide's presidencies, the earthquake of 2010 that killed some 200,000, and gang rule after President Moïse was murdered in 2021.

periods.name: Taíno Hispaniola
periods.note: Taíno chiefdoms, the five cacicazgos, ruled Hispaniola; the map calls the peoples before them Ciboney.

periods.name: Spanish Santo Domingo
periods.note: Columbus landed in 1492; Santo Domingo, founded in 1496, is the oldest European city in the Americas, with their first cathedral and university.

periods.name: Haitian rule and independence
periods.note: Ceded to France in 1795 and ruled by Haiti from 1822, the Dominicans declared independence in 1844; Spain took the country back from 1861 to 1865.

periods.name: Occupation and Trujillo
periods.note: US Marines occupied it from 1916 to 1924. Rafael Trujillo ruled by terror from 1930 until he was shot in 1961, and ordered the massacre of thousands of Haitians in 1937.

periods.name: Dominican Republic
periods.note: After civil war and an American invasion in 1965, Joaquín Balaguer ruled for 22 years; elections have been free since 1996.

periods.name: Taíno Xaymaca
periods.note: Taíno farmers called the island Xaymaca, "land of wood and water".

periods.name: Spanish Jamaica
periods.note: Columbus landed in 1494, and Spain kept the island as a cattle ranch.

periods.name: British Jamaica
periods.note: England took Jamaica in 1655. Port Royal was a buccaneers' haven, sugar grew on the labour of slaves, Maroons held the mountains, and the Baptist War of 1831 hastened the end of slavery in 1834.
states: ~United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

periods.name: Jamaica
periods.note: Independent in 1962; Bob Marley's reggae carried its music around the world.

periods.name: Taíno Borikén
periods.note: Taíno farmers called the island Borikén.

periods.name: Spanish Puerto Rico
periods.note: Juan Ponce de León founded the first settlement in 1508; San Juan's fortress, El Morro, guarded the Caribbean.

periods.name: American Puerto Rico
periods.note: Taken by the United States in 1898; Puerto Ricans became American citizens in 1917, and the island has been a self-governing commonwealth since 1952.

periods.name: Early peoples
periods.note: The people of San Jacinto made some of the oldest pottery in the Americas, around 4000 BC.

periods.name: Chiefdoms of gold
periods.note: The San Agustín culture carved giant stone statues; later the Muisca of the highlands, whose gilded chief's offering at Lake Guatavita began the legend of El Dorado, and the Tairona of the Sierra Nevada worked gold.

periods.name: New Granada
periods.note: Spaniards founded Santa Marta in 1525, Cartagena in 1533 and Bogotá in 1538; New Granada became a viceroyalty of its own in 1717.

periods.name: Independence and Gran Colombia
periods.note: Simón Bolívar won the battle of Boyacá in 1819 and founded Gran Colombia with Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama, which broke apart in 1830–31.

periods.name: Republic of Colombia
periods.note: Liberals and Conservatives fought civil wars, the worst the Thousand Days' War of 1899–1902, and Panama broke away in 1903.

periods.name: La Violencia and the armed conflict
periods.note: The murder of Jorge Eliécer Gaitán in 1948 began La Violencia. Guerrillas such as the FARC, paramilitaries and drug cartels like Pablo Escobar's fought for decades.

periods.name: Peace
periods.note: A peace agreement with the FARC was signed in 2016.

periods.name: Early peoples
periods.note: Carib and Arawak peoples lived on the coast and the plains, and the Timoto-Cuica farmed terraces in the Andes.

periods.name: Spanish Venezuela
periods.note: Columbus reached the coast in 1498, and explorers named it "little Venice" after villages built on stilts; the German bankers of the Welser family ruled it from 1528 to 1546. It was governed from Santo Domingo, then from Bogotá after 1739.

periods.name: Independence
periods.note: Venezuela declared independence in 1811; Simón Bolívar, born in Caracas, won it at Carabobo in 1821.

periods.name: Republic and caudillos
periods.note: Strongmen ruled after Venezuela left Gran Colombia in 1830; under Juan Vicente Gómez, from 1908 to 1935, oil was found and Venezuela became a great exporter.

periods.name: Democracy and Chávez
periods.note: Democracy from 1958; Hugo Chávez's "Bolivarian revolution" from 1999, then economic collapse under Nicolás Maduro drove millions to emigrate.

periods.name: Valdivia and Chorrera
periods.note: The Valdivia villagers of the coast made some of the oldest pottery in the Americas, from around 3500 BC; the Chorrera potters followed them.

periods.name: Regional chiefdoms
periods.note: Seafaring Manteño traders sailed the Pacific coast on balsa rafts, and the Cañari and Caranqui ruled the highlands.

periods.name: Inca rule
periods.note: Topa Inca conquered the land in the 1460s; Atahualpa, born in the north, won the war of succession against his brother Huáscar just as the Spanish came.

periods.name: Spanish Quito
periods.note: Sebastián de Benalcázar founded Spanish Quito in 1534; its Royal Audiencia was famed for its school of religious art.

periods.name: Republic of Ecuador
periods.note: Sucre won independence at Pichincha in 1822, and Ecuador left Gran Colombia in 1830; Eloy Alfaro's Liberal Revolution of 1895 split Church and state, and a war of 1941 lost Amazon lands to Peru.

periods.name: Democratic Ecuador
periods.note: Civilian rule returned in 1979; Ecuador adopted the US dollar in 2000.

periods.name: Norte Chico
periods.note: Caral and the other towns of the Norte Chico, from around 3000 BC, built pyramids as old as Egypt's; they were the oldest civilisation in the Americas.

periods.name: Chavín
periods.note: The temple of Chavín de Huántar spread the worship of jaguar and serpent gods across the Andes, and the Paracas culture wove fine textiles on the south coast.

periods.name: Moche and Nazca
periods.note: The Moche of the north coast built adobe pyramids and buried the Lord of Sipán in gold; the Nazca drew giant lines in the desert.

periods.name: Wari
periods.note: The Wari built the first Andean empire from Ayacucho, with roads and towns that the Incas later followed.

periods.name: Chimú and regional states
periods.note: The Chimú ruled the north coast from Chan Chan, the largest adobe city in the Americas.

periods.name: Inca Empire
periods.note: Pachacuti made Cusco the capital of Tawantinsuyu in 1438; within a century the Incas ruled from Ecuador to central Chile, joined by 40,000 km of roads, and built Machu Picchu.

periods.name: Spanish Peru
periods.note: Francisco Pizarro seized Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532. Lima, founded in 1535, ruled Spanish South America, the silver of Potosí paid for Spain's wars, and Túpac Amaru II led a great revolt in 1780.

periods.name: Republic of Peru
periods.note: San Martín declared independence in 1821, and Sucre won it at Ayacucho in 1824; Peru lost its southern nitrate provinces to Chile in the War of the Pacific of 1879–84.

periods.name: Military rule, Shining Path and after
periods.note: The left-wing military government of 1968–80 gave land to the peasants; the Shining Path's war killed some 70,000 people, and Alberto Fujimori, who crushed it, ruled from 1990 to 2000.

periods.name: Wankarani and Chiripa
periods.note: Villagers of the Wankarani and Chiripa cultures herded llamas and farmed by Lake Titicaca.

periods.name: Tiwanaku
periods.note: Tiwanaku, near Lake Titicaca, with its Gateway of the Sun, led the southern Andes for five centuries.

periods.name: Aymara kingdoms
periods.note: Aymara kingdoms such as the Lupaca and the Colla ruled the high plain.

periods.name: Inca rule
periods.note: The Incas conquered the Aymara kingdoms in the 15th century, and the land became the southeast of their empire, Collasuyu.

periods.name: Upper Peru
periods.note: Potosí, founded below a mountain of silver in 1545, became one of the largest cities in the world, its mines worked by forced Indian labour, the mita.
states: ~Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata

periods.name: Republic of Bolivia
periods.note: Named after Simón Bolívar in 1825, Bolivia lost its coast to Chile in 1879–84 and the Chaco to Paraguay in 1932–35.

periods.name: Revolution and after
periods.note: The revolution of 1952 gave land and the vote to the Indian majority; Evo Morales, the first indigenous president, ruled from 2006 to 2019.

periods.name: Chinchorro
periods.note: The Chinchorro fishers of the Atacama coast mummified their dead from around 5000 BC, two thousand years before the Egyptians.

periods.name: Mapuche and the Inca
periods.note: The Mapuche farmed the south, and stopped the Incas, who ruled the north, at the Maule river.

periods.name: Spanish Chile
periods.note: Pedro de Valdivia founded Santiago in 1541 and was killed by the Mapuche, who held the land south of the Biobío for more than three centuries.

periods.name: Republic of Chile
periods.note: O'Higgins and San Martín won independence in 1818. Chile took the nitrate north in the War of the Pacific, conquered the Mapuche lands of Araucanía in 1883 and annexed Easter Island in 1888.

periods.name: Pinochet
periods.note: General Augusto Pinochet overthrew Salvador Allende on 11 September 1973 and ruled for 17 years, killing or "disappearing" more than 3,000 people.

periods.name: Democratic Chile
periods.note: Democracy returned after the plebiscite of 1988 voted Pinochet out.

periods.name: First peoples
periods.note: Hunters stencilled their hands on the walls of the Cueva de las Manos in Patagonia; Diaguita farmers lived in the northwest.

periods.name: Inca northwest
periods.note: The Incas conquered the northwest around 1480.

periods.name: Spanish Río de la Plata
periods.note: Pedro de Mendoza founded Buenos Aires in 1536; abandoned and founded again in 1580, it became the capital of the new Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776.
states: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata

periods.name: Independence and civil wars
periods.note: The May Revolution of 1810 was followed by the declaration of independence at Tucumán in 1816; Juan Manuel de Rosas ruled Buenos Aires as a dictator until 1852.
states: United Provinces of the Río de la Plata

periods.name: Argentine Republic
periods.note: The army conquered Patagonia from its native peoples in 1878–85. Millions of Italian and Spanish immigrants came, and beef and wheat made Argentina one of the richest countries in the world by 1914.

periods.name: Perón and the juntas
periods.note: Juan and Eva Perón built a movement of the workers; coups followed, and the junta of 1976–83 "disappeared" some 30,000 people and lost the Falklands War with Britain in 1982.

periods.name: Democratic Argentina
periods.note: Democracy returned in 1983; the economy crashed in 2001.

periods.name: Charrúa lands
periods.note: Charrúa hunters lived on the grasslands east of the Uruguay river.

periods.name: Banda Oriental
periods.note: Portugal founded Colonia in 1680 and Spain Montevideo in 1726; José Artigas led the fight for independence, and Brazil held the land from 1817 to 1828.
states: ~Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata
~United Provinces of the Río de la Plata

periods.name: Republic of Uruguay
periods.note: Independent in 1828 as a buffer between Argentina and Brazil; José Batlle y Ordóñez made it a welfare state, the "Switzerland of America", and it won the first football World Cup in 1930.

periods.name: Dictatorship and democracy
periods.note: A military dictatorship ruled from 1973 to 1985; José Mujica, a former guerrilla, was president in 2010–15.

periods.name: Guaraní lands
periods.note: Guaraní farmers lived here; their language is still spoken by most Paraguayans.

periods.name: Spanish Paraguay and the Jesuit missions
periods.note: Asunción was founded in 1537; Jesuits gathered the Guaraní into mission towns until they were expelled in 1767.
states: ~Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata

periods.name: Francia and the López
periods.note: Dr Francia sealed Paraguay off from the world. Francisco Solano López's war against Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay, in 1864–70, killed perhaps half the people.

periods.name: Republic of Paraguay
periods.note: Paraguay won the Chaco War against Bolivia in 1932–35.

periods.name: Stroessner and after
periods.note: Alfredo Stroessner ruled for 35 years, until 1989.

periods.name: First peoples
periods.note: Hunters painted the rocks of Serra da Capivara; shell-mound builders lived on the coast, and the Marajoara culture built mounds at the mouth of the Amazon.

periods.name: Tupi and the Amazon peoples
periods.note: Tupi-Guarani farmers spread along the coast; in the Amazon, large towns left fertile "black earth" soils behind them.

periods.name: Colonial Brazil
periods.note: Pedro Álvares Cabral landed in 1500. Sugar plantations worked by millions of African slaves made the northeast rich, the Dutch held it from 1630 to 1654, and gold was found in Minas Gerais in the 1690s.

periods.name: Kingdom and Empire of Brazil
periods.note: The Portuguese court fled Napoleon to Rio in 1808. Pedro I declared Brazil an independent empire in 1822, and Pedro II reigned until 1889, a year after slavery was abolished.

periods.name: Old Republic and Vargas
periods.note: The army proclaimed the republic in 1889; coffee planters ruled until Getúlio Vargas took power in 1930, and Brasília was built as the new capital in 1960.

periods.name: Military rule and democracy
periods.note: A military dictatorship ruled from 1964 to 1985; democratic Brazil has become one of the ten largest economies in the world.

periods.name: First peoples
periods.note: Arawak and Carib peoples lived along the rivers and the coast.

periods.name: Dutch Essequibo
periods.note: The Dutch founded Essequibo in 1616, and later Berbice and Demerara, with sugar plantations worked by slaves; Coffy led the Berbice slave revolt of 1763.

periods.name: British Guiana
periods.note: Britain took the colonies in 1796 and united them in 1831; after slavery ended in 1834, workers came from India, whose descendants are now the largest community.

periods.name: Co-operative Republic of Guyana
periods.note: Independent in 1966; oil found offshore in 2015 has made it one of the fastest-growing economies in the world.

periods.name: First peoples
periods.note: Arawak and Carib peoples lived along the rivers and the coast.

periods.name: Dutch Suriname
periods.note: The English founded the colony in 1651 and gave it to the Dutch for New Amsterdam in 1667; escaped slaves, the Maroons, built free communities in the forest.

periods.name: Republic of Suriname
periods.note: Independent in 1975; Dési Bouterse led a coup in 1980 and was later elected president.

periods.name: First peoples
periods.note: Arawak, Carib and Wayana peoples lived along the rivers and the coast.

periods.name: French colony
periods.note: France settled Cayenne in 1643. From 1852 the colony was a penal settlement, with the prison of Devil's Island, where Alfred Dreyfus was held.

periods.name: Overseas department
periods.note: A department of France since 1946; Europe's rockets are launched from Kourou.

periods.name: Lucayans
periods.note: Taíno settlers from Cuba and Hispaniola reached the islands around AD 800 and became the Lucayans. Columbus made his first landfall in the Americas here, on Guanahani, in October 1492; within thirty years the Spanish had carried nearly all of them off as slaves.

periods.name: British colony
periods.note: Puritans from Bermuda, the Eleutheran Adventurers, settled in 1648. Nassau was a pirate haven, home to Blackbeard, until Woodes Rogers arrived as governor in 1718; Loyalists brought enslaved Africans after the American Revolution, and slavery ended in 1834.
states: ~United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

periods.name: Commonwealth of the Bahamas
periods.note: Majority rule came in 1967 under Lynden Pindling, who led the islands to independence in 1973. Tourism and offshore banking became the mainstays, and Hurricane Dorian devastated Abaco and Grand Bahama in 2019.

periods.name: First peoples
periods.note: Banwari Trace, a shell midden about 7,000 years old, is the oldest known human site in the Caribbean. Arawak-speaking farmers came later from the Orinoco, and Caribs lived on Tobago; Columbus sighted Trinidad in 1498 and named it for the Holy Trinity.

periods.name: Spanish Trinidad
periods.note: Spain founded San José de Oruña in 1592 but left the island nearly empty until 1783, when it invited Catholic planters, mostly French, and their enslaved Africans. Tobago changed hands between the Dutch, Courlanders, French and British more than thirty times.

periods.name: British colony
periods.note: Britain took Trinidad in 1797 and joined Tobago to it in 1889. After slavery ended, about 144,000 indentured workers came from India for the sugar estates, oil was drilled from 1908, and Carnival gave birth to calypso and the steelpan.
states: ~United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

periods.name: Independent Trinidad and Tobago
periods.note: Eric Williams led the country to independence in 1962, and it became a republic in 1976. Oil and gas made it one of the richest nations in the Caribbean; in 1990 Islamist rebels held the prime minister and parliament hostage for six days.

periods.name: First peoples
periods.note: People first reached Barbados around 1600 BC; Arawak-speaking farmers from South America followed, and later the Kalinago (Island Caribs). Spanish slave raids had emptied the island by the time the Portuguese named it Os Barbados, "the bearded ones", after its fig trees.

periods.name: English sugar colony
periods.note: English settlers landed in 1627, and from the 1640s enslaved Africans worked the first great sugar plantations of the English Caribbean, under a slave code of 1661 that other colonies copied. Bussa led a great revolt in 1816, and slavery ended in 1834.
states: ~United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

periods.name: Independent Barbados
periods.note: Errol Barrow led Barbados to independence in 1966. A stable parliamentary democracy living from tourism and finance, it became a republic in 2021, with Sandra Mason as its first president.

periods.name: Botai and the Bronze Age steppe
periods.note: Around 3500 BC the Botai people of the northern steppe kept herds of horses, among the first people known to have done so. In the Bronze Age the herders and copper miners of the Andronovo culture, probably early speakers of Indo-Iranian languages, spread across the whole steppe.

periods.name: Saka
periods.note: Saka (Scythian) horse nomads ruled the steppe and buried their chiefs in great mounds; the "Golden Man" of the Issyk kurgan near Almaty wore a suit of 4,000 gold plates. Herodotus tells how Tomyris, queen of the Massagetae, beat and killed Cyrus the Great of Persia in 530 BC.

periods.name: Wusun, Kangju and the Huns
periods.note: The Wusun ruled the Ili valley and the Kangju the Syr Darya, and both traded and fought with Han China. Yueban, a remnant of the northern Xiongnu, held the steppe north of the Wusun into the 400s, and the Huns crossed the land on their way west.

periods.name: Turkic khaganates
periods.note: Bumin Qaghan founded the Turkic Khaganate in 552, and the Western Turks ruled the steppe from Suyab and Talas. In 751 the Abbasids and their Karluk allies beat a Tang Chinese army on the Talas river; legend has it that Chinese prisoners taught the Arabs to make paper.

periods.name: Oghuz, Kimeks and Karluks
periods.note: The Oghuz ruled the lower Syr Darya from Yangikent, the Kimeks the Irtysh and the Karluks the southeast, while the Pechenegs roamed the west. Islam spread from the oasis towns; the philosopher al-Farabi, the "Second Teacher" after Aristotle, probably came from Farab (Otrar). The Seljuks, who conquered Persia, were Oghuz from here.

periods.name: Kipchak steppe
periods.note: Kipchak (Cuman) tribes took the steppe, which Persian writers called the Desht-i Kipchak, the Kipchak plain, from the Irtysh to the Danube. The Karakhanids and then the Kara Khitai held the southern towns, and in 1218 the Khwarazmshah's governor of Otrar killed a caravan of Genghis Khan's merchants.

periods.name: Mongol rule and the White Horde
periods.note: Genghis Khan razed Otrar in 1219–20, and the steppe passed to his son Jochi's heirs, the Golden Horde in the west and the White Horde in the east. Timur built the great shrine of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi at Turkistan, and died at Otrar in 1405.

periods.name: Kazakh Khanate
periods.note: Kerei and Janibek founded the Kazakh Khanate in 1465; under Kasym Khan it counted a million people. The Dzungar invasion of 1723 began the "years of great disaster" and drove the Junior Juz, one of the three Kazakh hordes, to seek Russian protection in 1731; Ablai Khan reunited the hordes until 1781.

periods.name: The last khans
periods.note: Russia advanced with lines of forts from the north and abolished the khans of the Middle Juz in 1822 and of the Junior Juz in 1824. Ablai's grandson Kenesary Kasymov, the last khan, fought Russia for ten years until he was killed in 1847.

periods.name: Russian rule
periods.note: Russia took the Senior Juz in the south, founded the fort of Verny (Almaty) in 1854 and gave the herders' pastures to Russian and Ukrainian settlers. When the tsar ordered Central Asians to dig trenches behind the front in 1916, the Kazakhs and Kyrgyz rose, and Amangeldy Imanov besieged Turgai.

periods.name: Alash and Soviet Kazakhstan
periods.note: The Alash Orda briefly ruled an autonomous Kazakhstan. Collectivisation caused a famine in 1930–33 that killed about 1.5 million people, some 40 percent of the Kazakhs; Stalin deported whole peoples here, and the Soviets launched Gagarin from Baikonur in 1961 and set off 456 nuclear tests near Semipalatinsk.

periods.name: Republic of Kazakhstan
periods.note: Kazakhstan was the last republic to leave the Soviet Union, in December 1991. Nursultan Nazarbayev ruled until 2019, gave up the nuclear weapons left on its soil and moved the capital north to Astana in 1997; protests in January 2022 ended in a deadly crackdown.

periods.name: Oxus civilization
periods.note: Neanderthals buried a child in the cave of Teshik-Tash some 70,000 years ago. In the Bronze Age the walled towns of the Oxus civilization, such as Sapalli Tepe, farmed the southern oases, while Andronovo herders roamed the north.

periods.name: Sogdiana and Khwarazm
periods.note: Iranian peoples, the Sogdians around Samarkand (Afrasiab) and the Chorasmians on the lower Amu Darya, built oasis cities from the 700s BC; Zoroastrianism may have begun in this land or in neighbouring Bactria. Cyrus the Great made them Persian satrapies around 540 BC.

periods.name: Alexander and the Greco-Bactrians
periods.note: Alexander the Great took Marakanda (Samarkand) in 329 BC, fought the Sogdian rebel Spitamenes for two years and married Roxana, the daughter of a local lord. Greek kings of Bactria ruled the south after him.

periods.name: Kangju and the Kushans
periods.note: The Silk Road opened as Han China sent envoys west; in 104–101 BC Han armies marched to Fergana for its "heavenly horses". The Kangju ruled Sogdiana, and the Kushans the south, where Buddhist monasteries rose at Termez.

periods.name: Sogdian cities and the Turks
periods.note: Sogdian merchants ran the Silk Road trade as far as China, and the kings of Samarkand covered their palace at Afrasiab with paintings of foreign envoys. The Hephthalites and then the Western Turks were their overlords, and the Afrighid kings ruled Khwarazm.

periods.name: Arab conquest
periods.note: Qutayba ibn Muslim took Bukhara in 709 and Samarkand and Khwarazm in 712, and Islam slowly took the place of the old faiths. Al-Khwarizmi, from Khwarazm, wrote the book that gave algebra its name, and "algorithm" comes from his own.

periods.name: Samanid Empire
periods.note: The Persian Samanids ruled from Bukhara, whose brick mausoleum of Ismail Samani still stands; their court revived Persian as a language of poetry, with Rudaki. Ibn Sina (Avicenna) was born near Bukhara in 980, and al-Biruni in Khwarazm in 973.

periods.name: Karakhanids and Khwarazmshahs
periods.note: The Turkic Karakhanids took Bukhara in 999 and built its Kalyan minaret in 1127; the Kara Khitai beat the Seljuk sultan near Samarkand in 1141. The Khwarazmshahs of Gurganj made the region the centre of an empire from the Aral Sea to the Persian Gulf, until Genghis Khan destroyed it.

periods.name: Mongols and the Chagatai Khanate
periods.note: Genghis Khan took Bukhara and Samarkand in 1220 and told the people of Bukhara that he was the punishment of God. The land became part of the khanate of his son Chagatai.

periods.name: Timurid Empire
periods.note: Timur (Tamerlane), whose armies reached from Delhi to Ankara, made Samarkand his capital and filled it with blue-tiled buildings such as the Bibi-Khanym mosque and his tomb, the Gur-e-Amir. His grandson Ulugh Beg built an observatory there, and Babur, born in Andijan, went on to found the Mughal Empire in India.

periods.name: Khanates of Bukhara and Khiva
periods.note: Muhammad Shaybani's Uzbeks took Samarkand and Bukhara in 1500 and gave the country its name; their khans ruled from Bukhara, and another line from Khiva from 1511. The Sher-Dor and Tilya-Kori madrasas completed Samarkand's Registan, while the Kazakhs held Tashkent and a khanate of Kokand broke away in Fergana in 1709.

periods.name: Emirate of Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand
periods.note: The Manghit emirs ruled Bukhara from 1785, and Kokand took Tashkent in 1809; the slave markets of Bukhara and Khiva sold captured Persians and Russians. Britain and Russia played their "Great Game" here, and the emir of Bukhara beheaded two British officers, Stoddart and Conolly, in 1842.

periods.name: Russian Turkestan
periods.note: General Chernyayev stormed Tashkent in 1865, and it became the capital of Russian Turkestan; Bukhara (1868) and Khiva (1873) became Russian protectorates and Kokand was annexed in 1876. Railways reached Samarkand in 1888, and the land was turned over to cotton.

periods.name: Soviet Uzbekistan
periods.note: The Bolsheviks crushed the Kokand Autonomy in 1918 and ended the emir of Bukhara and the khan of Khiva in 1920; the Basmachi fought them for years. The Uzbek SSR was formed in 1924; irrigation for cotton drained the Aral Sea, and an earthquake levelled much of Tashkent in 1966.

periods.name: Republic of Uzbekistan
periods.note: Uzbekistan became independent in 1991. Islam Karimov ruled it harshly until his death in 2016, and his troops killed hundreds of protesters at Andijan in 2005; Shavkat Mirziyoyev opened the country and ended the forced labour of the cotton harvest.

periods.name: Jeitun, Namazga and Margiana
periods.note: Jeitun, near Ashgabat, was the first farming village in Central Asia, around 6000 BC. Towns such as Namazga and Altyn-Depe grew along the Kopet Dag, and Gonur Depe in the Murghab delta was a great centre of the Oxus civilization around 2000 BC.

periods.name: Margiana and Parthava
periods.note: Iranian peoples farmed the oasis of Margiana (Merv) and Parthava below the Kopet Dag; both became Persian satrapies, and Darius I crushed a revolt in Margiana in 521 BC.

periods.name: Alexander and the Seleucids
periods.note: Alexander's men founded an Alexandria at Merv, and the Seleucids rebuilt it as Antiochia in Margiana.

periods.name: Parthian Empire
periods.note: The Parni nomads under Arsaces founded the Parthian dynasty around 247 BC; their royal fortress of Nisa, near Ashgabat, held palaces, shrines and carved ivory drinking horns. Roman soldiers captured at Carrhae in 53 BC were sent to guard Merv.

periods.name: Sasanian Merv
periods.note: Merv was the Sasanians' great frontier city, with Zoroastrian fire temples, Buddhist stupas and a Christian bishop; the last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, was murdered near Merv in 651.

periods.name: Arab caliphates
periods.note: Merv became the Arab capital of Khorasan; Abu Muslim raised the black banners of the Abbasid revolution there in 747, and the caliph al-Ma'mun ruled the empire from Merv until 818.

periods.name: Samanids, Ghaznavids and the Oghuz
periods.note: The Tahirids, the Samanids and the Ghaznavids ruled the oases in turn, while Oghuz Turks moved in from the north; the Muslims among them came to be called Turkmen.

periods.name: Seljuk Empire
periods.note: Oghuz Turkmen of the Seljuk clan took Merv in 1037 and beat the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan in 1040, then conquered Persia. Merv, capital of Sultan Sanjar, may have been the largest city in the world around 1150; his mausoleum still stands.

periods.name: Khwarazmshahs and Mongols
periods.note: The Khwarazmshahs ruled from Gurganj (Konye-Urgench). In 1221 Genghis Khan's son Tolui destroyed Merv, and chroniclers claimed he killed hundreds of thousands of people; the Ilkhans and the Golden Horde then held the land.

periods.name: Timurids
periods.note: Timur and his heirs ruled the oases, and his son Shah Rukh rebuilt Merv.

periods.name: Turkmen tribes
periods.note: Turkmen tribes, the Teke, Yomut, Ersari and others, lived as herders and raiders between Safavid Persia, Khiva and Bukhara, selling captives in the slave markets; Magtymguly (1724–1807), the national poet, called them to unite. The Teke routed a Persian army at Merv in 1861.

periods.name: Russian Transcaspia
periods.note: General Skobelev stormed the Teke fortress of Geok Tepe in January 1881 and thousands of Turkmen were killed; Russia founded Ashgabat that year, took Merv in 1884 and ran a railway across the desert, while Khiva and Bukhara kept the north and east as Russian protectorates.

periods.name: Soviet Turkmenistan
periods.note: The Turkmen SSR was formed in 1924. An earthquake destroyed Ashgabat in 1948, killing tens of thousands of people; the Karakum Canal, dug from 1954, carried the Amu Darya's water into the desert, and a gas crater at Darvaza has been burning since about 1971.

periods.name: Independent Turkmenistan
periods.note: Saparmurat Niyazov, "Turkmenbashi", ruled with a cult of his own person, renaming the months after himself and his mother and raising a golden statue that turned to face the sun; the UN recognised the country's permanent neutrality in 1995. Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov followed him in 2006, and his son Serdar in 2022.

periods.name: Bronze Age herders
periods.note: Herders carved thousands of pictures of animals and hunters into the rocks of Saimaluu-Tash, high in the Tian Shan, from the Bronze Age on.

periods.name: Saka and Wusun
periods.note: Saka nomads, then the Wusun, whose capital Chigu stood by Lake Issyk-Kul, grazed the mountain pastures. The Wusun were allies of Han China; the Han princess Liu Xijun, married to their old king around 105 BC, wrote a famous lament about her exile.

periods.name: Turkic khaganates
periods.note: Suyab, in the Chuy valley, was the capital of the Western Turkic khagans and later of the Türgesh, and a Tang Chinese garrison town for forty years; the poet Li Bai was probably born there in 701.

periods.name: Karluks and Karakhanids
periods.note: The Karluks took Suyab in 766. Then the Karakhanids, one of the first Turkic dynasties to become Muslim, ruled from Balasagun (with its Burana tower), Kashgar and Uzgen; Yusuf of Balasagun wrote the "Kutadgu Bilig" for them in 1069, the first great work of Turkic literature.

periods.name: Kara Khitai
periods.note: Yelü Dashi, a prince of the fallen Khitan Liao dynasty of China, took Balasagun in the 1130s and founded the Kara Khitai, who ruled Central Asia in the Chinese manner. The Naiman prince Kuchlug seized their throne in 1211, and the Mongols killed him in 1218.

periods.name: Mongols and Moghulistan
periods.note: Balasagun surrendered to the Mongols in 1218, and the land passed to Chagatai's khanate and from 1347 to Moghulistan, its eastern half. The Kyrgyz, whose ancestors lived on the Yenisei in Siberia, became the main people of the Tian Shan by the 1500s and told their past in the epic of Manas.

periods.name: Dzungars and Kokand
periods.note: The Buddhist Oirat Dzungars raided and ruled the Kyrgyz until the Qing destroyed them in the 1750s; then the khans of Kokand took the valleys and built the fort of Pishpek (Bishkek) in 1825. Kurmanjan Datka, "the queen of the Alay", led the southern Kyrgyz.

periods.name: Russian rule
periods.note: Russia took the northern Kyrgyz lands in the 1860s and the south when it annexed Kokand in 1876, and settlers took the best pastures. In the revolt of 1916 tens of thousands of Kyrgyz were killed or died fleeing over the mountains to China, the Urkun.

periods.name: Soviet Kyrgyzstan
periods.note: The Soviets made the Kara-Kirghiz autonomous region in 1924 and the Kirghiz SSR in 1936, and renamed Pishpek Frunze. Chinghiz Aitmatov's novels made Kyrgyz life known around the world.

periods.name: Kyrgyz Republic
periods.note: Kyrgyzstan became independent in 1991. Street revolutions overthrew its presidents in 2005 (the Tulip Revolution), 2010 and 2020, and hundreds of people, most of them Uzbeks, were killed in clashes around Osh in 2010.

periods.name: Sarazm and the Oxus civilization
periods.note: Sarazm, near Panjakent, was one of the first towns in Central Asia, from about 3500 BC, trading turquoise and copper; the farmers of the Oxus civilization worked the southern valleys.

periods.name: Bactria and Sogdiana
periods.note: The Bactrians and Sogdians, Iranian peoples and ancestors of the Tajiks, lived here, and both became Persian satrapies. The gold and silver Oxus Treasure, now in the British Museum, was found by the Amu Darya in 1877.

periods.name: Alexander and Greco-Bactria
periods.note: Alexander the Great founded Alexandria Eschate, "the Furthest", at Khujand in 329 BC, and Greek kings of Bactria built the Temple of the Oxus at Takht-i Sangin.

periods.name: Kushan Empire
periods.note: The Yuezhi conquered Bactria and founded the Kushan Empire, which spread Buddhism along the Silk Road.

periods.name: Hephthalites, Sogdians and Turks
periods.note: The Hephthalites and then the Western Turks ruled the land; Sogdian Panjakent was rich in painted houses, and the monastery of Ajina Tepa held a Buddha 13 metres long.

periods.name: Arab conquest
periods.note: Devashtich, the last Sogdian ruler of Panjakent, held out against the Arabs on Mount Mugh, where his letters were found in 1933, until he was taken and killed in 722.

periods.name: Samanid Empire
periods.note: Tajiks honour the Persian Samanids of Bukhara as their first state: the currency, the somoni, and the country's highest peak are named after Ismail Samani, and Rudaki, the father of Persian poetry, was born at Panjrud.

periods.name: Karakhanids to Khwarazmshahs
periods.note: Turkic dynasties ruled, but Persian culture flourished; the poet Nasir Khusraw spread Ismaili Islam in the Pamirs, where Ismailis still honour him.

periods.name: Mongols and Timurids
periods.note: Timur Malik held Khujand against Genghis Khan in 1220; Chagatai's khans and then Timur and his heirs ruled the land.

periods.name: Bukhara and Kokand
periods.note: The Uzbek khans and emirs of Bukhara ruled the south, Kokand the north from the 1700s, and small mountain principalities such as Darvaz, Karategin and Badakhshan kept their own rulers.

periods.name: Russian Turkestan and the Emirate of Bukhara
periods.note: Russia took Khujand in 1866 and made the emir of Bukhara, who held the rest, its vassal in 1868; Russia and Britain divided the Pamirs in 1895. Dushanbe was a village named for its Monday market.

periods.name: Soviet Tajikistan
periods.note: The Red Army drove out the emir in 1920–21, and the Basmachi fought it in the mountains. Tajikistan became a Soviet republic in 1929, but Samarkand and Bukhara, centres of Tajik culture, were left in Uzbekistan; the Nurek dam was the tallest in the world.

periods.name: Republic of Tajikistan
periods.note: Independence in 1991 was followed by a civil war (1992–97) that killed tens of thousands of people; Emomali Rahmon has ruled since 1992.

periods.name: First Australians
periods.note: People reached Australia more than 50,000 years ago, and their descendants make up the oldest living cultures on Earth, with more than 250 languages and the stories of the Dreaming. The Gunditjmara built stone eel traps at Budj Bim 6,600 years ago, and rising seas cut Tasmania off about 12,000 years ago.

periods.name: Convict colonies
periods.note: Arthur Phillip's First Fleet landed some 1,400 people, most of them convicts, at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788; Britain sent 162,000 convicts in all. Smallpox and frontier wars killed many thousands of Aboriginal people as settlers spread inland, and new colonies were founded in Tasmania, Western Australia and South Australia.

periods.name: Gold rushes and self-governing colonies
periods.note: Gold was found in 1851, and Victoria's gold rush made Melbourne one of the richest cities in the world; miners rebelled at the Eureka Stockade in 1854. The six colonies governed themselves, and South Australia gave women the vote in 1894.

periods.name: Federation and the world wars
periods.note: The colonies united as the Commonwealth of Australia on 1 January 1901, with a "White Australia" policy against Asian migrants. The landing of the ANZACs at Gallipoli in 1915 became a founding legend; Canberra became the capital in 1927, and Japanese planes bombed Darwin in 1942.

periods.name: Modern Australia
periods.note: Millions of migrants came from Europe and later Asia, and the White Australia policy was ended by 1973. A referendum in 1967 counted Aboriginal people in the census, the High Court's Mabo decision recognised native title in 1992, and the government apologised to the Stolen Generations in 2008.

periods.name: Polynesian settlers
periods.note: Voyagers from eastern Polynesia, steering by the stars, reached Aotearoa around 1250–1300, the last large land on Earth to be settled. They hunted the giant flightless moa to extinction within about two centuries.

periods.name: Classic Māori
periods.note: Māori lived in tribes (iwi), built hilltop forts (pā), carved meeting houses and worked greenstone; in 1642 they drove off Abel Tasman's Dutch ships at Golden Bay.

periods.name: Cook, traders and the Musket Wars
periods.note: James Cook charted the islands in 1769–70, and whalers, traders and missionaries followed. Tribes armed with muskets fought the Musket Wars (1807–42), which killed tens of thousands, and northern chiefs declared their independence in 1835.

periods.name: British colony
periods.note: More than 500 chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi with Britain in 1840, but wars over land (1845–72) and confiscations followed. Gold was found in Otago in 1861, and in 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country where women could vote.

periods.name: Dominion of New Zealand
periods.note: New Zealand became a dominion in 1907, and its ANZAC soldiers fought at Gallipoli in 1915; the first Labour government built a welfare state in the 1930s.

periods.name: Independent New Zealand
periods.note: Full independence came in 1947; Edmund Hillary climbed Everest in 1953. New Zealand banned nuclear ships in the 1980s, and since 1975 the Waitangi Tribunal has heard Māori claims under the treaty.

periods.name: First farmers
periods.note: People reached New Guinea more than 50,000 years ago, when it was joined to Australia. At Kuk Swamp in the highlands they drained the land to grow bananas and taro thousands of years ago, one of the few places on Earth where farming was invented on its own.

periods.name: Papuans and Lapita voyagers
periods.note: The Lapita people, ancestors of the Polynesians, made their stamped pottery in the Bismarck islands from about 1500 BC. Hundreds of peoples speaking more than 800 languages lived in villages of farmers and traders, such as the Trobriand islanders of the Kula ring, and the sweet potato let the highland valleys fill with people.

periods.name: German and British New Guinea
periods.note: In 1884 Germany took the northeast and the Bismarck islands, and Britain the southeast; the Dutch had claimed the western half of the island in 1828. Australia took over British New Guinea, as Papua, in 1906.

periods.name: Australian rule
periods.note: Australia seized German New Guinea in 1914. Gold prospectors entering the highlands in the 1930s found about a million people unknown to the outside world; Japan invaded in 1942, and Australians fought it back along the Kokoda Track.

periods.name: Independent Papua New Guinea
periods.note: Papua New Guinea became independent in 1975 under Michael Somare. A war over the Panguna copper mine on Bougainville (1988–98) ended in autonomy, and the island voted for independence in 2019.

periods.name: Polynesian settlers
periods.note: Voyagers in double-hulled canoes, steering by the stars, reached Hawaii from the Marquesas and Tahiti around 1000–1200, bringing taro, sweet potatoes, pigs and dogs. They built fishponds and stone temples (heiau).

periods.name: Ruling chiefs
periods.note: Each island was ruled by chiefs (aliʻi) under the strict laws of kapu; ʻUmi-a-Līloa united the island of Hawaiʻi around 1500. James Cook reached the islands in 1778 and was killed at Kealakekua Bay the next year.

periods.name: Kamehameha unites the islands
periods.note: Kamehameha, a chief of the island of Hawaiʻi, won his first battle in 1782, took Maui and Oʻahu, where his enemies were driven over the Nuʻuanu cliffs in 1795, and became king of all the islands when Kauaʻi submitted in 1810.

periods.name: Kingdom of Hawaii
periods.note: Kamehameha's heirs abolished the kapu in 1819, welcomed American missionaries and gave the kingdom a constitution in 1840; sugar planters brought workers from China, Japan and Portugal. Diseases brought by foreigners killed most Native Hawaiians.

periods.name: Overthrow and annexation
periods.note: American planters, backed by US Marines, overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani in 1893, and the United States annexed their Republic of Hawaii in 1898.

periods.name: Territory of Hawaii
periods.note: Hawaii was an American territory; Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941 brought the United States into the Second World War.

periods.name: State of Hawaii
periods.note: Hawaii became the 50th state in 1959, and tourism took the place of sugar; the Hawaiian language, nearly lost, was brought back in schools from the 1980s. Barack Obama, born in Honolulu in 1961, was the first president from Hawaii.

periods.name: Lapita settlers and chiefdoms
periods.note: Lapita voyagers settled Fiji around 1000 BC, and later migrants from Melanesia mixed with them. Fijians lived in warring chiefdoms, built great canoes and traded with and fought the Tongans to the east.

periods.name: Cakobau and the Tongan wars
periods.note: Traders came for sandalwood and sea cucumbers; Cakobau, chief of the little island of Bau, rose to power, while the Tongan prince Enele Maʻafu took the Lau islands. Cakobau was proclaimed king of Fiji in 1871.

periods.name: British colony
periods.note: Cakobau handed Fiji to Britain in 1874, and a measles epidemic killed a third of the Fijians the next year; from 1879 Britain brought 60,000 Indian labourers to work the sugar fields, and their descendants became almost half the people.

periods.name: Independent Fiji
periods.note: Fiji became independent in 1970. Two coups in 1987 and another in 2000 were made in the name of indigenous Fijians against governments backed by Indo-Fijians, and the army seized power again in 2006.

periods.name: Lapita settlers
periods.note: Lapita voyagers settled Tonga around 900 BC; from here and Samoa their descendants, the Polynesians, went on to settle the Pacific.

periods.name: Tuʻi Tonga Empire
periods.note: The sacred kings (Tuʻi Tonga), said to descend from the god Tangaloa, ruled from Muʻa, where their stone tombs still stand, and raised the trilithon of Haʻamonga ʻa Maui. Their seafaring power reached Samoa, Fiji and ʻUvea; James Cook called Tonga the Friendly Islands in 1773.

periods.name: Civil wars
periods.note: The chiefs fought a long civil war, while Methodist missionaries won converts.

periods.name: Kingdom of Tonga
periods.note: Tāufaʻāhau, baptised George, united the islands as King George Tupou I in 1845 and gave them a constitution in 1875 that is still in force. Tonga was a British protected state from 1900 but was never a colony; Queen Sālote rode through the rain in an open carriage at Elizabeth II's coronation in 1953.

periods.name: Independent Tonga
periods.note: Tonga regained full independence in 1970 and became a more democratic monarchy in 2010; the huge undersea eruption of Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai in 2022 was heard around the world.

periods.name: Lapita settlers and Tongan rule
periods.note: Lapita voyagers settled Samoa around 800 BC. Tongan kings ruled the islands for centuries until, Samoans say, the brothers Tuna and Fata drove them out and founded the Malietoa title.

periods.name: Paramount chiefs
periods.note: High chiefs held the great titles of the islands; around 1500 Queen Salamasina held all four of them at once.

periods.name: Missionaries and the rival powers
periods.note: John Williams brought Christianity in 1830. Germany, Britain and the United States backed rival chiefs, and German and American warships were wrecked in a cyclone at Apia in 1889; the writer Robert Louis Stevenson lived and died there.

periods.name: German and New Zealand Samoa
periods.note: In 1899 the powers split the islands: Germany took the west and the United States the east (American Samoa). New Zealand seized German Samoa in 1914; the 1918 flu killed a fifth of the people, and New Zealand police shot the peaceful Mau independence movement's leader in 1929.

periods.name: Independent Samoa
periods.note: Samoa became the first Pacific island country to win independence, in 1962.
